lessons.title: What Is a Stock?
lessons.celebration: You understand what a share actually is!

screens.title: A Piece of the Company
screens.text: A stock is a small slice of ownership in a company. Owning a share makes you a partial owner, not an employee or a lender.

screens.question: A share of stock represents partial ownership in a company.
screens.explanation: Buying stock literally means buying a small ownership stake.

screens.question: Owning stock means owning a small [___] of a company.
screens.explanation: "Share" describes that fractional ownership stake.

screens.question: What does buying one share of a company generally represent?
options: A one-day job working for the company.
A small, fractional ownership stake in that company.
A loan you've given the company that must be repaid.
screens.explanation: Shareholders own a slice of the company, not a debt owed to them or a job.

screens.question: Match the term to its meaning.
pairs: A small unit of ownership in a company
Someone who owns at least one share
The business whose ownership is divided into shares
screens.explanation: These three terms describe the basic relationship between a business and its owners.

screens.template: A stock's [__1__] reflects what someone is willing to pay right now, not a fixed [__2__] set by the company.
screens.explanation: Price is a live, constantly negotiated number, not something the company dictates.

screens.question: A simplified path for how a share ends up in your hands:
items: A company decides to sell ownership stakes to raise money
Shares are created and offered to investors
Investors buy shares through an exchange
Those shares can later be resold to other investors
correct_order: A company decides to sell ownership stakes to raise money
Shares are created and offered to investors
Investors buy shares through an exchange
Those shares can later be resold to other investors
screens.explanation: After the initial offering, most shares trade between investors rather than involving the company directly.

screens.question: Which best describes owning a single share of a company?

options.label: A coupon for company products
options.wrong_explanation: Owning stock doesn't entitle you to discounts or products.

options.label: A small, fractional ownership stake in that company
options.detail: You own a tiny piece of the business

options.label: A loan you gave the company
options.wrong_explanation: Stock ownership isn't a loan; that's closer to a bond.

screens.explanation: Stock ownership is equity — a piece of the business itself.

screens.scenario: Someone believes owning one share means they help run the company's daily operations.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Owning shares generally doesn't give an individual shareholder control over daily operations.
They should contact the company to request a job.
They should buy even more shares to get more control.
screens.explanation: Day-to-day operations are run by management, not by individual shareholders.

screens.question: Which of these is an example of equity ownership, like a stock?
options: A share representing partial ownership in a company.
screens.explanation: Equity ownership means owning a stake in the business, unlike a deposit or membership.

screens.question: All shareholders of a company automatically get an equal say in daily decisions.
screens.explanation: Ownership doesn't equal management control; influence often scales with how many shares are owned and formal voting processes.

screens.question: A person or entity that owns at least one share is called a [___].
screens.explanation: "Shareholder" is the standard term for anyone owning stock in a company.

lessons.title: What Is a Chart?
lessons.celebration: You can read what a chart actually shows!

screens.title: A Picture of Price Over Time
screens.text: A chart is simply a visual plot of price against time — nothing more mysterious than that.

screens.question: A chart is a visual plot of price over time.
screens.explanation: That's the entire function of a price chart, at its core.

screens.question: Charts plot price against [___].
screens.explanation: The two axes of a standard price chart are price and time.

screens.question: What does a stock chart primarily show?
options: A guarantee of the company's future earnings.
The exact identities of everyone currently trading it.
Historical price movement over a chosen time period.
screens.explanation: A chart is a record of what price has already done, not a prediction or a directory of traders.

screens.question: Match the chart element to what it represents.
pairs: The recorded price at that moment
screens.explanation: These are the basic building blocks of any price chart.

screens.template: Charts describe what has [__1__] happened, not what will [__2__] happen next.
screens.explanation: A chart is a historical record, not a guarantee about the future.

screens.question: A simple way to approach an unfamiliar chart for the first time:
items: Check the price range on the vertical axis
Check the time range on the horizontal axis
Note the overall shape of the price movement
Look for any labeled events or notable points
correct_order: Check the price range on the vertical axis
Check the time range on the horizontal axis
Note the overall shape of the price movement
Look for any labeled events or notable points
screens.explanation: Orienting yourself to scale and timeframe first makes the shape of the chart easier to interpret.

screens.question: What is the main purpose of a price chart?

options.label: Guaranteeing what the future price will be
options.wrong_explanation: Charts show history, not guaranteed futures.

options.label: Visualizing how price has moved over a period of time
options.detail: A historical picture, not a forecast

options.label: Replacing the need to understand the underlying company
options.wrong_explanation: A chart is one tool among several, not a full substitute.

screens.explanation: A chart's core job is visualization of price history.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a chart alone tells them everything they need to know about a company's health.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should ignore the chart entirely from now on.
They should look at an even shorter timeframe instead.
A chart shows price history, not the full picture of the underlying business.
screens.explanation: Charts are one useful tool, but they don't capture everything about a company.

screens.question: If you wanted to see the very first data point on a chart, where would you look?
options: The leftmost edge of the chart.
The rightmost edge of the chart.
The top of the chart only.
screens.explanation: Charts are typically read left-to-right as time progressing forward.

screens.question: A chart can only display one single timeframe and can never be adjusted.
screens.explanation: Most charting tools let you switch between many different timeframes for the same asset.

screens.question: The vertical axis of a standard price chart represents [___].
screens.explanation: The Y-axis (vertical) shows price; the X-axis (horizontal) shows time.

lessons.title: Why Prices Move
lessons.celebration: You understand the tug-of-war behind every price!

screens.title: Buyers vs. Sellers
screens.text: Price moves because of an ongoing back-and-forth between buyers and sellers — not because of a single decision-maker.

screens.question: Price moves because of an ongoing negotiation between buyers and sellers.
screens.explanation: Every trade is an agreement between someone willing to buy and someone willing to sell.

screens.question: When more people want to buy than sell at a given price, price tends to move [___].
screens.explanation: More buying pressure than selling pressure tends to push price higher.

screens.question: What generally happens when sellers outnumber buyers at a price?
screens.explanation: More selling pressure than buying pressure tends to push price lower.

screens.question: Match the balance of buyers/sellers to the common price effect.
screens.explanation: Price is commonly described as a reflection of this shifting balance.

screens.template: Price is often described as a live [__1__] between buyers and sellers, not a value set by [__2__].
screens.explanation: No single party sets the price; it emerges from many participants trading.

screens.question: A simplified view of how a new price forms:
items: Buyers submit the prices they're willing to pay
Sellers submit the prices they're willing to accept
A trade occurs when a buyer and seller agree on a price
That agreed price becomes the new "last traded price"
correct_order: Buyers submit the prices they're willing to pay
Sellers submit the prices they're willing to accept
A trade occurs when a buyer and seller agree on a price
That agreed price becomes the new "last traded price"
screens.explanation: Each new trade is the result of buyers and sellers finding common ground.

screens.question: Which best explains a sudden, sharp price move?

options.label: The chart being recalibrated
options.wrong_explanation: Charts display real trades, not arbitrary recalibrations.

options.label: A shift in the balance between buyers and sellers
options.detail: More pressure on one side than the other

options.label: The company changing its logo
options.wrong_explanation: Branding changes don't directly move price like this.

screens.explanation: Price moves reflect shifts in buying and selling pressure.

screens.scenario: Someone believes a single company employee personally sets the stock's price each day.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Price emerges from many buyers and sellers trading, not one person's decision.
They should assume the price is fixed once set.
They should ask a different employee instead.
screens.explanation: No individual sets the price directly — it comes from collective trading activity.

screens.question: What would you expect if buying and selling pressure were perfectly balanced?
options: Price would tend to stay relatively steady.
screens.explanation: Balanced pressure between buyers and sellers tends to produce calmer, steadier price behavior.

screens.question: A single large seller entering the market can shift the balance toward more selling pressure.
screens.explanation: Any participant's buying or selling activity contributes to the overall balance driving price.

screens.question: Price is often described as emerging from the ongoing [___] between buyers and sellers.
screens.explanation: No single authority sets price — it comes from continuous trading activity.

lessons.title: What Is Volume?
lessons.celebration: You understand what volume tells you!

screens.title: How Much Traded, Not Where
screens.text: Volume measures how many shares changed hands during a period — a separate idea from price itself.

screens.question: Volume measures how many shares changed hands during a period.
screens.explanation: That's the definition of volume — a count of shares traded, not a price level.

screens.question: Higher volume generally means more shares were [___].
screens.explanation: Volume counts the number of shares that actually changed hands.

screens.question: What does very low volume commonly suggest about a price move?
options: The move is guaranteed to reverse immediately.
The chart's data must be incorrect.
Fewer participants were involved in that particular move.
screens.explanation: Low volume simply describes fewer shares trading, not a guaranteed outcome.

screens.question: Match the volume description to its meaning.
pairs: Many shares traded in that period
Few shares traded in that period
A sudden jump in trading activity
screens.explanation: Volume is a separate dimension from price, describing activity level.

screens.template: Volume describes [__1__] of trading activity, while price describes [__2__].
screens.explanation: Volume and price answer two different questions about the same period.

screens.question: A simple way to read a volume bar under a candle:
items: Note the height of the volume bar
Compare it to nearby volume bars
Note whether the price candle above it was bullish or bearish
Consider volume and price movement together
correct_order: Note the height of the volume bar
Compare it to nearby volume bars
Note whether the price candle above it was bullish or bearish
Consider volume and price movement together
screens.explanation: Volume is usually read alongside price action, not in isolation.

screens.question: What does a volume spike alongside a large price move commonly suggest?

options.label: A chart data error
options.wrong_explanation: A volume spike is a normal, valid occurrence.

options.label: A guarantee that the move will continue forever
options.wrong_explanation: Volume describes activity, not a guaranteed future direction.

options.label: A larger number of participants were involved in that particular move

screens.explanation: Volume spikes are commonly read as a sign of increased participation, not a certainty about what happens next.

screens.scenario: Someone claims volume numbers are meaningless and should always be ignored.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should only look at volume and ignore price entirely.
Volume is commonly used as one added piece of context, not something to dismiss outright.
They should stop looking at charts altogether.
screens.explanation: Volume adds useful context; the mistake is dismissing it entirely, not the reverse.

screens.question: Which of these would most likely show HIGH volume?
options: A widely-traded, popular stock during active market hours.
An obscure stock with almost no interested traders.
A market that is currently closed.
screens.explanation: Popular assets during active trading hours commonly see more shares change hands.

screens.question: Volume and price are actually the same measurement, just displayed differently.
screens.explanation: Volume counts shares traded; price measures the level shares traded at — two separate dimensions.

screens.question: A sudden, unusually large increase in volume is often called a volume [___].
screens.explanation: "Volume spike" is the standard term for a sudden jump in trading activity.

lessons.title: What Is Liquidity?
lessons.celebration: You understand how easily a market can be traded!

screens.title: How Easily You Can Get In or Out
screens.text: Liquidity describes how easily an asset can be bought or sold without significantly moving its price.

screens.question: Liquidity describes how easily an asset can be bought or sold without significantly moving its price.
screens.explanation: That's the standard definition of liquidity.

screens.question: A market with many active buyers and sellers is generally described as [___].
screens.explanation: "Liquid" describes an asset that's easy to trade without big price impact.

screens.question: What is a commonly cited downside of low liquidity?
options: It removes the need for a bid and ask price.
Larger price swings can result from relatively small trades.
screens.explanation: In illiquid markets, even modest trades can move the price more noticeably.

screens.question: Match the liquidity level to its common description.
pairs: Easy to buy or sell without much price impact
Trades can move price more easily
The general ease of entering or exiting a position
screens.explanation: These describe the same underlying concept from different angles.

screens.template: [__1__] liquidity generally means tighter bid/ask spreads, while [__2__] liquidity often means wider ones.
screens.explanation: More active participation tends to narrow the gap between bid and ask.

screens.question: A simple way to evaluate how liquid an asset is:
items: Check how many buyers and sellers are currently active
Check the size of the bid/ask spread
Check typical trading volume for that asset
Form a view on how liquid it currently is
correct_order: Check how many buyers and sellers are currently active
Check the size of the bid/ask spread
Check typical trading volume for that asset
Form a view on how liquid it currently is
screens.explanation: These three signals together give a rough sense of liquidity.

screens.question: Which is generally a sign of low liquidity?

options.label: A wide gap between the highest bid and lowest ask
A very tight bid/ask spread
options.wrong_explanation: A tight spread is more commonly associated with higher liquidity.

options.label: Very high daily trading volume
options.wrong_explanation: High volume is more commonly associated with higher liquidity.

screens.explanation: Wide spreads are commonly linked to thinner, less liquid markets.

screens.scenario: Someone buys a large position in a very illiquid stock, expecting to exit instantly at the same price.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should have bought an even larger position.
They should have ignored the bid/ask spread entirely.
Low liquidity can make it harder to exit a large position without affecting the price.
screens.explanation: Illiquid markets can make large trades harder to exit cleanly at the expected price.

screens.question: Which is a more likely sign of HIGH liquidity?
options: Many active buyers and sellers with a tight bid/ask spread.
Very few participants and a wide bid/ask spread.
A market that hasn't traded in days.
screens.explanation: Active participation with tight spreads is a hallmark of high liquidity.

screens.question: Liquidity has no effect on how much a large trade might move the price.
screens.explanation: Lower liquidity generally means large trades can move price more noticeably.

screens.question: An asset that's easy to buy or sell without moving its price much is described as highly [___].
screens.explanation: "Liquid" specifically describes ease of trading without big price impact.

lessons.title: Bid vs Ask
lessons.celebration: You understand the two-sided price!

screens.title: Two Prices, Not One
screens.text: Most markets quote two prices at once: the bid (what buyers offer) and the ask (what sellers want).

screens.question: The ask price is what buyers are offering to pay.
screens.explanation: The ask is what sellers want to receive; the bid is what buyers are offering.

screens.question: The gap between the highest bid and the lowest ask is called the [___].
screens.explanation: "Spread" is the standard term for that price gap.

screens.question: Why does a spread generally exist?
options: Trading halts require it by law.
Buyers and sellers don't always fully agree on price.
It's a fee charged only on weekends.
screens.explanation: The spread reflects the natural difference between what each side is willing to accept.

screens.question: Match the term to its meaning.
pairs: The price buyers are currently offering to pay
The price sellers are currently asking to receive
The gap between the bid and the ask
screens.explanation: These three terms describe the two-sided nature of most markets.

screens.template: The [__1__] is generally lower than the [__2__] at any given moment.
screens.explanation: Buyers typically offer slightly less than sellers ask, creating the spread.

screens.question: A simple way to read a live quote:
items: Check the current bid
Check the current ask
Note the size of the gap between them
Understand a market order typically fills near one of these prices
correct_order: Check the current bid
Check the current ask
Note the size of the gap between them
Understand a market order typically fills near one of these prices
screens.explanation: This explains why an executed price can differ slightly from what you expected.

screens.question: What does a "wide spread" generally suggest?

options.label: A guarantee of profit on the next trade
options.wrong_explanation: Spread size doesn't guarantee an outcome.

options.label: Bid and ask being identical
options.wrong_explanation: A wide spread means a bigger gap, not an identical price.

options.label: A larger-than-usual gap between the bid and ask prices
options.detail: More distance between what buyers offer and sellers ask

screens.explanation: "Spread" specifically refers to the bid/ask gap.

screens.scenario: Someone expects to always buy at the exact last traded price shown on a chart.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should refresh the page many times instead.
Actual fills happen near the current bid or ask, which can differ slightly from the last traded price.
The chart itself must be broken.
screens.explanation: A small gap between the last trade and the current bid/ask is a normal part of how markets work.

screens.question: If the bid is $10.00 and the ask is $10.05, what is the spread?
screens.explanation: The spread is simply the difference between the ask and the bid.

screens.question: A market order will typically fill near the current bid or ask, not necessarily the last traded price.
screens.explanation: Market orders match against the best currently available bid or ask, which can differ slightly from the last trade.

screens.question: The price sellers are currently willing to accept is called the [___].
screens.explanation: "Ask" is the price sellers want; "bid" is what buyers offer.

lessons.title: Market vs Limit Orders (Intro)
lessons.celebration: You understand the two basic order types!

screens.title: Speed vs Price Control
screens.text: A market order and a limit order are two basic ways to place a trade, trading off speed against price control.

screens.question: A market order lets you name the exact price you want to pay.
screens.explanation: A market order executes at the best currently available price, not a chosen price.

screens.question: An order that only executes at a specific price (or better) is called a [___] order.
screens.explanation: "Limit" refers to the price limit you've set.

screens.question: What does a market order prioritize?
options: Immediate execution, at whatever the current price happens to be.
Waiting indefinitely for a price target.
screens.explanation: A market order trades price certainty for speed of execution.

screens.question: Match the order type to its trade-off.
pairs: Executes only at your chosen price or better, but may not fill at all
An instruction to buy or sell under certain conditions
screens.explanation: Each order type balances speed against price control differently.

screens.template: A market order prioritizes [__1__], while a limit order prioritizes [__2__].
screens.explanation: This is the core trade-off between the two order types.

screens.question: What happens when you place a market order:
items: You submit the order
It matches against the best currently available price
It executes right away
You receive confirmation of the fill
correct_order: You submit the order
It matches against the best currently available price
It executes right away
You receive confirmation of the fill
screens.explanation: Market orders are designed to execute quickly without waiting for a specific price.

screens.question: When might a limit order simply never execute?

options.label: If the market price never reaches your specified level
If you set the price too close to the current price
options.wrong_explanation: Being close to the current price makes filling more likely, not less.

options.label: Limit orders always execute immediately
options.wrong_explanation: That describes a market order, not a limit order.

screens.explanation: A limit order only fills if the market actually reaches your specified price.

screens.scenario: Someone is confused why their limit order never filled, even though they set a specific price.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Limit orders must be broken and shouldn't be used.
If the market price never reached their limit, the order simply remained unfilled — that's expected behavior.
They should have set an even lower limit price regardless of the market.
screens.explanation: An unfilled limit order usually just means price never reached that level.

screens.question: Which order type guarantees a specific price (or better), but not necessarily a fill?
screens.explanation: A limit order only executes at your specified price or better, which means it might not fill at all.

screens.question: A market order guarantees the price you'll pay, down to the exact cent.
screens.explanation: A market order guarantees speed of execution, not an exact guaranteed price.

screens.question: An order designed to execute immediately at the best available price is called a [___] order.
screens.explanation: "Market" orders prioritize speed over price certainty.

lessons.title: What Is Volatility?
lessons.celebration: You understand how "choppy" a market can be!

screens.title: How Big and Fast the Swings Are
screens.text: Volatility describes how much — and how quickly — price moves, in either direction.

screens.question: Volatility describes how much and how quickly price moves, regardless of direction.
screens.explanation: Volatility is about the size and speed of movement, not which direction it goes.

screens.question: A market moving through large price swings quickly is often described as [___].
screens.explanation: "Volatile" describes large, fast price swings.

screens.question: What does "low volatility" commonly describe?
options: A market that has stopped trading.
Smaller, slower price movements over time.
screens.explanation: Low volatility simply means calmer, smaller price movement.

screens.question: Match the volatility level to its description.
pairs: The overall size and speed of price movement
screens.explanation: Volatility is a measurement of movement, not a directional signal.

screens.template: [__1__] volatility can mean bigger potential price swings in [__2__] time.
screens.explanation: Higher volatility often means more movement can happen within a shorter window.

screens.question: A simple way to gauge current volatility on a chart:
items: Look at the size of recent candles
Compare them to that asset's typical candle size
Note if swings currently look unusually large or small
Form a rough view on current volatility
correct_order: Look at the size of recent candles
Compare them to that asset's typical candle size
Note if swings currently look unusually large or small
Form a rough view on current volatility
screens.explanation: Comparing recent movement to what's typical is a simple way to estimate volatility.

screens.question: Which chart is more likely to be described as "volatile"?

options.label: One with small, steady, gradual movement
options.wrong_explanation: That would more likely be described as low volatility.

options.label: One that hasn't moved at all
options.wrong_explanation: No movement is the lowest possible volatility, not high.

options.label: One with large, fast price swings

screens.explanation: Larger, faster swings are the hallmark of higher volatility.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes high volatility guarantees a specific direction for price.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should assume volatility always means a downtrend.
Volatility describes the size and speed of movement, not which direction it goes.
They should assume volatility always means an uptrend.
screens.explanation: A highly volatile market can move sharply in either direction — volatility alone doesn't determine direction.

screens.question: Which market condition would most likely be described as "volatile"?
options: Large, fast price swings in a short period.
screens.explanation: Volatility is about the size and speed of price movement, regardless of direction.

screens.question: Volatility can be high even if a market is trending strongly upward.
screens.explanation: A strong uptrend can still include large, fast swings — volatility measures movement size, not direction.

screens.question: Markets with small, slow price movement are often described as having [___] volatility.
screens.explanation: "Low volatility" describes calmer, smaller price movement.

lessons.title: Market Hours
lessons.celebration: You understand when markets are actually open!

screens.title: Not Always Open
screens.text: Most stock markets have set trading hours, with additional (often thinner) trading happening outside them.

screens.question: Every stock market is open for trading 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
screens.explanation: Most stock markets have defined standard trading hours, with limited activity outside them.

screens.question: Trading that happens outside standard hours is often called [___] hours trading.
screens.explanation: "Extended hours" (or after-hours/pre-market) describes trading outside the standard session.

screens.question: Why do market hours generally matter?
options: Prices freeze completely during standard hours.
Liquidity and volatility can differ noticeably outside standard hours.
Order types stop functioning outside standard hours.
screens.explanation: Extended-hours sessions commonly have thinner trading, which can affect price behavior.

screens.question: Match the trading period to its common characteristic.
pairs: Typically the highest liquidity of the day
Often lower liquidity than standard hours
Market typically closed for regular trading
screens.explanation: Liquidity commonly varies a lot depending on which period you're trading in.

screens.template: Trading outside standard hours can mean [__1__] liquidity and [__2__] spreads.
screens.explanation: Thinner participation outside standard hours commonly widens the bid/ask spread.

screens.question: A simple habit around market hours:
items: Check whether the market is currently open
Note whether it's standard or extended hours
Adjust expectations for liquidity accordingly
Proceed with that context in mind
correct_order: Check whether the market is currently open
Note whether it's standard or extended hours
Adjust expectations for liquidity accordingly
Proceed with that context in mind
screens.explanation: Knowing which session you're in helps set realistic expectations about liquidity.

screens.question: What's commonly true about extended-hours trading compared to standard hours?

options.label: It always has higher liquidity than standard hours
options.wrong_explanation: Extended hours are more commonly thinner, not thicker.

options.label: It often has lower liquidity than the standard session
Spreads are always identical to standard hours
options.wrong_explanation: Spreads are commonly wider during thinner extended-hours trading.

screens.explanation: Extended-hours sessions are commonly described as having thinner liquidity.

screens.scenario: Someone is surprised that a trade placed during after-hours filled at a very different price than expected.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Extended hours should have identical liquidity to standard hours.
Lower liquidity outside standard hours can lead to bigger differences between expected and actual fill prices.
The trading platform must be broken.
screens.explanation: Thinner participation outside standard hours is a commonly cited reason for wider price gaps on fills.

screens.question: Which is more likely true of pre-market trading hours?
options: Typically thinner liquidity than the standard session.
Always identical liquidity to standard hours.
Guaranteed higher volume than standard hours.
screens.explanation: Extended hours commonly see fewer active participants than the standard session.

screens.question: Some markets are completely closed on certain holidays.
screens.explanation: Most stock exchanges observe scheduled holidays when regular trading doesn't occur.

screens.question: Trading hours before the standard session opens are often called [___]-market hours.
screens.explanation: "Pre-market" describes the extended session before the standard open.

lessons.title: Timeframes
lessons.celebration: You understand how timeframes change the view!

screens.title: Zooming In and Out
screens.text: The same chart can look very different depending on which timeframe you're viewing it on.

screens.question: A 1-minute chart and a 1-day chart of the same asset will always look identical.
screens.explanation: Different timeframes summarize price differently, so the same asset can look quite different across them.

screens.question: Choosing a shorter timeframe generally shows [___] detail over a shorter period.
screens.explanation: Shorter timeframes zoom in, showing more granular detail over less total time.

screens.question: What determines how much time a single candlestick represents?
options: The number of wicks it has.
screens.explanation: Switching the timeframe changes what one candlestick summarizes.

screens.question: Match the timeframe choice to its trade-off.
pairs: A way to combine both views
screens.explanation: Each timeframe offers a different balance of detail versus context.

screens.template: Zooming to a [__1__] timeframe shows more detail over a shorter period, while a [__2__] timeframe shows less detail over a longer period.
screens.explanation: Timeframe choice is a trade-off between detail and overall context.

screens.question: A sensible way to look at a new chart across timeframes:
items: Check a longer timeframe first for general context
Zoom into a shorter timeframe for more detail
Compare what you see across both timeframes
Form an overall view combining both
correct_order: Check a longer timeframe first for general context
Zoom into a shorter timeframe for more detail
Compare what you see across both timeframes
Form an overall view combining both
screens.explanation: Looking at multiple timeframes is a common way to build a fuller picture.

screens.question: Which best describes why traders often check more than one timeframe?

options.label: To combine broader context with more detailed, recent price action
Because longer timeframes replace the need for candles entirely
options.wrong_explanation: Candles still apply on any timeframe.

options.label: Because shorter timeframes are always more accurate
options.wrong_explanation: Shorter timeframes aren't inherently more accurate, just more detailed.

screens.explanation: Different timeframes are complementary, not competing, sources of context.

screens.scenario: Someone judges an asset's entire long-term direction using only a 1-minute chart.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should have ignored the chart entirely.
A very short timeframe mostly shows recent detail, not the bigger long-term picture.
They should have used an even shorter timeframe instead.
screens.explanation: Judging the bigger picture usually calls for checking a longer timeframe as well.

screens.question: Which timeframe would show the LEAST detail per candle, but the MOST overall historical context?
options: A very short timeframe, like a 1-minute chart.
A long timeframe, like a weekly or monthly chart.
screens.explanation: Longer timeframes compress more history into each candle, showing less granular detail but more overall context.

screens.question: Switching timeframes changes how much time a single candlestick represents.
screens.explanation: Each timeframe defines what period of time one candle summarizes.

screens.question: A very short timeframe, like 1-minute, shows [___] detail over a shorter period.
screens.explanation: Shorter timeframes zoom in, offering finer detail over a smaller total window.

lessons.title: Candlestick Basics (Intro)
lessons.celebration: You can read a single candlestick!

screens.title: Reading a Candle
screens.text: A candlestick is a compact picture of price during a fixed period of time — a preview before Unit 2 goes deeper.

screens.question: A candlestick only shows the price at one single instant in time.
screens.explanation: A candlestick summarizes an entire time period, not a single instant.

screens.question: The thick middle part of a candlestick is called the [___].
screens.explanation: The body spans between the open and close prices for that period.

screens.question: What does the color of a candlestick commonly indicate?
options: Whether the close was higher (bullish) or lower (bearish) than the open.
The exact number of shares traded.
screens.explanation: Color is a quick visual summary of direction for that period.

screens.question: Match the candlestick part to what it shows.
pairs: The range between the open and close price
The high or low reached during that period
Whether that period closed higher or lower than it opened
screens.explanation: Each part of a candle encodes a different piece of information.

screens.template: A [__1__] candle typically means the close was higher than the open, while a [__2__] candle means the close was lower.
screens.explanation: Color convention (usually green/red) quickly summarizes direction.

screens.question: A simple way to read a single candle's story:
items: Identify the open and close (the body)
Identify the high and low reached (the wicks)
Compare the wick length to the body length
Note which direction any long wick points
correct_order: Identify the open and close (the body)
Identify the high and low reached (the wicks)
Compare the wick length to the body length
Note which direction any long wick points
screens.explanation: Reading a candle means examining all four price points, not just its color.

screens.question: Which term describes a candlestick with a very small body and long wicks on both sides?

options.label: Doji
options.detail: Open and close are close together

options.label: Hammer
options.wrong_explanation: A hammer typically has one long wick, not two.

options.label: Marubozu
options.detail: A candle with almost no wicks
options.wrong_explanation: This is the opposite — a marubozu has little to no wick.

screens.explanation: A doji is one of the most commonly referenced single-candle patterns.

screens.scenario: Someone says "this one candle proves price will definitely go up next."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should have used a different-colored candle.
No single candlestick can reliably predict future price with certainty.
They should have looked at an even longer wick.
screens.explanation: Candlesticks describe what already happened — they aren't guarantees about what happens next.

screens.question: What does a candlestick's wick represent?
options: The high and/or low price reached during that period.
The exact trading volume for that period.
screens.explanation: Wicks mark the extreme high and low prices reached, beyond the body.

screens.question: Every single candlestick must have at least one visible wick.
screens.explanation: A candle can have a tiny or nonexistent wick if price barely moved beyond the open/close range.

screens.question: The colored, thick part of a candlestick between the open and close is called the [___].
screens.explanation: "Body" specifically refers to the open-to-close range.

lessons.title: Open, High, Low, Close
lessons.celebration: You know your OHLC!

screens.title: The Four Numbers Behind Every Candle
screens.text: Every candlestick is built from exactly four numbers: the open, high, low, and close for that period.

screens.question: Every candlestick is built from exactly four price values.
screens.explanation: Open, high, low, and close are the four numbers that define a candle.

screens.question: The price at the very start of a candle's period is called the [___].
screens.explanation: "Open" is the first traded price of that period.

screens.question: What does "close" refer to on a candlestick?
options: The highest price reached during the period.
The final traded price at the end of that period.
The very first traded price of that period.
screens.explanation: "Close" specifically refers to the ending price of that timeframe.

screens.question: Match the OHLC term to its meaning.
pairs: First traded price of the period
Highest price reached during the period
Lowest price reached during the period
screens.explanation: Together with the close, these four values fully describe a candle.

screens.template: The [__1__] and [__2__] together define the wick's extremes on a candle.
screens.explanation: The high and low mark the top and bottom reach of the wick.

screens.question: How one candle's OHLC values are set, over its time period:
items: The period begins at the open price
Price moves up and down, setting the high and low
The period ends at the close price
All four values are then locked in for that candle
correct_order: The period begins at the open price
Price moves up and down, setting the high and low
The period ends at the close price
All four values are then locked in for that candle
screens.explanation: OHLC values are only finalized once that period's candle has fully closed.

screens.question: Which best describes the "high" of a candlestick?

options.label: The price the candle opened at
options.wrong_explanation: That's the "open," not the "high."

options.label: The highest price reached at any point during that period
options.detail: Even if it didn't close there

options.label: The average of open and close
options.wrong_explanation: The high is a single peak value, not an average.

screens.explanation: The high specifically marks the peak price reached, regardless of where it closed.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes the "close" of a candle is always the same as its highest price.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: The close and the high are often different values — the close is simply where price ended.
They should assume close always equals the low instead.
They should ignore the close value entirely.
screens.explanation: A candle can close well below its high if price pulled back before the period ended.

screens.question: Which value marks the LOWEST price reached during a candle's period?
screens.explanation: "Low" specifically marks the lowest price touched during that period.

screens.question: The open and close values are always the same as the high and low values.
screens.explanation: Open/close and high/low are often different; a candle's body and wicks can differ in position.

screens.question: The very last traded price within a candle's period is called the [___].
screens.explanation: "Close" refers to the final price of that period.

lessons.title: Why Gaps Happen
lessons.celebration: You understand price gaps!

screens.title: The Space Between Candles
screens.text: A gap happens when price opens noticeably above or below where it previously closed, often due to news or events between sessions.

screens.question: A gap occurs when a candle opens at the exact same price the previous candle closed at.
screens.explanation: A gap specifically describes a noticeable difference between the prior close and the new open.

screens.question: A jump between one candle's close and the next candle's open is called a [___].
screens.explanation: "Gap" is the standard term for this kind of jump.

screens.question: Why do gaps commonly occur between trading sessions?
options: Volume always drops to zero between sessions.
The chart software resets randomly overnight.
News or events can shift buyer/seller sentiment while the market is closed.
screens.explanation: News overnight or over a weekend is a common reason expectations shift before the next open.

screens.question: Match the gap type to its description.
pairs: Next open is noticeably higher than the prior close
Next open is noticeably lower than the prior close
Price later trades back to close that gap
screens.explanation: These are standard descriptive terms for gap behavior.

screens.template: Gaps often form when the market is [__1__], and information arrives that shifts sentiment before the [__2__].
screens.explanation: The information can't be traded on until the market reopens, causing a jump at the open.

screens.question: A simple way to notice a gap on a chart:
items: Compare where the prior candle closed
Compare where the next candle opened
Note whether there's a noticeable jump between them
Classify it as a gap up or gap down accordingly
correct_order: Compare where the prior candle closed
Compare where the next candle opened
Note whether there's a noticeable jump between them
Classify it as a gap up or gap down accordingly
screens.explanation: A gap is identified by comparing two specific price points across the session break.

screens.question: Which best describes a "gap fill"?

options.label: A gap that never closes
options.wrong_explanation: That would simply be described as an unfilled gap.

options.label: Price later trading back to the level before the gap occurred
options.detail: Closing the price space that was skipped

options.label: A candle with no wick
options.wrong_explanation: That's a separate candlestick concept, not about gaps.

screens.explanation: "Gap fill" specifically describes price retracing back through the skipped range.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes every gap must always get filled eventually, as a guaranteed rule.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Not every gap gets filled — some do, some don't; there's no guarantee either way.
They should assume no gap is ever filled instead.
They should ignore gaps entirely from now on.
screens.explanation: Treating "gaps always fill" as a certainty overstates what is really just a commonly observed tendency, not a rule.

screens.question: Which scenario would most likely cause a stock to gap up at the next open?
options: Strong positive news released after the market closed.
screens.explanation: News released while the market is closed is a common cause of a gap at the next open.

screens.question: A "gap down" means the next candle opens noticeably higher than the prior close.
screens.explanation: A gap down means the next open is noticeably LOWER than the prior close, not higher.

screens.question: Price later trading back through a gap's skipped range is called a gap [___].
screens.explanation: "Gap fill" describes price retracing back through the previously skipped range.

lessons.title: What "Trend" Means
lessons.celebration: You understand the basic idea of a trend!

screens.title: Which Way Is It Going, Generally?
screens.text: A trend is simply a description of the general direction price has been moving over some period.

screens.question: A trend is a description of the general direction price has been moving.
screens.explanation: That's the core, descriptive meaning of "trend."

screens.question: A chart generally moving from lower prices to higher prices is described as being in an [___] trend.
screens.explanation: "Uptrend" is the standard descriptive term for that general direction.

screens.question: What does a "downtrend" commonly describe?
options: A pattern of price generally moving lower over time.
A single red candle appearing anywhere on the chart.
A guarantee that price will never rise again.
screens.explanation: Downtrend describes an overall pattern, not a single candle or a certain future.

screens.question: Match the trend type to its general description.
pairs: Price generally moving higher over time
Price generally moving lower over time
Price moving without a clear overall direction
screens.explanation: These are the three standard descriptive labels for overall price direction.

screens.template: "Trend" is a [__1__] label for a pattern that has [__2__] happened, not a guarantee of what comes next.
screens.explanation: Trend describes the past and present pattern, not a certain future.

screens.question: A simple way to get an initial read on a chart's trend:
items: Look at the overall shape across a longer timeframe
Note whether it's generally moving up, down, or sideways
Assign the matching descriptive label
Treat that label as a description, not a guarantee
correct_order: Look at the overall shape across a longer timeframe
Note whether it's generally moving up, down, or sideways
Assign the matching descriptive label
Treat that label as a description, not a guarantee
screens.explanation: This keeps the exercise descriptive rather than predictive.

screens.question: Which best describes what "trend" means as a term?

options.label: A description of the general direction price has recently moved
A specific candlestick shape
options.wrong_explanation: Trend describes multiple candles together, not one shape.

options.label: A guarantee that price will keep moving that way forever
options.wrong_explanation: A trend describes the past pattern, not a certain future.

screens.explanation: "Trend" is a useful descriptive shorthand, not a promise about what happens next.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes that because a chart has trended upward for months, it can never turn downward.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should have used a shorter timeframe instead.
A trend describes what has already happened — it doesn't guarantee it will continue forever.
They should have looked at a totally different asset.
screens.explanation: Trends can and do change; treating a past trend as a permanent guarantee is a common misconception.

screens.question: Which best describes a "sideways" or range-bound market?
options: Price moving without a clear overall upward or downward direction.
Price moving strongly and consistently lower.
Price moving strongly and consistently higher.
screens.explanation: Sideways/range describes a lack of clear directional progress, unlike an uptrend or downtrend.

screens.question: A downtrend can eventually turn into an uptrend over time.
screens.explanation: Trends can and do change; a past trend doesn't lock in the future direction forever.

screens.question: Price generally moving from higher levels to lower levels over time is called a [___].
screens.explanation: "Downtrend" describes an overall pattern of declining price.

lessons.title: Mini Simulation: Identify Direction
lessons.celebration: You can classify chart direction on sight!

screens.title: Putting It Together
screens.text: Let's practice classifying a chart's overall direction — purely a descriptive exercise, not a prediction of what comes next.

screens.question: What is the overall direction shown in this chart?
options: An uptrend — price generally moving higher over time
A downtrend — price generally moving lower over time
A sideways range with no clear direction
screens.explanation: The overall shape here moves generally higher over the period shown.

screens.question: What is the overall direction shown in this chart?
options: An uptrend — price generally moving higher over time
A downtrend — price generally moving lower over time
A sideways range with no clear direction
screens.explanation: The overall shape here moves generally lower over the period shown.

screens.question: How would you classify the price action in this chart?
options: A sideways range, without a clear overall direction
screens.explanation: Price here stays within a similar band rather than clearly trending.

screens.question: A chart can only ever be classified as one of exactly three directions: up, down, or sideways.
screens.explanation: These three descriptive labels are the standard way charts are broadly classified by overall direction.

screens.question: Match the classification to its defining shape.
pairs: Generally moving from lower prices to higher prices
Generally moving from higher prices to lower prices
Bouncing within a similar band without a clear direction
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the three classifications from this unit.

screens.question: A simple process for classifying any new chart's direction:
items: Look at where price started on the chart
Look at where price ended on the chart
Note whether it moved mostly up, down, or stayed within a band
Assign the matching classification
correct_order: Look at where price started on the chart
Look at where price ended on the chart
Note whether it moved mostly up, down, or stayed within a band
Assign the matching classification
screens.explanation: Comparing the start and end of a period is a simple first step toward classifying direction.

screens.question: What is the purpose of this kind of classification exercise?

options.label: Predicting the next candle with total certainty
options.wrong_explanation: Classification describes the past, not a guaranteed future.

options.label: Deciding whether to buy or sell right now
options.wrong_explanation: This drill is about reading direction, not making a trade decision.

options.label: Practicing a clear, descriptive read of what a chart has already done
options.detail: A literacy skill, not a forecast

screens.concern: Understanding the point of the drill
screens.explanation: This exercise builds descriptive chart-reading skill, not predictive or trading decisions.

screens.scenario: Someone finishes this drill and claims they can now predict every future chart's direction with certainty.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: This drill practices describing direction that has already happened — it doesn't grant predictive certainty about the future.
They should have practiced on an even smaller chart.
They should have skipped straight to a real account instead.
screens.explanation: This is a literacy exercise in reading what already happened, not a predictive skill.

screens.question: What's the most reliable first step when classifying a chart's direction?
options: Guess based on the chart's color scheme.
Ignore the chart and check the news instead.
Compare where price started versus where it ended over the period.
screens.explanation: Comparing the start and end points is a simple, direct way to gauge overall direction.

screens.question: Classifying a chart's direction is the same thing as predicting its next move.
screens.explanation: Classification describes what has already happened; it is not a prediction of the future.

screens.question: A chart bouncing within a similar band with no clear direction is classified as [___].
screens.explanation: "Sideways" (or range-bound) is the classification for directionless bouncing.

lessons.title: What Is a Candlestick?
lessons.celebration: You can read the anatomy of a candle off a chart!

screens.title: The Full Anatomy
screens.text: Every candle has a body (the open-to-close range) and wicks (the highs and lows it reached). Reading both off the chart is the core skill of this unit.

screens.question: Look at the tall highlighted candle above. Its thick middle section represents what?
options: The trading volume for that period.
The single highest price of the day only.
screens.explanation: The thick body always spans the open and close; the thin wicks show the extremes.

screens.question: On the chart above, the thin lines poking out of each candle's body are the wicks (the high/low reach).
screens.explanation: Wicks (or shadows) mark how far price stretched beyond the body.

screens.question: A green (or hollow) candle like the highlighted one closed [___] than it opened.
screens.explanation: By convention a bullish/green candle closes above its open.

screens.question: Match each part of the candle above to what it shows.
pairs: The high reached above the body
The low reached below the body
screens.explanation: Body and wicks together tell the full story of the period.

screens.question: The highlighted candle has a large body and almost no wicks. What does that shape suggest?

options.label: That nothing happened that period
options.wrong_explanation: A large body shows a big move, not a quiet one.

options.label: Price moved decisively one way and held there into the close
That the chart data is broken
options.wrong_explanation: A near-wickless candle is a normal, valid shape.

screens.explanation: A big body with tiny wicks means price pushed one direction and stayed there.

screens.scenario: Someone glances at the chart and reads only the wicks, ignoring the bodies entirely.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should only ever look at the very first candle.
The body and wicks are read together — the body shows the net move, the wicks the extremes.
They should ignore the wicks too and just guess.
screens.explanation: Reading body and wick together gives a fuller picture than either alone.

screens.question: A candlestick with a small body and long wicks on both sides would generally NOT be called a marubozu.
screens.explanation: A marubozu specifically needs a large body and almost no wicks — the opposite of that description.

screens.question: Wicks show the [___] and low reached during the period, beyond the body.
screens.explanation: Wicks mark the high and low extremes; the body marks the open-to-close range.

screens.question: If a candle's open and close are far apart, its body will be...
screens.explanation: A bigger gap between open and close makes for a larger body.

lessons.title: Reading a Doji
lessons.celebration: You can spot a doji on a chart instantly!

screens.title: When Neither Side Wins
screens.text: A doji has a tiny body — open and close almost equal — with wicks on both sides. It's commonly read as a moment of balance. The highlighted candle below is a doji.

screens.question: The highlighted candle above is best described as a...
options: Bullish engulfing — a big candle swallowing the one before it.
Marubozu — a large body with no wicks.
Doji — a tiny body with wicks on both sides.
screens.explanation: The near-nonexistent body is what makes the highlighted candle a doji.

screens.question: The chart above shows a candle with a large, decisive body.
screens.explanation: The highlighted candle is a doji — its body is tiny, the opposite of decisive.

screens.question: The tiny body on the highlighted candle is commonly read as market [___] between buyers and sellers.
screens.explanation: Neither side pushed price clearly higher or lower by the close.

screens.question: Reading the doji on the chart above, what does it tell you on its own?

options.label: That buyers and sellers finished that period roughly balanced
That the market is closed
options.wrong_explanation: A doji is a normal candle, not a closed market.

options.label: That a reversal is guaranteed next
options.wrong_explanation: No single candle guarantees what comes next.

screens.concern: Interpreting a doji from the chart
screens.explanation: A doji describes balance in that period; it doesn't predict the next move by itself.

screens.scenario: Looking at this chart, someone calls the highlighted doji a "100% guaranteed reversal."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A doji can only ever appear at the start of a chart.
A doji describes balance — no single candle is a guaranteed signal of what happens next.
The doji should have an even bigger body to count.
screens.explanation: A doji is a useful descriptive clue, not a certainty.

screens.question: Tap the doji on the chart.
screens.explanation: The middle candle has an almost nonexistent body with wicks on both sides — that's the doji.

screens.question: A doji's open and close prices are nearly identical.
screens.explanation: The near-equal open and close is exactly what makes the tiny body of a doji.

screens.question: Which best describes what "indecision" means for a doji?
options: The candle has no high or low.
Neither buyers nor sellers clearly won that period.
screens.explanation: Indecision describes a balanced tug-of-war, not missing data.

screens.question: A doji can appear at any point in a chart, [___] just at the very start.

lessons.title: Reading a Hammer
lessons.celebration: You can identify a hammer on a chart!

screens.title: A Long Lower Wick
screens.text: A hammer has a small body near the top and a long lower wick, appearing after a down-move. The long wick shows price was pushed down, then recovered by the close. The highlighted candle is a hammer.

screens.question: The highlighted candle above — small body up top, long lower wick, after a drop — is a...
screens.explanation: A long lower wick with the body near the top, after a decline, is the hammer shape.

screens.question: The long lower wick on the highlighted candle shows price was pushed down but [___] by the close.
screens.explanation: The body finishing near the top means buyers pulled price back up before the close.

screens.question: The chart above shows a candle with a long upper wick and body near the bottom.
screens.explanation: This is a hammer — a long LOWER wick with the body near the top.

screens.question: What does the hammer on the chart above describe?

options.label: That the candle has no body at all
options.wrong_explanation: A hammer has a small but real body near the top.

options.label: A guarantee price rises from here
options.wrong_explanation: The shape is descriptive, not a promise.

options.label: Sellers pushed price down, but buyers recovered much of it by the close
options.detail: A descriptive read of the wick

screens.explanation: The hammer describes a failed push lower that buyers largely reversed.

screens.question: Match each candle feature above to what it represents.
pairs: The close finished back near the high
The context that makes it a "hammer"
screens.explanation: Shape plus context together define the hammer.

screens.question: Tap the hammer on the chart.
screens.explanation: The last candle has a small body up top and a long lower wick — the hammer.

screens.question: A hammer's long wick points downward, below the body.
screens.explanation: The long lower wick is what defines the hammer shape.

screens.question: Where does a hammer's small body sit relative to the candle's overall range?
screens.explanation: A hammer's body sits near the top, with the long wick trailing below it.

screens.question: A hammer commonly appears after a [___] in price.
screens.explanation: The hammer shape is read in the context of a preceding down-move.

lessons.title: Reading a Shooting Star
lessons.celebration: You can identify a shooting star on a chart!

screens.title: A Long Upper Wick
screens.text: A shooting star is the hammer's mirror image: a small body near the bottom and a long upper wick, appearing after an up-move. Price was pushed up but slid back by the close. The highlighted candle is a shooting star.

screens.question: The highlighted candle above — small body near the bottom, long upper wick, after a rise — is a...
screens.explanation: A long upper wick with the body near the bottom, after a rise, is the shooting star shape.

screens.question: The long upper wick on the highlighted candle shows price was pushed up but [___] by the close.
screens.explanation: The body finishing near the low means the higher prices were rejected before the close.

screens.question: The chart above shows the same shape as a hammer.
screens.explanation: It's the mirror image — a long UPPER wick (shooting star), not a long lower wick (hammer).

screens.question: What does the shooting star on the chart above describe?

options.label: The exact volume traded
options.wrong_explanation: Candle shape doesn't show volume directly.

options.label: Buyers pushed price up, but it was rejected back down by the close
options.detail: A descriptive read of the upper wick

options.label: A guarantee price falls from here
options.wrong_explanation: The shape describes, it doesn't promise.

screens.explanation: The shooting star describes an upward push that got rejected.

screens.scenario: Someone sees this chart and labels the highlighted candle a hammer.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Wick direction doesn't matter when naming a candle.
A shooting star and a hammer are the exact same shape.
The long wick here is on top, after a rise — that's a shooting star, not a hammer.
screens.explanation: Which side the long wick is on (and the preceding move) is what separates the two.

screens.question: A shooting star's long wick points upward, above the body.
screens.explanation: The long upper wick is what defines the shooting star shape.

screens.question: A shooting star commonly appears after what kind of move?
screens.explanation: The shooting star is read in the context of a preceding up-move.

screens.question: Match each shape to its wick position.
pairs: Wicks on both sides, tiny body
screens.explanation: Wick position (and preceding trend) is what names each shape.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a shooting star's long wick means volume was extremely high.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Wick length shows price extremes, not trading volume — they're two separate ideas.
Volume can't be measured separately from wicks.
screens.explanation: Wicks describe price reach, not trading volume.

screens.question: Match each shape to the trend it commonly follows.
screens.explanation: Preceding trend is part of what gives each shape its common reading.

lessons.title: Reading Bullish Engulfing
lessons.celebration: You can spot a bullish engulfing on a chart!

screens.title: One Candle Swallows the Last
screens.text: A bullish engulfing is a small down candle followed by a larger up candle whose body fully covers it. The highlighted candle is the engulfing one.

screens.question: On the chart above, the highlighted candle's body fully covers the previous candle's body, and it closed up. This is a...
screens.explanation: A larger up-candle body swallowing the prior down candle is the bullish engulfing shape.

screens.question: In a bullish engulfing like the one shown, the second (highlighted) candle's body is smaller than the first.
screens.explanation: The whole point is the second body is LARGER — it engulfs the first.

screens.question: A bullish engulfing pattern needs the up candle to fully [___] the prior candle's body.
screens.explanation: "Engulfing" means the second body completely covers the first.

screens.question: What does the bullish engulfing on the chart above describe?

options.label: Buyers overwhelmed the prior down candle within one period
options.detail: A descriptive read of the two candles

options.label: A guaranteed uptrend from here
options.wrong_explanation: A pattern describes; it doesn't guarantee.

options.label: That both candles are red
options.wrong_explanation: The engulfing candle here is an up (green) candle.

screens.explanation: The pattern describes buyers taking over that period, nothing guaranteed.

screens.question: Tap the candle that engulfs the one before it.
screens.explanation: The second candle's larger up body fully covers the prior down candle.

screens.question: A bullish engulfing pattern involves exactly two candles.
screens.explanation: The pattern is specifically a two-candle relationship — a small one, then a larger engulfing one.

screens.question: In a bullish engulfing, which candle comes first?
screens.explanation: The smaller down candle is followed by the larger engulfing up candle.

screens.question: The word "engulfing" describes one candle's body completely [___] another's.
screens.explanation: "Engulfing" specifically means the second body fully covers the first.

screens.question: The candle that gets engulfed in a bullish engulfing pattern is the [___] one.
screens.explanation: The smaller, earlier down candle is the one that gets engulfed.

screens.question: Bullish engulfing can only occur after an uptrend, never after a decline.
screens.explanation: Bullish engulfing is commonly read in the context of a prior decline, not an uptrend.

lessons.title: Reading Bearish Engulfing
lessons.celebration: You can spot a bearish engulfing on a chart!

screens.title: The Mirror Image
screens.text: A bearish engulfing is a small up candle followed by a larger down candle whose body fully covers it. The highlighted candle is the engulfing one.

screens.question: On the chart above, the highlighted down candle fully covers the previous up candle's body. This is a...
screens.explanation: A larger down-candle body swallowing the prior up candle is the bearish engulfing shape.

screens.question: The chart above shows an up (green) candle engulfing a down candle.
screens.explanation: Here a DOWN candle engulfs an up candle — that's bearish engulfing.

screens.question: A bearish engulfing is commonly read as [___] taking over from buyers for that period.
screens.explanation: The larger down candle shows selling pressure overwhelmed the prior up candle.

screens.question: Match each engulfing pattern to its description.
pairs: Larger up candle covers a prior down candle
Larger down candle covers a prior up candle
Two candles of the same small size, no engulfing
screens.explanation: The engulfing direction depends on which candle swallows the other.

screens.scenario: Someone sees this chart and calls it bullish because "there's a big candle."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Size alone isn't the point — here the big candle is a DOWN candle engulfing an up one, which is bearish.
A big candle always means bullish.
The color of the engulfing candle never matters.
screens.explanation: Direction of the engulfing candle, not just its size, sets bullish vs bearish.

screens.question: A bearish engulfing pattern involves exactly two candles.
screens.explanation: Like bullish engulfing, this is a two-candle relationship.

screens.question: In a bearish engulfing, which candle comes first?
screens.explanation: The smaller up candle is followed by the larger engulfing down candle.

screens.question: What does a bearish engulfing describe about that period?

options.label: Sellers overwhelmed the prior up candle within one period
That both candles are the same color
options.wrong_explanation: One is up, one is down — that's the point.

options.label: A guaranteed downtrend forever
options.wrong_explanation: A pattern describes, it doesn't guarantee.

screens.explanation: The pattern describes selling pressure taking over, not a guaranteed outcome.

screens.question: The candle that gets engulfed in a bearish engulfing pattern is the [___] one.
screens.explanation: The smaller, earlier up candle is the one that gets engulfed.

screens.question: Tap the engulfing candle on the chart.
screens.explanation: The second, larger down candle is the one that engulfs the first.

lessons.title: Reading a Spinning Top
lessons.celebration: You can identify a spinning top on a chart!

screens.title: A Small Body, Wicks Both Sides
screens.text: A spinning top has a small body with wicks of similar length on both sides — like a doji but with a slightly larger body. It's commonly read as hesitation. The highlighted candle is a spinning top.

screens.question: The highlighted candle — small body, similar wicks on both sides — is a...
screens.explanation: A small body centered between two similar wicks is the spinning top shape.

screens.question: The chart above shows a candle with a large body and no wicks.
screens.explanation: A spinning top has a SMALL body with wicks on both sides — the opposite of a marubozu.

screens.question: A spinning top is commonly read as [___], with neither side clearly in control.
screens.explanation: The small body and balanced wicks suggest an indecisive period.

screens.question: How does the spinning top on the chart differ from a marubozu?

options.label: They are exactly the same shape
options.wrong_explanation: One shows hesitation, the other decisiveness.

options.label: The spinning top has a small body and wicks; a marubozu has a big body and almost none
The spinning top has no body at all
options.wrong_explanation: It has a small but visible body.

screens.explanation: Body size and wick presence are what separate hesitation from decisiveness.

screens.question: A spinning top has wicks of roughly similar length on both sides.
screens.explanation: Balanced wicks on both sides, with a small body, is the spinning top shape.

screens.question: Compared to a doji, a spinning top's body is...
screens.explanation: A spinning top has a bit more body than a doji, but still small overall.

screens.scenario: Someone claims a spinning top always signals an immediate reversal.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A spinning top describes hesitation, not a guaranteed reversal signal.
Spinning tops only appear once per chart.
Spinning tops always reverse the trend immediately.
screens.explanation: Like other single candles, a spinning top is descriptive, not a certainty.

screens.question: A spinning top's wicks are roughly [___] in length on both sides.
screens.explanation: Balanced wick length on both sides is part of the spinning top's definition.

screens.question: Which is closest in meaning to a spinning top's "hesitation" reading?
options: Neither buyers nor sellers clearly won that period.
screens.explanation: Hesitation means neither side won decisively.

lessons.title: Reading a Marubozu
lessons.celebration: You can identify a marubozu on a chart!

screens.title: All Body, No Wick
screens.text: A marubozu has a large body and almost no wicks — price opened at one end, closed at the other, and barely looked back. The highlighted candle is a marubozu.

screens.question: The highlighted candle — big body, almost no wicks — is a...
screens.explanation: A large body with virtually no wicks is the marubozu shape.

screens.question: A marubozu is commonly read as a [___], one-sided period.
screens.explanation: The full body with no wicks shows price moved one way and held.

screens.question: The chart above shows more hesitation than a spinning top would.
screens.explanation: A marubozu shows decisiveness — far less hesitation than a small-bodied spinning top.

screens.question: Match each candle to how decisive it looks.
screens.explanation: Body size is a quick read of how one-sided a period was.

screens.scenario: Someone treats a single marubozu on this chart as a promise the trend continues.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Big candles never mean anything at all.
A marubozu can only appear once per chart.
A marubozu describes one decisive period — it doesn't guarantee what the next candle does.
screens.explanation: Even a decisive candle is descriptive, not a guarantee of the future.

screens.question: A marubozu has virtually no wicks on either side.
screens.explanation: Almost no wick, with a large body, is exactly what defines a marubozu.

screens.question: Which best describes the price action inside a marubozu candle?
options: Price moved in one direction steadily and closed near its extreme.
Price bounced back and forth with no clear direction.
screens.explanation: A marubozu reflects steady, one-directional movement through the period.

screens.question: A marubozu's lack of wicks suggests neither side pushed price [___] before the close.
screens.explanation: With no meaningful wick, price wasn't pushed back from its extreme before closing.

screens.question: A marubozu's open is at (or very near) one extreme, and its close is at the [___] extreme.
screens.explanation: Opening at one extreme and closing at the other, with little wick, is the marubozu shape.

screens.question: Tap the marubozu on the chart.
screens.explanation: The big-bodied, near-wickless candle is the marubozu.

lessons.title: Rejection Wicks in Context
lessons.celebration: You can read rejection wicks off a chart!

screens.title: Where Price Got Pushed Back
screens.text: A long wick is often called a "rejection" — price reached a level, then got pushed back before the close. The highlighted candle below has a long lower wick: a rejection of the lows.

screens.question: The highlighted candle's long lower wick is commonly read as a rejection of the...
options: lows — price dipped, then buyers pushed it back up.
highs — price spiked, then sellers pushed it back down.
volume — the number of shares traded.
screens.explanation: A long LOWER wick means the low was rejected and price closed back up.

screens.question: A long upper wick is commonly read as a rejection of the highs.
screens.explanation: Here the highlighted candle spiked up and got pushed back down — the highs were rejected.

screens.question: A rejection wick shows price [___] a level but failed to hold there into the close.
screens.explanation: The wick marks a level price touched but couldn't sustain.

screens.question: Reading the rejection wick on the chart above, what is the safe takeaway?

options.label: The wick shows the trading volume
options.wrong_explanation: Wicks show price extremes, not volume.

options.label: Price is certain to reverse now
options.wrong_explanation: A rejection is a clue, not a promise.

options.label: A level was tested and rejected that period — useful context, not a guarantee

screens.explanation: Rejection wicks describe where price failed to hold — context, not certainty.

screens.question: A rejection wick shows price failed to hold at an extreme it briefly reached.
screens.explanation: The wick marks a level price touched but couldn't sustain into the close.

screens.question: A long lower wick on a candle is commonly called a rejection of the...
screens.explanation: A long lower wick specifically shows the lows were tested and rejected.

screens.question: Match the wick type to what it rejects.
screens.explanation: Wick length and direction show which extreme was tested and rejected.

screens.template: A rejection of the [__1__] shows a long lower wick; a rejection of the [__2__] shows a long upper wick.
screens.explanation: Lower wick = lows rejected; upper wick = highs rejected.

screens.question: A rejection wick can appear on candles of either color.
screens.explanation: Rejection is about wick length/position, not the candle's overall color.

lessons.title: Identification Drill: Reversal Shapes
lessons.celebration: You can tell reversal candles apart at a glance!

screens.title: Name the Shape
screens.text: Time to read charts fast. For each chart, identify the highlighted candle.

screens.question: Which candle is highlighted on the chart above?
options: Hammer — long lower wick, body up top.
Shooting star — long upper wick, body down low.
screens.explanation: Long lower wick with the body near the top is a hammer.

screens.question: Which candle is highlighted on the chart above?
options: Hammer — long lower wick, body up top.
Shooting star — long upper wick, body down low.
screens.explanation: Long upper wick with the body near the bottom is a shooting star.

screens.question: Which candle is highlighted on the chart above?
options: Spinning top — small body, even wicks.
Inverted hammer — small body low, long upper wick, after a drop.
screens.explanation: A long upper wick with a small low body after a decline is an inverted hammer.

screens.question: Which candle is highlighted on the chart above?
options: Hanging man — small body up top, long lower wick, after a rise.
Bullish engulfing — big up candle covering the last.
screens.explanation: A hammer shape appearing after a rise is called a hanging man.

screens.question: The chart above shows a doji.
screens.explanation: Tiny body with wicks both sides — that's a doji.

screens.question: Tap the shooting star on the chart.
screens.explanation: Long upper wick, small body near the bottom — the shooting star.

screens.question: Tap the inverted hammer on the chart.
screens.explanation: Long upper wick with a small low body after a drop — the inverted hammer.

screens.question: A hanging man and a hammer share the exact same candle shape.
screens.explanation: Same shape, different context — a hammer after a decline, a hanging man after a rise.

screens.question: What separates a hanging man from a hammer?
options: The trend context it appears in (a rise vs. a decline).
screens.explanation: Both share the same shape; only the preceding trend differs.

screens.question: Correctly identifying a candle shape means checking both its form and its [___].
