screens.explanation: Shape alone isn't enough — the surrounding trend matters too.

lessons.title: Identification Drill: Engulfing & Bodies
lessons.celebration: You can classify body-driven candles fast!

screens.title: Name the Pattern
screens.text: These charts are all about body size and engulfing. Read each one.

screens.question: Which pattern is shown on the chart above?
options: Bullish engulfing — big up candle covers the prior down candle.
Bearish engulfing — big down candle covers the prior up candle.
Spinning top — small body, even wicks.
screens.explanation: A larger up candle swallowing the prior down candle is bullish engulfing.

screens.question: Which pattern is shown on the chart above?
options: Bullish engulfing — big up candle covers the prior down candle.
Bearish engulfing — big down candle covers the prior up candle.
Marubozu — one big body, no wicks.
screens.explanation: A larger down candle swallowing the prior up candle is bearish engulfing.

screens.question: Which candle is highlighted on the chart above?
options: Marubozu — big body, almost no wicks.
screens.explanation: A full body with virtually no wicks is a marubozu.

screens.question: Which candle is highlighted on the chart above?
options: Spinning top — small body, similar wicks both sides.
screens.explanation: A small body centered between two wicks is a spinning top.

screens.question: The chart above shows a bearish engulfing.
screens.explanation: The big candle here is an UP candle engulfing a down one — that's bullish engulfing.

screens.question: Tap the bearish engulfing candle.
screens.explanation: The second candle's larger down body fully covers the prior up candle.

screens.question: Tap the marubozu on the chart.
screens.explanation: The big-bodied, near-wickless candle is the marubozu.

screens.question: Both bullish and bearish engulfing patterns involve one candle's body fully covering another's.
screens.explanation: "Engulfing" means full coverage in both the bullish and bearish versions.

screens.question: What's the fastest way to tell bullish engulfing from bearish engulfing?
options: Check which direction (up or down) the larger, engulfing candle closed.
screens.explanation: The engulfing candle's direction (up vs down) names the pattern.

screens.question: A marubozu is identified mainly by its [___] body and lack of wicks.
screens.explanation: A big body with almost no wick is the marubozu's defining feature.

lessons.title: Identification Drill: Speed Round
lessons.celebration: You crushed the mixed speed round!

screens.title: Mixed Charts, Fast
screens.text: A mix of everything so far. Read each chart and name what you see.

screens.question: Which candle is highlighted on the chart above?
screens.explanation: A tiny body with wicks both sides is a doji.

screens.explanation: This is a hammer — the long wick is on the bottom, not the top.

screens.question: Which candle is highlighted on the chart above?
screens.explanation: A big down candle covering the prior up candle is bearish engulfing.

screens.question: The chart above shows a marubozu — a big body with almost no wicks.
screens.explanation: Full body, no meaningful wicks — that's a marubozu.

screens.explanation: A long upper wick with a low body after a rise is a shooting star.

screens.question: Tap the spinning top on the chart.
screens.explanation: The small body with even wicks on both sides is the spinning top.

screens.question: Tap the rejection candle (long lower wick).
screens.explanation: The middle candle's long lower wick shows a rejection of the lows.

screens.question: Reading candlestick shapes quickly is a skill that improves with practice.
screens.explanation: Like any pattern recognition, speed and accuracy build with repetition.

screens.question: A rejection wick and a long wick on a hammer describe a similar underlying idea. What is it?
options: The candle has no real body.
Price never moved during the period.
Price was pushed to an extreme, then didn't hold there.
screens.explanation: Both describe a push to an extreme that then reversed before the close.

screens.question: Speed rounds like this one build [___] recognition of common shapes.
screens.explanation: Repeated practice speeds up pattern recognition.

lessons.title: What This Candle Suggests — Rejection Shapes
lessons.celebration: You can read what a rejection candle suggests!

screens.title: From Shape to Meaning
screens.text: Now go past naming — read what each chart suggests, always descriptively.

screens.question: The highlighted candle on the chart above has a long lower wick. What does it suggest, descriptively?

options.label: Price is guaranteed to rise next
options.wrong_explanation: A rejection is a clue, not a promise.

options.label: Sellers pushed price down, but buyers recovered it by the close
options.detail: A read of the lower wick

options.label: The market data is broken
options.wrong_explanation: A long wick is a normal, valid candle.

screens.explanation: A long lower wick describes a failed push down that buyers reversed.

screens.question: The highlighted candle on the chart above has a long upper wick. What does it suggest?

options.label: That volume was zero
options.wrong_explanation: Wicks show price extremes, not volume.

options.label: Buyers pushed price up, but sellers rejected it by the close
options.detail: A read of the upper wick

options.label: A guaranteed crash
options.wrong_explanation: Descriptive, not a promise.

screens.explanation: A long upper wick describes an upward push that got rejected.

screens.question: The hammer on the chart above suggests sellers stayed fully in control into the close.
screens.explanation: The body closing back near the top shows BUYERS recovered the move — not sellers staying in control.

screens.scenario: Someone reads the rejection wick on this chart as a guaranteed reversal.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Rejection wicks always mean the trend reverses.
The wick shows the exact future price.
A rejection wick is descriptive context — it doesn't guarantee the direction of the next candle.
screens.explanation: Rejection describes what happened at a level, not what happens next.

screens.question: "What a candle suggests" is always a certain, guaranteed prediction.
screens.explanation: These reads are descriptive clues, never guarantees about the future.

screens.question: Reading a rejection wick's "suggestion" means considering...
options: only the wick's exact pixel length.
what the wick implies about buyer/seller behavior that period.
screens.explanation: The suggestion is about behavior (who got rejected), not a measurement exercise.

screens.question: Moving from naming a shape to reading its suggestion adds a layer of [___].
screens.explanation: Interpreting what a shape implies goes beyond simply naming it.

screens.question: What's the difference between "naming" a candle and reading its "suggestion"?
options: Naming identifies the shape; suggestion interprets what it implies about behavior.
Suggestion is about volume, naming is about color.
They are exactly the same task.
screens.explanation: Naming is identification; suggestion is interpretation of the shape's meaning.

screens.question: A rejection wick's suggestion is read [___], not as a certainty.
screens.explanation: All single-candle suggestions in this unit stay descriptive, not certain.

lessons.title: What This Candle Suggests — In Trend Context
lessons.celebration: You can read a candle against its trend!

screens.title: The Same Shape, Different Context
screens.text: Context changes the read. The same shape after a rise vs a drop carries a different name and meaning.

screens.question: The chart above shows a hammer shape appearing after a rise. That is specifically called a...
screens.explanation: The hammer shape after an up-move is named a hanging man.

screens.question: The chart above shows a small-body, long-upper-wick candle after a drop. That is specifically called an...
screens.explanation: That shape after a down-move is an inverted hammer (the shooting star is the after-a-rise version).

screens.question: Where a candle appears in the trend can change what it's called and what it suggests.
screens.explanation: Identical shapes (hammer vs hanging man) get different names based on the preceding move.

screens.question: Why read a candle alongside the trend around it, as on the chart above?

options.label: Because it guarantees the next move
options.wrong_explanation: Context informs, it doesn't guarantee.

options.label: Because the trend never matters
options.wrong_explanation: Context is central to reading candles.

options.label: The same shape can mean different things depending on what came before it

screens.explanation: Reading a candle in context is what turns a shape into a meaningful description.

screens.question: The same candle shape can carry a different name depending on the preceding trend.
screens.explanation: Hammer vs. hanging man, and shooting star vs. inverted hammer, are exactly this kind of pair.

screens.question: Which pair of shapes shares an identical form but different context-based names?
screens.explanation: Hammer/hanging man is the classic same-shape-different-context pair.

screens.question: Reading candles "in context" means considering the trend that came [___] them.
screens.explanation: The preceding trend is the context that shapes a candle's meaning.

screens.question: An inverted hammer appears after a [___], while a shooting star appears after a rise.
screens.explanation: Same upper-wick shape, but the inverted hammer's context is a preceding decline.

screens.question: Context can change a candle's name even when its shape stays identical.
screens.explanation: Hammer/hanging man and shooting star/inverted hammer are examples of this.

lessons.title: What This Candle Suggests — Reading Momentum
lessons.celebration: You can read momentum from candle bodies!

screens.title: Bodies Tell the Momentum Story
screens.text: Big bodies suggest momentum; small bodies suggest hesitation. Read the charts for how one-sided each period was.

screens.question: The big, near-wickless candle highlighted above suggests...
options: Deep hesitation with neither side in control.
screens.explanation: A marubozu's full body reads as decisive momentum.

screens.question: The small-bodied candle with wicks on both sides above suggests...
screens.explanation: A spinning top's small body reads as indecision.

screens.template: A [__1__] body suggests stronger momentum, while a [__2__] body suggests more hesitation.
screens.explanation: Body size is a quick read of how one-sided the period was.

screens.question: The doji on the chart above suggests strong one-directional momentum.
screens.explanation: A doji's near-zero body suggests balance, not strong momentum.

screens.scenario: Someone reads a single big marubozu as a promise that momentum continues forever.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Body size has nothing to do with momentum.
A big body describes one strong period — it doesn't guarantee momentum keeps going.
screens.explanation: A decisive candle is descriptive; it doesn't lock in the future.

screens.question: Reading momentum from candle bodies is one useful, descriptive tool among several.
screens.explanation: Body-size reading is one piece of a broader chart-reading toolkit.

screens.question: A series of large bodies in the same direction would suggest...
screens.explanation: Repeated large bodies in one direction reflect ongoing momentum.

screens.question: Reading momentum from bodies is a [___] read, not a guaranteed forecast.
screens.explanation: Like other candle reads in this unit, it's descriptive context, not certainty.

screens.question: Momentum reading pairs body size with the [___] of the move.
screens.explanation: Body size shows how one-sided the move was; direction shows which way.

screens.question: A series of small bodies would most likely suggest...
screens.explanation: Small bodies repeated over time suggest continued hesitation, not strong momentum.

lessons.title: Mixed Candle Recognition — Round One
lessons.celebration: You can read any single candle in context!

screens.title: Put It All Together
screens.text: A full mix — name the shape and read what it suggests.

screens.question: Which candle is highlighted on the chart above?
options: Hanging man — hammer shape after a rise.
Inverted hammer — upper wick after a drop.
screens.explanation: A small body up top with a long lower wick after a rise is a hanging man.

screens.question: Which pattern is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: A larger up candle covering the prior down candle is bullish engulfing.

screens.question: The highlighted doji on the chart above is best read as...

options.label: A guaranteed top
options.wrong_explanation: A doji doesn't guarantee a turn.

options.label: Proof of a data error
options.wrong_explanation: A doji is a valid candle.

options.label: A balanced period with neither side in control

screens.explanation: A doji describes balance, nothing more on its own.

screens.question: The chart above shows a hammer (long lower wick, body up top).
screens.explanation: That's the hammer shape.

screens.question: Match each shape to its one-line read.
screens.explanation: Naming the shape and reading it are two halves of the same skill.

screens.question: Combining shape recognition with contextual reading is more useful than either alone.
screens.explanation: Naming the shape and reading its context together give the fullest picture.

screens.question: Which skill does this lesson combine?
options: Only interpreting, without identifying any shape.
Only naming shapes, with no interpretation.
Naming a candle shape and reading what it suggests.
screens.explanation: This lesson explicitly combines identification with interpretation.

screens.question: Round One mixes recognition with [___] to build a fuller reading skill.
screens.explanation: Interpretation alongside recognition is the point of this mixed round.

screens.question: "Round One" is meant to check both shape [___] and contextual reading together.
screens.explanation: This lesson combines identification with interpretation, as the title suggests.

screens.question: Reviewing mixed candles helps reinforce skills from earlier in the unit.
screens.explanation: Mixed review rounds reinforce and test everything taught so far.

lessons.title: Mixed Candle Recognition — Round Two
lessons.celebration: You've mastered reading single candles!

screens.title: Final Recognition Round
screens.text: Last set — read each chart and lock in the skill.

screens.question: Which candle is highlighted on the chart above?
options: Hanging man — long lower wick after a rise.
Inverted hammer — long upper wick, small low body, after a drop.
screens.explanation: A long upper wick with a small low body after a decline is an inverted hammer.

screens.question: The chart above shows a bullish engulfing.
screens.explanation: A big DOWN candle engulfing an up candle is bearish engulfing.

screens.question: Which candle is highlighted on the chart above?
options: Spinning top — small body, even wicks.
screens.explanation: A small body centered between two wicks is a spinning top.

screens.question: Reading the shooting star on the chart above, the safe, descriptive takeaway is...

options.label: The candle shows trading volume
options.wrong_explanation: Wicks show price extremes, not volume.

options.label: Price will definitely fall now
options.wrong_explanation: Descriptive, not a promise.

options.label: An upward push was rejected by the close — useful context

screens.explanation: The shooting star describes a rejected push up — context, not a guarantee.

screens.scenario: Someone names every candle correctly but never once looks at the surrounding chart.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Naming candles is the only thing that ever matters.
Candles are read alongside the surrounding trend and levels, not in total isolation.
The surrounding chart should always be ignored.
screens.explanation: Context from the surrounding chart is part of reading any single candle well.

screens.question: This final round is meant to lock in both shape recognition and context reading.
screens.explanation: It's the capstone drill combining everything covered in this unit.

screens.question: What is the single most important habit this unit has emphasized?
options: Reading candles together with their surrounding context.
screens.explanation: Context-aware reading has been the throughline of the whole unit.

screens.question: Completing this unit means you can both name a shape and read its [___].
screens.explanation: Both identification and interpretation are the two halves of this unit's skill.

screens.question: Completing this final round means you can recognize shapes [___] read their context.
screens.explanation: The unit's goal is combining recognition with contextual reading, not choosing one.

screens.question: What comes next after mastering single-candle reading?
options: Applying this skill to multi-candle patterns and levels.
screens.explanation: Single-candle reading is a foundation for reading multi-candle patterns and levels next.

lessons.title: Market Orders (Deep Dive)
lessons.celebration: You understand market orders in depth!

screens.title: Prioritizing Speed
screens.text: A market order executes immediately at the best currently available price — a deeper look at the order type introduced back in Unit 1.

screens.question: A market order guarantees a specific, pre-chosen execution price.
screens.explanation: A market order executes at the best available price at that moment, not a chosen one.

screens.question: A market order prioritizes [___] of execution above all else.
screens.explanation: Speed is the defining trade-off a market order makes.

screens.question: Why might a market order fill at a slightly different price than the last quote you saw?
options: Price can shift in the brief moment between placing and executing the order.
Market orders always execute exactly one minute later.
Market orders are only valid on weekends.
screens.explanation: Prices can move quickly, so the fill may differ slightly from what was last displayed.

screens.question: Match the order concern to its relevance to market orders.
pairs: The main priority of a market order
Not guaranteed with a market order
Affects how much the fill price may differ from the last quote
screens.explanation: These concepts together explain how market orders behave in practice.

screens.template: In a fast-moving, [__1__] liquidity market, a market order's fill price may differ [__2__] from the last quote.
screens.explanation: Thinner liquidity can mean bigger gaps between the last quote and the actual fill.

screens.question: What happens step by step with a market order:
items: The order is submitted
It matches against the best currently available price
It executes without waiting for a specific level
Confirmation of the fill is received
correct_order: The order is submitted
It matches against the best currently available price
It executes without waiting for a specific level
Confirmation of the fill is received
screens.explanation: Market orders are built for immediate execution, not price precision.

screens.question: When might a market order's fill differ most from the last displayed price?

options.label: Only on public holidays
options.wrong_explanation: Holiday scheduling isn't what drives this gap.

options.label: In a fast-moving or thin-liquidity market
options.detail: Price can shift quickly with fewer participants

options.label: In a very calm, highly liquid market
options.wrong_explanation: Calm, liquid markets tend to have smaller gaps between quote and fill.

screens.explanation: Fast-moving or thin markets are where the gap between expected and actual fill price tends to be largest.

screens.scenario: Someone is surprised their market order filled at a noticeably different price during a very fast-moving moment.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: The order must have been placed incorrectly.
Market orders prioritize speed over exact price, so some difference is expected in fast conditions.
Market orders should never be used under any circumstances.
screens.explanation: This is a normal trade-off of the order type, not evidence of an error.

screens.question: Once submitted, a market order typically executes [___] rather than waiting.
screens.explanation: Immediate execution is the whole point of a market order.

screens.question: A market order can be used to both buy and sell.
screens.explanation: Market orders apply to both buying and selling; speed of execution is the shared trait.

lessons.title: Limit Orders (Deep Dive)
lessons.celebration: You understand limit orders in depth!

screens.title: Prioritizing Price
screens.text: A limit order only executes at your chosen price or better — trading execution certainty for price control.

screens.question: A limit order is guaranteed to execute immediately once placed.
screens.explanation: A limit order only executes if the market reaches your specified price — it may never fill.

screens.question: A limit order to buy will only execute at your set price or [___].
screens.explanation: A buy limit order fills at your specified price or better (lower).

screens.question: What is the main trade-off of using a limit order?
options: You gain price control but risk the order never filling.
There is no trade-off at all.
You gain guaranteed execution but lose all price control.
screens.explanation: Limit orders trade execution certainty for a chosen price level.

screens.question: Match the order type to its execution behavior.
pairs: Fills at your price or lower
Fills at your price or higher
Fills immediately at the best available price
screens.explanation: Reviewing how each order type behaves once triggered.

screens.template: A [__1__] order may never fill, while a [__2__] order fills almost immediately.
screens.explanation: This is the central speed-versus-price trade-off between the two order types.

screens.question: What happens step by step with a limit order:
items: The order is submitted with a specific price
It waits until the market reaches that price (or better)
If reached, it executes at that price or better
If never reached, it remains unfilled
correct_order: The order is submitted with a specific price
It waits until the market reaches that price (or better)
If reached, it executes at that price or better
If never reached, it remains unfilled
screens.explanation: A limit order is patient by design, unlike a market order.

screens.question: Which best describes a limit order that never fills?

options.label: Limit orders are broken and unreliable
options.wrong_explanation: This is normal, expected order behavior.

options.label: The market simply never reached the specified price
The order was corrupted by the platform
options.wrong_explanation: An unfilled limit order is usually just a matter of price never being reached.

screens.explanation: An unfilled limit order most commonly just reflects price never reaching that level.

screens.scenario: Someone is frustrated that their limit order didn't fill even though price came close to their level.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Limit orders should always be replaced with market orders.
"Close" isn't the same as reaching the exact specified price — the order was working as designed.
screens.explanation: A limit order requires the exact specified price (or better) to be reached, not just approached.

screens.question: A sell limit order will only execute at your set price or [___].
screens.explanation: A sell limit order fills at your specified price or better (higher).

screens.question: A limit order can remain unfilled indefinitely if price never reaches it.
screens.explanation: Without a time limit, a limit order simply waits until price reaches the specified level (or is cancelled).

lessons.title: Stop-Loss Orders
lessons.celebration: You understand stop-loss orders!

screens.title: A Planned Exit
screens.text: A stop-loss order triggers a trade once price reaches a specified level, commonly used to define risk in advance.

screens.question: A stop-loss order exists specifically to guarantee a profit.
screens.explanation: A stop-loss is commonly used to limit potential losses, not to guarantee profit.

screens.question: An order that triggers a sale once price falls to a specified level is called a [___] order.
screens.explanation: "Stop-loss" is the standard term for this kind of risk-defining order.

screens.question: Why might someone place a stop-loss order in advance?
options: To define, ahead of time, the price at which they'd exit if the position moves against them.
To guarantee the exact fill price no matter what.
To prevent the market from ever moving against them.
screens.explanation: A stop-loss is a plan set in advance — it defines a level, not a guaranteed price or outcome.

screens.question: Match the order concept to its description.
pairs: Triggers an exit once a specific price level is reached
Triggers an exit once a specific favorable price level is reached
How a triggered stop typically then executes
screens.explanation: These three concepts are commonly compared together as planning tools.

screens.template: A stop-loss order is often described as a way to define [__1__] in advance, not to guarantee a specific [__2__].
screens.explanation: Once triggered, a stop-loss commonly behaves like a market order, so the final fill price isn't guaranteed.

screens.question: A simple way to think through setting a stop-loss level:
items: Decide on a price level that would change your view of the position
Set that level as your stop-loss
If price reaches it, the order triggers
The resulting exit executes based on available market prices
correct_order: Decide on a price level that would change your view of the position
Set that level as your stop-loss
If price reaches it, the order triggers
The resulting exit executes based on available market prices
screens.explanation: This describes the mechanical process, without implying any particular outcome.

screens.question: Which best describes what a stop-loss order is used for, conceptually?

options.label: Defining a price level in advance, as part of a risk plan
Guaranteeing you will never lose money
options.wrong_explanation: A stop-loss limits how a plan unfolds; it doesn't guarantee outcomes.

options.label: Guaranteeing the exact same fill price every time
options.wrong_explanation: Once triggered, actual fill price can vary depending on market conditions.

screens.explanation: A stop-loss order is a planning tool, not a guarantee of outcome or price.

screens.scenario: Someone believes setting a stop-loss means they can never lose more than expected, no matter what.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should have avoided using any stop-loss at all.
They should have only used a stop-loss on weekends.
Fast-moving markets can sometimes fill a triggered stop-loss at a worse price than expected — it isn't an absolute guarantee.
screens.explanation: A stop-loss defines an intended exit level, but the exact executed price can still vary in fast-moving conditions.

screens.question: A stop-loss is commonly placed at a level that would [___] the original trade idea.
screens.explanation: A stop-loss is commonly tied to the point where the reasoning for the trade no longer holds.

screens.question: Once triggered, a basic stop-loss order commonly behaves like a market order.
screens.explanation: A triggered stop typically executes at the best available price, like a market order.

lessons.title: Take-Profit Orders
lessons.celebration: You understand take-profit orders!

screens.title: A Planned Exit on the Upside
screens.text: A take-profit order triggers an exit once price reaches a specified favorable level, commonly used to lock in a planned target in advance.

screens.question: A take-profit order is the same thing as a stop-loss order.
screens.explanation: A take-profit targets a favorable exit level; a stop-loss targets an unfavorable one.

screens.question: An order set to exit once price reaches a favorable target is called a [___] order.
screens.explanation: "Take-profit" describes exiting at a pre-planned favorable level.

screens.question: Why might someone set a take-profit level in advance?
options: To define, ahead of time, a target price at which they'd be satisfied exiting.
To prevent any further price movement from happening.
To guarantee the position will always reach that price.
screens.explanation: A take-profit is a plan set in advance — it defines a target, not a guaranteed outcome.

screens.question: Match the order type to its general purpose.
pairs: Plans an exit at a favorable target level
Plans an exit at an unfavorable level, to limit loss
Define a full risk/reward plan for a position
screens.explanation: These two order types are commonly used together to bracket a planned trade.

screens.template: A take-profit order defines a [__1__] exit level, while a stop-loss defines an [__2__] one.
screens.explanation: These two orders bracket the planned range of outcomes for a position.

screens.question: A simple way to think through setting a take-profit level:
items: Decide on a price level that would represent a satisfying outcome
Set that level as your take-profit
If price reaches it, the order triggers
The position exits based on that plan
correct_order: Decide on a price level that would represent a satisfying outcome
Set that level as your take-profit
If price reaches it, the order triggers
The position exits based on that plan
screens.explanation: This describes the mechanical process, without guaranteeing that price will reach it.

screens.question: Which best describes what a take-profit order is used for?

options.label: Guaranteeing that price will always reach that level
options.wrong_explanation: Setting a target doesn't guarantee price gets there.

options.label: Preventing any losses from ever occurring
options.wrong_explanation: A take-profit addresses the upside target, not downside risk.

options.label: Defining a favorable target level in advance, as part of a plan

screens.explanation: A take-profit order is a planning tool for a target, not a guarantee that price reaches it.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes setting a take-profit guarantees price will eventually reach that level.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should set an even higher take-profit level instead.
They should remove all take-profit orders from now on.
Setting a target doesn't guarantee price will ever reach it — the order simply waits until (and unless) it does.
screens.explanation: A take-profit order defines an intended target; it doesn't guarantee that target will be reached.

screens.question: A take-profit order is commonly placed at a level considered a [___] outcome.
screens.explanation: The take-profit level represents a planned, satisfying exit point.

screens.question: A take-profit and a stop-loss can be used together on the same position.
screens.explanation: Using both together is a common way to bracket a planned trade's range of outcomes.

lessons.title: Stop-Limit Orders
lessons.celebration: You understand stop-limit orders!

screens.title: Combining Stop and Limit
screens.text: A stop-limit order combines a trigger price with a limit price, adding price control at the cost of a chance it may not fill.

screens.question: A stop-limit order guarantees execution once the stop price is reached.
screens.explanation: Once triggered, a stop-limit becomes a limit order, which may not fill if price moves past the limit price too quickly.

screens.question: A stop-limit order combines a trigger price with a specified [___] price.
screens.explanation: The "limit" part adds price control once the stop is triggered.

screens.question: What happens once a stop-limit order's trigger price is reached?
options: It becomes a guaranteed, immediate market order.
It becomes a limit order at the specified limit price.
screens.explanation: A stop-limit order converts into a limit order once triggered, not a market order.

screens.question: Match the order type to what it becomes once triggered.
pairs: Becomes a limit order at the specified limit price
Was already a limit order from the start
screens.explanation: This distinction is what separates a stop-limit from a basic stop order.

screens.template: A stop-limit order adds [__1__] control, but with the risk of not [__2__] if price moves too fast.
screens.explanation: The trade-off is price precision versus a chance of no execution at all.

screens.question: What happens step by step with a stop-limit order:
items: The stop price is reached, triggering the order
It converts into a limit order at your specified limit price
If the market reaches that limit price, it fills
If not, it may remain unfilled
correct_order: The stop price is reached, triggering the order
It converts into a limit order at your specified limit price
If the market reaches that limit price, it fills
If not, it may remain unfilled
screens.explanation: This shows how a stop-limit order differs from a plain stop order that becomes a market order.

screens.question: Which best describes the main risk of a stop-limit order compared to a basic stop order?

options.label: It always fills instantly regardless of price movement
options.wrong_explanation: That describes a basic stop order becoming a market order, not a stop-limit.

options.label: It guarantees a better price than a market order every time
options.wrong_explanation: There's no such guarantee; it may simply not fill.

options.label: It may not fill at all if price moves quickly past the limit price
options.detail: Trading execution certainty for price control

screens.explanation: The added price control comes with the risk of the order not filling in a fast move.

screens.scenario: Someone is confused why their stop-limit order didn't fill during a very fast price drop.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: The platform must have a bug.
Stop-limit orders always behave exactly like market orders.
If price moved past the limit price too quickly, the order can remain unfilled — that's a known trade-off of this order type.
screens.explanation: A fast move past the limit price is a well-known way a stop-limit order can fail to fill.

screens.question: Once a stop-limit's trigger price is hit, it converts into a [___] order.
screens.explanation: The defining feature of a stop-limit is converting into a limit order once triggered.

screens.question: A stop-limit order guarantees a fill, just like a market order does.
screens.explanation: Unlike a market order, a stop-limit may not fill if price moves past the limit price too fast.

lessons.title: Slippage
lessons.celebration: You understand slippage!

screens.title: The Gap Between Expected and Actual
screens.text: Slippage describes the difference between the price you expected and the price you actually got.

screens.question: Slippage means you always get exactly the price you expected.
screens.explanation: Slippage specifically refers to getting a different price than expected, usually during fast price movement.

screens.question: The difference between the expected price and the actual executed price is called [___].
screens.explanation: "Slippage" is the standard term for this gap.

screens.question: Why does slippage tend to increase during fast-moving markets?
options: Prices can change quickly between when an order is placed and when it executes.
Charts stop updating during fast moves.
Fees are automatically higher on weekends.
screens.explanation: Rapid price movement is a common reason execution price can differ from the expected price.

screens.question: Match the condition to its typical effect on slippage.
screens.explanation: These conditions are commonly linked to how much slippage tends to occur.

screens.template: Ignoring slippage can make a trading plan look [__1__] on paper than it performs in [__2__].
screens.explanation: Slippage is a real-world cost that's easy to overlook when reviewing a plan only on paper.

screens.question: A simple way to account for slippage when reviewing a trade idea:
items: Note the expected entry and exit price
Consider potential slippage during fast moves
Compare the more realistic total cost to the original plan
Adjust expectations accordingly
correct_order: Note the expected entry and exit price
Consider potential slippage during fast moves
Compare the more realistic total cost to the original plan
Adjust expectations accordingly
screens.explanation: This gives a more complete, honest picture than looking at expected prices alone.

screens.question: Which best describes when slippage is likely to be largest?

options.label: Only during scheduled maintenance windows
options.wrong_explanation: Maintenance windows aren't what drives slippage.

options.label: During calm, highly liquid conditions
options.wrong_explanation: Calm, liquid conditions tend to have smaller slippage.

options.label: During fast-moving, low-liquidity conditions
options.detail: Bigger, quicker price changes with fewer participants

screens.explanation: Fast-moving, thin markets are where the gap between expected and actual price tends to be largest.

screens.scenario: Someone calculates a trading plan's results using only the exact prices shown on a chart, ignoring slippage entirely.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should only look at longer wicks.
They should use an even older chart instead.
Ignoring slippage makes a plan look better on paper than it would likely perform in practice.
screens.explanation: A realistic picture accounts for costs like slippage beyond just the chart's displayed prices.

screens.question: Slippage tends to be [___] in calm, liquid markets.
screens.explanation: Calmer, more liquid conditions are commonly linked to smaller slippage.

screens.question: Slippage can occur on both market and other order types once triggered.
screens.explanation: Any order that ends up executing like a market order can experience slippage.

lessons.title: Why Execution Differs From Chart Price
lessons.celebration: You understand why real fills can differ from the chart!

screens.title: The Chart Isn't the Whole Story
screens.text: Several factors — spread, slippage, and order type — can all cause your actual execution price to differ from what a chart displays.

screens.question: The price shown on a chart always exactly matches every trader's actual execution price.
screens.explanation: Spread, slippage, and order type can all cause real execution to differ from the displayed chart price.

screens.question: The gap between bid and ask is one commonly cited reason execution can differ from the [___] chart price.
screens.explanation: The displayed "last price" on a chart isn't necessarily the exact bid or ask you'd transact at.

screens.question: Which of these commonly contributes to execution differing from the chart price?
options: The number of indicators displayed on screen.
Bid/ask spread, slippage, and the type of order used.
screens.explanation: These three factors are commonly cited reasons real fills can differ from a displayed price.

screens.question: Match the factor to how it can affect execution.
pairs: Bid and ask differ from the single "last price" shown
Price can shift between order placement and execution
Market vs. limit orders behave differently around a specific price
screens.explanation: Each of these factors contributes a different piece of the gap between chart and execution.

screens.template: Combining [__1__], [__2__], and order type together explains most differences between chart price and actual fills.
screens.explanation: These three factors together commonly explain most of the gap.

screens.question: A simple way to set realistic expectations before placing an order:
items: Note the current bid/ask spread
Consider potential slippage given current volatility/liquidity
Consider how the chosen order type will behave
Expect some difference from the exact displayed chart price
correct_order: Note the current bid/ask spread
Consider potential slippage given current volatility/liquidity
Consider how the chosen order type will behave
Expect some difference from the exact displayed chart price
screens.explanation: This builds a habit of realistic expectations rather than assuming an exact match.

screens.question: Which best explains why a market order's fill might differ from the "last price" on a chart?

options.label: Spread and potential slippage between placing and executing the order
The chart is always inaccurate and unreliable
options.wrong_explanation: Charts are generally accurate; small execution gaps are a separate, normal phenomenon.

options.label: Market orders never actually execute at all
options.wrong_explanation: Market orders do execute — just not always at the exact last displayed price.

screens.explanation: Spread and slippage together are the most commonly cited reasons for this gap.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes any difference between chart price and their actual fill means the platform cheated them.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should stop using charts entirely.
They should assume all trading platforms are identical in this regard.
Small differences between chart price and fills are commonly explained by spread, slippage, and order type — not platform wrongdoing.
screens.explanation: These small gaps are a normal, well-understood part of how markets and order types work.

screens.question: Order type is one of [___] factors that can explain a gap between chart price and fill price.
screens.explanation: Spread, slippage, and order type together are commonly cited as the reasons for this gap.

screens.question: A limit order and a market order can behave differently around the very same price level.
screens.explanation: A market order fills immediately regardless of exact price, while a limit order waits for a specific level.

lessons.title: Orders & Execution Review
lessons.celebration: You've completed the Orders & Execution unit!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of the order types and execution concepts from this unit.

screens.question: Every order type in this unit guarantees a specific outcome once placed.
screens.explanation: Each order type has its own trade-offs; none guarantees a specific price or fill with certainty.

screens.question: The order type that prioritizes speed over price is the [___] order.
screens.explanation: A market order specifically prioritizes fast execution over a chosen price.

screens.question: What do market, limit, stop-loss, take-profit, and stop-limit orders all have in common?
options: They're all tools for defining how and when a trade executes, each with its own trade-offs.
They only apply to one specific asset class.
They all guarantee execution at the exact price you want.
screens.explanation: Each order type is a tool with a distinct trade-off, not a guarantee.

screens.question: Match the order type to its primary purpose.
pairs: Immediate execution at the best available price
Execution only at a chosen price or better
Planning an exit level in advance
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the core order types from this unit.

screens.template: Reading order types well means understanding their [__1__], not expecting a [__2__] outcome from any of them.
screens.explanation: Each order type balances speed, price control, and risk differently — none is a guarantee.

screens.question: The general path this unit followed:
items: Learn the basic trade-off between market and limit orders
Learn about stop-loss, take-profit, and stop-limit orders
Learn about slippage and why real fills can differ from the chart
Combine all of it into a realistic view of execution
correct_order: Learn the basic trade-off between market and limit orders
Learn about stop-loss, take-profit, and stop-limit orders
Learn about slippage and why real fills can differ from the chart
Combine all of it into a realistic view of execution
screens.explanation: Each lesson built on the one before it toward a fuller understanding of execution mechanics.

screens.question: Which best summarizes the overall theme of this unit?

options.label: Order types are tools with trade-offs, not guarantees of a specific outcome
Order types don't matter and can be chosen at random
options.wrong_explanation: Choosing the right order type for the situation does matter.

options.label: Every order type guarantees an exact, predictable result
options.wrong_explanation: This directly contradicts what every lesson covered.

screens.explanation: This balanced view has been the throughline of every lesson in this unit.

screens.scenario: Someone finishes this unit and assumes there's one single "best" order type to use in every situation.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should only ever use limit orders from now on.
They should only ever use market orders from now on.
Different order types suit different situations — there's no single type that's best in every case.
screens.explanation: This unit covered several order types precisely because each fits different situations and priorities.

screens.question: This unit's order types each balance speed, price control, and [___] differently.
screens.explanation: Speed, price control, and risk are the three dimensions each order type trades off.

screens.question: Knowing multiple order types lets you choose the one that fits a given situation.
screens.explanation: Different situations call for different trade-offs, which is why multiple order types exist.

lessons.title: Uptrend Basics
lessons.celebration: You understand uptrends!

screens.title: Climbing Step by Step
screens.text: An uptrend is commonly described as a series of higher swing highs and higher swing lows.

screens.question: An uptrend is commonly described as higher swing highs and higher swing lows over time.
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive definition of an uptrend's structure.

screens.question: In an uptrend, each pullback often finds a [___] low than the one before.
screens.explanation: Higher lows stepping up is part of the classic uptrend description.

screens.question: What would commonly lead a chart reader to classify a chart as an uptrend?
options: A single green candle appearing anywhere on the chart.
The asset's name containing a positive-sounding word.
A pattern of higher swing highs and higher swing lows.
screens.explanation: Classification is based on the pattern of swings, not one candle or the name.

screens.question: Match the trend feature to its role in an uptrend.
pairs: Each rally reaches further than the last
Each pullback holds above the prior low
screens.explanation: These features together build the descriptive picture of an uptrend.

screens.template: An uptrend is a [__1__] label describing a pattern that has already [__2__] happened.
screens.explanation: Trend labels describe the past and present pattern, not a guaranteed future.

screens.question: A simple way to classify a chart as an uptrend:
items: Identify the recent sequence of swing highs and lows
Compare each swing to the one before it
Confirm both highs and lows are generally rising
Assign the "uptrend" label if so
correct_order: Identify the recent sequence of swing highs and lows
Compare each swing to the one before it
Confirm both highs and lows are generally rising
Assign the "uptrend" label if so
screens.explanation: This turns raw swing points into a simple, consistent classification process.

screens.question: Which best describes what "uptrend" means as a term?

options.label: A specific single candlestick shape
options.wrong_explanation: Trend describes multiple candles together, not one shape.

options.label: A description of a pattern of rising swing highs and lows
A guarantee that price will keep rising forever
options.wrong_explanation: A trend describes the past pattern, not a certain future.

screens.explanation: "Uptrend" is a useful descriptive shorthand, not a promise about what happens next.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a chart "can't" be in an uptrend just because one single candle closed red.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should have ignored the red candle's existence entirely.
One candle within an overall uptrend doesn't change the broader classification by itself.
They should have switched to a totally different asset.
screens.explanation: Trend classification is based on the broader swing pattern, not any single candle.

screens.question: Both the highs and the lows in an uptrend generally move [___] together.
screens.explanation: Both swing highs and swing lows rising together is the defining structure.

screens.question: A single lower low automatically disqualifies an otherwise clear uptrend.
screens.explanation: One isolated swing doesn't override the broader pattern; classification looks at the overall sequence.

screens.title: Stepping Down
screens.text: A downtrend is commonly described as a series of lower swing highs and lower swing lows.

screens.question: A downtrend is commonly described as lower swing highs and lower swing lows over time.
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive definition of a downtrend's structure.

screens.question: In a downtrend, each rally often reaches a [___] high than the one before.
screens.explanation: Lower highs stepping down is part of the classic downtrend description.

screens.question: What would commonly lead a chart reader to classify a chart as a downtrend?
options: The asset's name containing a negative-sounding word.
A pattern of lower swing highs and lower swing lows.
A single red candle appearing anywhere on the chart.
screens.explanation: Classification is based on the pattern of swings, not one candle or the name.

screens.question: Match the trend feature to its role in a downtrend.
pairs: Each decline reaches further than the last
Each rally fails to reach the prior high
screens.explanation: These features together build the descriptive picture of a downtrend.

screens.explanation: Trend labels describe the past and present, not a certain future.

options: One candle within an overall downtrend doesn't change the broader classification by itself.
They should have switched to a totally different asset.
They should have ignored the green candle's existence entirely.
screens.explanation: Trend classification is based on the broader swing pattern, not any single candle.

screens.question: Both the highs and the lows in a downtrend generally move [___] together.
screens.explanation: Both swing highs and swing lows falling together is the defining structure.

screens.question: A single higher high automatically disqualifies an otherwise clear downtrend.
screens.explanation: One isolated swing doesn't override the broader pattern; classification looks at the overall sequence.

lessons.title: Sideways Markets
lessons.celebration: You can spot sideways price action!

screens.title: Going Nowhere (For Now)
screens.text: A sideways market bounces between a rough high and low without a clear overall direction.

screens.question: A sideways market shows a clear upward direction.
screens.explanation: A sideways market describes a lack of clear direction, bouncing within a band instead.

screens.question: Price moving back and forth between a rough ceiling and floor is often called a [___].
screens.explanation: "Range" (or sideways/consolidation) describes this kind of bounded movement.

screens.question: What generally characterizes a sideways market?
options: Swing highs and lows staying within a similar band over time.
Swing highs and lows both rising steadily.
Swing highs and lows both falling steadily.
screens.explanation: A lack of clear directional progress in the swings is the hallmark of sideways action.

screens.question: Match the market phase to its swing description.
pairs: Swing highs and lows both rising
Swing highs and lows both falling
Swing highs and lows staying roughly similar
screens.explanation: Comparing all three side by side highlights what makes sideways distinct.

screens.template: During a range, price tends to stay between a rough [__1__] and a rough [__2__].
screens.explanation: This floor/ceiling description matches the earlier support/resistance concept.

screens.question: A simple way to identify a sideways market:
items: Look for a period without clear higher highs or lower lows
Note the rough high and low it's bouncing between
Confirm price has touched each side more than once
Label it as sideways/range for that period
correct_order: Look for a period without clear higher highs or lower lows
Note the rough high and low it's bouncing between
Confirm price has touched each side more than once
Label it as sideways/range for that period
screens.explanation: Multiple touches on both sides is what distinguishes a range from a brief pause.

screens.question: Which best describes a chart currently moving sideways?

options.label: Falling to zero without pause
options.wrong_explanation: That would be an extreme downtrend, not sideways action.

options.label: Making new all-time highs every single candle
options.wrong_explanation: That would describe a strong uptrend, not sideways action.

options.label: Bouncing between a rough high and low without a clear direction
options.detail: The standard description of sideways action

screens.explanation: Sideways action specifically describes bounded, directionless movement.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a sideways market will stay sideways forever.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should have widened their definition of the range instead.
They should have only looked at a shorter timeframe.
Sideways periods are commonly followed by a move in one direction or another — they don't last forever.
screens.explanation: Treating any market phase as permanent overstates what is really just a temporary description.

screens.question: A sideways market is sometimes also called a [___].
screens.explanation: "Range" is a common alternate term for sideways price action.

screens.question: A sideways market can eventually break into either an uptrend or a downtrend.
screens.explanation: Ranges are commonly described as temporary, eventually resolving in one direction or another.

lessons.title: Higher Highs & Higher Lows
lessons.celebration: You can spot the building blocks of an uptrend!

screens.title: The Uptrend's Signature
screens.text: "Higher highs and higher lows" is the specific swing pattern behind every uptrend classification.

screens.question: "Higher highs and higher lows" describes the swing pattern behind an uptrend.
screens.explanation: This phrase is the standard descriptive shorthand for uptrend structure.

screens.question: A swing high that is higher than the previous swing high is called a [___] high.
screens.explanation: "Higher high" specifically means it exceeds the prior swing high.

screens.question: Why does a rising sequence of swing lows matter for an uptrend?
options: It shows the asset is about to be delisted.
It shows pullbacks are holding at progressively higher levels.
It has no relationship to trend classification.
screens.explanation: Rising swing lows are part of the defining structure of an uptrend.

screens.question: Match the swing sequence to its label.
pairs: Each low holds above the last
screens.explanation: These two sequences combined are what define uptrend structure.

screens.template: If either swing highs or swing lows stop [__1__], the uptrend structure may be starting to [__2__].
screens.explanation: A break in this rising pattern is commonly noted as an early sign structure may be shifting.

screens.question: A simple way to check for higher-highs-and-higher-lows structure:
items: Mark the recent swing highs in order
Mark the recent swing lows in order
Check that each high exceeds the last
Check that each low holds above the last
correct_order: Mark the recent swing highs in order
Mark the recent swing lows in order
Check that each high exceeds the last
Check that each low holds above the last
screens.explanation: Confirming both sequences together is what verifies uptrend structure.

screens.question: Which best describes what "higher highs and higher lows" means?

options.label: Only the lows need to rise; highs don't matter
options.wrong_explanation: Both highs and lows rising together define this structure.

options.label: Each new swing high and swing low both exceed the prior ones
Only the highs need to rise; lows don't matter
options.wrong_explanation: Both highs and lows rising together define this structure.

screens.explanation: Both sequences rising together is what the phrase specifically describes.

screens.scenario: Someone claims a chart has "higher highs and higher lows" after checking only the swing highs.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should check the swing highs twice instead.
They should ignore swing lows entirely from now on.
Confirming this structure requires checking both the swing highs AND the swing lows, not just one.
screens.explanation: Both sequences need to be checked together to properly confirm this structure.

screens.question: Which best completes an uptrend's structure alongside higher highs?
screens.explanation: Higher highs paired with higher lows together define the uptrend structure.

screens.question: Checking only swing highs is enough to confirm an uptrend.
screens.explanation: Both swing highs and swing lows need to be checked together.

lessons.title: Lower Highs & Lower Lows
lessons.celebration: You can spot the building blocks of a downtrend!

screens.title: The Downtrend's Signature
screens.text: "Lower highs and lower lows" is the specific swing pattern behind every downtrend classification.

screens.question: "Lower highs and lower lows" describes the swing pattern behind a downtrend.
screens.explanation: This phrase is the standard descriptive shorthand for downtrend structure.

screens.question: A swing low that is lower than the previous swing low is called a [___] low.
screens.explanation: "Lower low" specifically means it falls below the prior swing low.

screens.question: Why does a falling sequence of swing highs matter for a downtrend?
options: It shows the asset is about to be delisted.
It has no relationship to trend classification.
It shows rallies are failing at progressively lower levels.
screens.explanation: Falling swing highs are part of the defining structure of a downtrend.

screens.question: Match the swing sequence to its label.
pairs: Each high falls below the last
Each low falls below the last
screens.explanation: These two sequences combined are what define downtrend structure.

screens.template: If either swing highs or swing lows stop [__1__], the downtrend structure may be starting to [__2__].
screens.explanation: A break in this falling pattern is commonly noted as an early sign structure may be shifting.

screens.question: A simple way to check for lower-highs-and-lower-lows structure:
items: Mark the recent swing highs in order
Mark the recent swing lows in order
Check that each high falls below the last
Check that each low falls below the last
correct_order: Mark the recent swing highs in order
Mark the recent swing lows in order
Check that each high falls below the last
Check that each low falls below the last
screens.explanation: Confirming both sequences together is what verifies downtrend structure.

screens.question: Which best describes what "lower highs and lower lows" means?

options.label: Only the lows need to fall; highs don't matter
options.wrong_explanation: Both highs and lows falling together define this structure.

options.label: Only the highs need to fall; lows don't matter
options.wrong_explanation: Both highs and lows falling together define this structure.

options.label: Each new swing high and swing low both fall below the prior ones

screens.explanation: Both sequences falling together is what the phrase specifically describes.

screens.scenario: Someone claims a chart has "lower highs and lower lows" after checking only the swing lows.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Confirming this structure requires checking both the swing highs AND the swing lows, not just one.
They should ignore swing highs entirely from now on.
They should check the swing lows twice instead.
screens.explanation: Both sequences need to be checked together to properly confirm this structure.

screens.question: Which best completes a downtrend's structure alongside lower highs?
screens.explanation: Lower highs paired with lower lows together define the downtrend structure.

screens.question: Checking only swing lows is enough to confirm a downtrend.
screens.explanation: Both swing highs and swing lows need to be checked together.

lessons.title: Trend Strength
lessons.celebration: You can gauge how strong a trend looks!

screens.title: Steep vs. Gradual
screens.text: Trends aren't just "up" or "down" — they can look stronger or weaker depending on how steadily price is moving.

screens.question: All uptrends move at exactly the same speed and steepness.
screens.explanation: Trends can vary widely in steepness and consistency, even when sharing the same overall direction.

screens.question: A trend with large, consistent moves in one direction is often described as [___].
screens.explanation: "Strong" commonly describes a trend with consistent, sizable moves in one direction.

screens.question: What might commonly suggest a trend is weakening?
options: Swings becoming smaller or less consistent than before.
The chart changing to a different color scheme.
The asset's name being mentioned in the news.
screens.explanation: Smaller, less consistent swings are commonly read as a sign of weakening momentum.

screens.question: Match the trend description to its common reading.
pairs: Large, consistent swings in one direction
Often read as a stronger trend
Often read as a weaker or fading trend
Often read as declining trend conviction
screens.explanation: These descriptions offer a rough, non-certain way to gauge trend strength.

screens.template: Trend strength is a matter of [__1__], not a simple [__2__] label.
screens.explanation: Trends exist on a spectrum from very strong to very weak, not just "on" or "off."

screens.question: A simple way to informally gauge trend strength:
items: Compare the size of recent swings to earlier ones
Note how consistently price is moving in one direction
Note whether pullbacks are getting larger or smaller
Form a general (not certain) sense of trend strength
correct_order: Compare the size of recent swings to earlier ones
Note how consistently price is moving in one direction
Note whether pullbacks are getting larger or smaller
Form a general (not certain) sense of trend strength
screens.explanation: These comparisons together give a rough sense of how strong a trend currently looks.

screens.question: Which best describes a "weakening" trend, as commonly read?

options.label: No candles forming at all
options.wrong_explanation: A lack of candles isn't how trend strength is measured.

options.label: Swings becoming larger and more consistent
options.wrong_explanation: That would more commonly be read as a strengthening trend.

options.label: Swings becoming smaller and less consistent than before
options.detail: A commonly cited sign of fading momentum

screens.explanation: Smaller, less consistent swings are the commonly cited sign of a weakening trend.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes trend strength is either "fully strong" or "fully weak," with nothing in between.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Trend strength exists on a spectrum, not as a simple two-option label.
They should only ever describe trends as strong.
They should only ever describe trends as weak.
screens.explanation: Treating strength as binary oversimplifies what's actually a matter of degree.

screens.question: Trend strength is commonly judged by comparing swing size to what's [___] for that chart.
screens.explanation: Comparing recent swings to what's typical gives a rough sense of relative strength.

screens.question: A trend can remain in the same direction while getting weaker over time.
screens.explanation: Direction and strength are separate ideas — a trend can persist in direction while losing steam.

lessons.title: Momentum Basics
lessons.celebration: You understand basic momentum!

screens.title: How Fast, Not Just Which Way
screens.text: Momentum describes how quickly and forcefully price is moving in its current direction.

screens.question: Momentum describes how quickly and forcefully price is currently moving.
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive meaning of momentum in this context.

screens.question: A market with fast, forceful moves in one direction is often described as having strong [___].
screens.explanation: "Momentum" describes the speed and force of a current move.

screens.question: How does momentum generally differ from trend?
options: They are exactly the same concept with different names.
Momentum describes the current speed/force of movement; trend describes overall direction over time.
Momentum only applies to downtrends, never uptrends.
screens.explanation: Trend and momentum describe related but distinct ideas — direction versus speed/force.

screens.question: Match the term to its focus.
pairs: Overall direction over a period of time
Current speed and force of movement
Size and speed of price swings generally
screens.explanation: These related terms each describe a slightly different angle on price behavior.

screens.template: Momentum can [__1__] even while the overall trend direction stays the [__2__].
screens.explanation: A trend can continue in the same direction while its momentum weakens or strengthens.

screens.question: A simple way to get a rough read on current momentum:
items: Compare the size of recent candles to earlier ones
Note how quickly price is covering distance
Note whether pullbacks are shallow or deep
Form a general (not certain) sense of current momentum
correct_order: Compare the size of recent candles to earlier ones
Note how quickly price is covering distance
Note whether pullbacks are shallow or deep
Form a general (not certain) sense of current momentum
screens.explanation: These comparisons together give a rough sense of how forceful the current move looks.

screens.question: Which best describes "momentum" as used here?

options.label: A guarantee of how long a move will last
options.wrong_explanation: Momentum describes the present, not a guaranteed duration.

options.label: The exact same concept as "trend"
options.wrong_explanation: Trend describes direction; momentum describes speed/force.

options.label: The current speed and force behind a price move
options.detail: A description of intensity, not direction alone

screens.explanation: Momentum specifically describes the intensity of a move, distinct from its direction.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes strong momentum today guarantees the same strong momentum tomorrow.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should assume momentum never changes once established.
Momentum can shift day to day — strong momentum now doesn't guarantee it continues at the same intensity.
They should assume momentum can only ever increase.
screens.explanation: Momentum is a current, changeable reading, not a fixed guarantee going forward.

screens.question: Momentum is often gauged by how [___] price is covering distance.
screens.explanation: Speed of movement is central to reading momentum.

screens.question: Momentum and volatility describe the exact same thing.
screens.explanation: Momentum is about directional speed/force; volatility is about the size and speed of swings generally, regardless of direction.

lessons.title: Pullbacks
lessons.celebration: You understand pullbacks within a trend!

screens.title: A Pause, Not Necessarily a Reversal
screens.text: A pullback is a temporary move against the prevailing trend, commonly followed by a resumption of that trend — though not guaranteed.

screens.question: A pullback means the overall trend has definitely and permanently reversed.
screens.explanation: A pullback is commonly described as a temporary move against the trend, not a guaranteed permanent reversal.

screens.question: A short-term move against the prevailing trend is commonly called a [___].
screens.explanation: "Pullback" is the standard term for this kind of temporary counter-move.

screens.question: What is commonly true about a pullback within an uptrend?
options: It only happens exactly once per uptrend.
It's a temporary dip that may be followed by the uptrend resuming.
It always means the uptrend has permanently ended.
screens.explanation: Pullbacks are commonly described as temporary pauses, not confirmed permanent reversals.

screens.question: Match the term to its relationship with the trend.
pairs: A temporary move against the current trend
The prevailing trend continuing after a pullback
The trend actually changing direction for good
screens.explanation: These three terms describe different possible outcomes after a counter-move.

screens.template: A pullback is commonly described as [__1__], while a full reversal describes the trend actually [__2__].
screens.explanation: The key distinction is whether the move is a pause or a genuine change in direction.

screens.question: A simple way to think through a pullback as it happens:
items: Notice price moving against the prevailing trend
Consider it a pullback candidate, not confirmed either way
Watch whether the prior trend direction resumes afterward
Only then describe it as a pullback or a reversal, after the fact
correct_order: Notice price moving against the prevailing trend
Consider it a pullback candidate, not confirmed either way
Watch whether the prior trend direction resumes afterward
Only then describe it as a pullback or a reversal, after the fact
screens.explanation: You typically can't be certain whether it's a pullback or reversal until after it's played out.

screens.question: Which best describes how to think about a fresh counter-trend move?

options.label: It could be a temporary pullback or the start of a reversal — often unclear at first
It's always guaranteed to be a full reversal
options.wrong_explanation: Many counter-moves are just temporary pullbacks.

options.label: It's always guaranteed to be just a pullback
options.wrong_explanation: Some counter-moves do turn into full reversals.

screens.explanation: In the moment, it's often genuinely unclear which one you're seeing — that's honest uncertainty, not a flaw.

screens.scenario: Someone labels every single counter-trend move a "pullback" no matter how it later plays out.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should label every counter-move a reversal instead.
Some counter-trend moves do turn into full reversals — not every one stays a temporary pullback.
They should ignore counter-trend moves entirely.
screens.explanation: Whether something was a pullback or a reversal is really only clear in hindsight.

screens.question: Whether a counter-trend move is a pullback or reversal is often only clear in [___].
screens.explanation: You typically can't be certain which one it is until after it plays out.

screens.question: A pullback is generally smaller in scale than the trend it's occurring within.
screens.explanation: Pullbacks are commonly described as smaller, temporary counter-moves relative to the larger trend.

lessons.title: Consolidation
lessons.celebration: You understand consolidation phases!

screens.title: Catching a Breath
screens.text: Consolidation describes a pause where price moves sideways within a tighter range, often after a stronger directional move.

screens.question: Consolidation describes price moving sideways within a tighter range.
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive meaning of consolidation.

screens.question: A period of sideways movement within a tighter range is commonly called [___].
screens.explanation: "Consolidation" is the standard term for this kind of pause.

screens.question: When does consolidation commonly appear on a chart?
options: Only at the very start of any chart.
Often after a stronger directional move, as a pause.
Only immediately before a market closes.
screens.explanation: Consolidation is commonly noted as a pause following a stronger directional move.

screens.question: Match the phase to its general description.
pairs: Swings generally moving in one direction
A tighter, sideways pause, often after a stronger move
Price clearly leaving a prior range or consolidation
screens.explanation: These three phases are commonly described together as parts of a market's ongoing cycle.

screens.template: Consolidation is often described as the market [__1__], before eventually [__2__] in one direction or another.
screens.explanation: Consolidation is commonly viewed as a temporary phase that eventually resolves.

screens.question: A simple way to identify a consolidation phase:
items: Look for a tightening, sideways range following a stronger move
Note how narrow the range is compared to the prior move
Confirm price is staying within that tighter band
Watch for how it eventually resolves
correct_order: Look for a tightening, sideways range following a stronger move
Note how narrow the range is compared to the prior move
Confirm price is staying within that tighter band
Watch for how it eventually resolves
screens.explanation: Comparing the range's width to the prior move helps confirm it's consolidation rather than just noise.

screens.question: Which best describes consolidation, as commonly used?

options.label: A guarantee that price will break upward next
options.wrong_explanation: Consolidation doesn't determine which direction it resolves.

options.label: A tighter, sideways pause, often following a stronger directional move
options.detail: A temporary phase, not a permanent state

options.label: The exact same thing as a full reversal
options.wrong_explanation: Consolidation is a pause, not necessarily a reversal.

screens.explanation: Consolidation describes a temporary, tighter pause — not a certain outcome afterward.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes consolidation always resolves in the same direction as the move that preceded it.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should ignore consolidation phases entirely.
They should assume it always reverses instead.
Consolidation can resolve in either direction — it doesn't guarantee a continuation of the prior move.
screens.explanation: Which direction consolidation resolves in isn't something that can be assumed in advance.

screens.question: Consolidation is commonly described as tighter than the [___] that preceded it.
screens.explanation: A consolidation range is typically narrower than the stronger move before it.

screens.question: Consolidation can only occur after an uptrend, never after a downtrend.
screens.explanation: Consolidation can follow either an uptrend or a downtrend as a pause.

lessons.title: Break of Structure (Intro)
lessons.celebration: You understand the basics of a structure break!

screens.title: When the Pattern Changes
screens.text: A break of structure describes price breaking the established pattern of swing highs/lows, commonly noted as an early sign the trend may be shifting.

screens.question: A break of structure means price has moved against the established pattern of recent swing highs/lows.
screens.explanation: That's the core descriptive meaning of a structure break.

screens.question: Breaking the established pattern of swing highs and lows is commonly called a break of [___].
screens.explanation: "Break of structure" is the standard term for this kind of shift.

screens.question: Why do chart readers commonly pay attention to a break of structure?
options: It's commonly noted as one of the earliest signs a trend's pattern may be shifting.
It means the chart's data has become invalid.
It guarantees the trend has permanently reversed.
screens.explanation: A structure break is a commonly cited early clue, not a certainty about the future.

screens.question: Match the structure event to its description.
pairs: Higher highs and higher lows holding
A swing low breaks below the prior swing low
The new pattern continuing after the break
screens.explanation: These terms describe a possible sequence of events as structure changes.

screens.template: A break of structure is commonly read as an early [__1__], not a guaranteed [__2__].
screens.explanation: It's commonly treated as a signal worth noting, not proof of what happens next.

screens.question: A simple way to think through a possible break of structure:
items: Confirm the established swing high/low pattern beforehand
Notice a swing breaking that established pattern
Treat it as an early, not yet confirmed, signal
Watch subsequent price action for further confirmation
correct_order: Confirm the established swing high/low pattern beforehand
Notice a swing breaking that established pattern
Treat it as an early, not yet confirmed, signal
Watch subsequent price action for further confirmation
screens.explanation: Patience before fully committing to a "confirmed" break is a commonly cited habit.

screens.question: Which best describes a break of structure, as commonly used?

options.label: A completely random, meaningless event
options.wrong_explanation: It's a commonly cited, useful piece of context.

options.label: Price breaking the established pattern of recent swing highs/lows
A guarantee the trend has permanently reversed
options.wrong_explanation: It's commonly read as an early signal, not a certainty.

screens.explanation: A break of structure is a descriptive early clue, not a guaranteed outcome.

screens.scenario: Someone treats every single break of structure as a guaranteed, permanent trend reversal.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Not every break of structure leads to a lasting trend change — some fail and the prior trend resumes.
They should ignore breaks of structure entirely.
They should look for an even bigger break to be sure.
screens.explanation: A break of structure is commonly read as an early signal, not a guaranteed permanent shift.

screens.question: A break of structure is commonly treated as an early, not [___], signal.
screens.explanation: It's read as an early clue that may or may not be confirmed by what follows.

screens.question: A break of structure can fail, with the prior trend resuming afterward.
screens.explanation: Not every structure break leads to a lasting change — some fail and the prior trend continues.

Swing highs and lows staying roughly similar

screens.question: Which best describes the purpose of these classification drills?

options.label: Building a consistent, descriptive habit for reading structure

screens.question: Classifying direction requires comparing multiple [___], not a single candle.
