lessons.title: Trend & Structure Drill — Momentum and Pauses
lessons.celebration: You can classify momentum-related phases!

screens.title: Practice Round
screens.text: Practice distinguishing pullbacks, consolidation, and momentum shifts across a mixed set of charts.

screens.question: How would the middle portion of this chart most likely be described?
options: Part of an ongoing uptrend structure, not a standalone phase
screens.explanation: The middle candles here are simply steps within the broader uptrend structure shown.

screens.question: How would this chart's overall price action most likely be described?
screens.explanation: The bounded, sideways movement here matches the description of consolidation.

screens.question: A pullback and a full trend reversal are always distinguishable the moment they begin.
screens.explanation: It's often genuinely unclear at first whether a counter-move is a pullback or the start of a reversal.

screens.question: A temporary counter-trend move that's often followed by the trend resuming is called a [___].
screens.explanation: "Pullback" is the standard term for this kind of temporary move.

screens.question: Match the phase to its general description.
pairs: Temporary move against the prevailing trend
Tighter, sideways pause, often after a stronger move
Price breaking the established swing pattern
screens.explanation: A quick recap of three related but distinct phases covered in this unit.

screens.question: Which best captures how to responsibly describe an in-progress counter-trend move?

options.label: "This could be a pullback or the start of a reversal — it's not yet clear"
"This is definitely just a pullback"

options.label: "This is definitely a full reversal"

Ignoring the broader trend context misses useful information that's commonly combined with level analysis.
They should ignore resistance levels entirely instead.

lessons.title: Levels Drill — Support or Resistance?

There is no support shown in this chart

screens.question: Where is the resistance level in this chart, in relation to price?

Above, where price has struggled to close beyond
Below, where price has never traded

Price falling below the prior level
Price staying entirely within the prior range

Above current price, acting as a ceiling
Can act as the opposite type after being broken

lessons.title: What Is a Double Top?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a double top on a chart!

screens.title: Two Peaks at the Same Level
screens.text: A double top is commonly described as price rising to a level, pulling back, rising to about the same level again, then turning down — an "M" shape. It's read as a possible reversal after an up-move.

screens.question: The chart above shows two peaks stalling at about the same price. This shape is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: Two peaks at the same level forming an "M" is the double top shape.

screens.question: A double top is commonly described as forming after an up-move, at resistance.
screens.explanation: The two peaks stall at the same resistance level after price has risen into it.

screens.question: The two peaks of a double top reach roughly the [___] price level.
screens.explanation: The defining feature is two peaks at about the same level.

screens.question: Match each part of the double top to what it is.
pairs: Highs that stall at the same resistance
A pullback before the second attempt
Price failing to break higher a second time
screens.explanation: These three parts together make the "M" shape.

screens.question: What does a double top describe, on its own?

options.label: A guaranteed crash from here
options.wrong_explanation: A pattern describes; it doesn't guarantee the next move.

options.label: Price tested a level twice and failed to break above it
options.detail: A descriptive read, not a guarantee

options.label: That both peaks are green candles
options.wrong_explanation: Candle color isn't what defines the pattern.

screens.explanation: A double top describes a level tested twice and rejected — context, not certainty.

screens.scenario: Someone sees one peak and immediately calls it a "double top."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A double top needs two peaks at about the same level — a single peak isn't one yet.
The number of peaks doesn't matter for a double top.
A double top only needs a single peak to count.
screens.explanation: The pattern is defined by two peaks at a similar level, not one.

lessons.title: What Is a Double Bottom?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a double bottom on a chart!

screens.title: Two Troughs at the Same Level
screens.text: A double bottom is the mirror image: price falls to a level, bounces, falls to about the same level again, then turns up — a "W" shape, read as a possible reversal after a down-move.

screens.question: The chart above shows two troughs holding at about the same price. This shape is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: Two troughs at the same level forming a "W" is the double bottom shape.

screens.question: A double bottom is commonly described as forming after a down-move, at support.
screens.explanation: The two troughs hold at the same support level after price has fallen into it.

screens.question: The two troughs of a double bottom reach roughly the [___] price level.
screens.explanation: The defining feature is two troughs at about the same level.

screens.question: What does a double bottom describe, on its own?

options.label: A guaranteed rally from here
options.wrong_explanation: A pattern describes; it doesn't guarantee the outcome.

options.label: That the chart data is broken
options.wrong_explanation: A double bottom is a normal, valid shape.

options.label: Price tested a level twice and held above it both times

screens.explanation: A double bottom describes support tested twice and held — context, not certainty.

screens.question: The chart above shows an "M" shape.
screens.explanation: A double bottom is a "W" shape; the "M" is a double top.

screens.scenario: Someone calls the chart a double top because "it has two turning points."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Two troughs at support form a double bottom (a "W"), not a double top.
Any two turning points always make a double top.
Double tops and double bottoms are the same thing.
screens.explanation: Direction matters — troughs at support is a double bottom, peaks at resistance is a double top.

lessons.title: The Neckline
lessons.celebration: You understand the neckline!

screens.title: The Level That Confirms
screens.text: The neckline is the level at the dip of a double top (or the peak of a double bottom). The pattern is commonly said to "complete" only if price breaks that neckline.

screens.question: In a double top, the neckline sits at the [___] between the two peaks.
screens.explanation: The neckline runs along the low of the pullback between the two peaks.

screens.question: Why is the neckline important when reading a double top?
options: The neckline guarantees the direction of the next candle.
The neckline is unrelated to the pattern.
The pattern is commonly said to complete only when price breaks the neckline.
screens.explanation: Breaking the neckline is the commonly cited confirmation step, descriptively.

screens.question: A double top is commonly said to be "confirmed" the instant the second peak forms, before any neckline break.
screens.explanation: Confirmation is commonly tied to the neckline breaking, not just the second peak appearing.

screens.question: Match the pattern to where its neckline sits.
pairs: Along the dip between the two peaks
Along the bounce peak between the two troughs
The commonly cited confirmation of either pattern
screens.explanation: The neckline is the shared "confirmation level" for both patterns.

screens.question: Which best describes the neckline's role?

options.label: The exact future price target
options.wrong_explanation: The neckline is a level, not a price prediction.

options.label: A level whose break is commonly read as confirming the pattern
A guarantee the pattern will play out
options.wrong_explanation: A break is a clue, not a guarantee.

screens.explanation: The neckline is the confirmation level, described — not a certainty.

screens.scenario: Someone treats a double top as complete even though price never broke the neckline.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Without a neckline break, the pattern isn't commonly considered confirmed yet.
A double top is always complete at the first peak.
The neckline never matters for a double top.
screens.explanation: The neckline break is the commonly cited confirmation, so calling it complete early skips that step.

lessons.title: Double Top vs. Resistance Rejection
lessons.celebration: You can tell these two apart!

screens.title: One Touch or Two?
screens.text: A single rejection at resistance touches the level once. A double top touches about the same level twice, with a dip in between. Reading how many times price tested the level is the skill here.

screens.question: The chart above shows price stalling at resistance and turning down after a single touch. This is best described as...
screens.explanation: One touch of resistance is a rejection; a double top needs two touches at the same level.

screens.question: The chart above shows two peaks at the same level with a dip between them. This is best described as...
screens.explanation: Two touches of the same level, forming an "M", is a double top.

screens.question: The main difference between a single resistance rejection and a double top is how many times the level was tested.
screens.explanation: One test = rejection; two tests at the same level = double top.

screens.template: A double top tests the level [__1__], while a single rejection tests it [__2__].
screens.explanation: Counting the tests of the level is what separates the two reads.

screens.question: Reading the chart above, which description fits?

options.label: Two tests of the same resistance — a double top
A support bounce
options.wrong_explanation: This is at resistance (top), not support.

options.label: A single test of resistance
options.wrong_explanation: There are two peaks here, not one.

screens.explanation: Two peaks at the same resistance is a double top, not a single rejection.

screens.scenario: Someone labels a two-peak "M" at resistance a "single rejection."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Two peaks at the same level is a double top, not a single rejection — they undercounted the tests.
A double top and a single rejection are identical.
The number of touches never matters.
screens.explanation: The count of tests at the level is exactly what distinguishes the two.

lessons.title: Double Bottom vs. Support Bounce
lessons.celebration: You can tell these two apart!

screens.title: One Bounce or Two?
screens.text: A single support bounce touches support once. A double bottom touches about the same support twice, with a bounce in between — the "W".

screens.question: The chart above shows price dipping to support and bouncing after a single touch. This is best described as...
screens.explanation: One touch of support is a bounce; a double bottom needs two touches at the same level.

screens.question: The chart above shows two troughs at the same level with a bounce between them. This is best described as...
screens.explanation: Two touches of the same support, forming a "W", is a double bottom.

screens.question: A double bottom and a single support bounce differ mainly in how many times support was tested.
screens.explanation: One test = bounce; two tests at the same level = double bottom.

screens.template: A double bottom tests support [__1__], while a single bounce tests it [__2__].
screens.explanation: Counting the tests of support is what separates the two reads.

screens.question: Reading the chart above, which description fits?

options.label: A single support bounce
options.wrong_explanation: There are two troughs here, not one.

options.label: A resistance rejection
options.wrong_explanation: This is at support (bottom), not resistance.

options.label: Two tests of the same support — a double bottom

screens.explanation: Two troughs at the same support is a double bottom, not a single bounce.

screens.scenario: Someone calls a two-trough "W" a "single bounce."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Two troughs at the same level is a double bottom, not a single bounce — they undercounted the tests.
A double bottom and a single bounce are identical.
Counting touches never matters at support.
screens.explanation: The count of tests at support is what distinguishes the two.

lessons.title: Reading the Two Peaks
lessons.celebration: You can judge whether the peaks match!

screens.title: Are They Really Equal?
screens.text: A cleaner double top has two peaks at about the same height. If the second peak is much higher or lower, the "double" read is weaker. Judging roughly-equal highs is the skill here.

screens.question: A double top is commonly described as having two peaks at roughly the same level.
screens.explanation: Roughly-equal peaks are what make it a "double" top.

screens.question: If the second peak is much higher than the first, the double top read is...
options: Weaker — the peaks aren't really at the same level.
screens.explanation: The pattern relies on the two peaks being at about the same level.

screens.question: For a clean double top, the two peaks should be at [___] the same height.
screens.explanation: "About the same" height is the practical standard, not perfectly identical.

screens.question: The two peaks on the chart above are at about the same level. What does that support?

options.label: A cleaner double top read, since the level was tested twice at the same height
A guaranteed reversal
options.wrong_explanation: Equal peaks strengthen the read, not guarantee an outcome.

options.label: That the pattern is invalid
options.wrong_explanation: Equal peaks support the pattern, not invalidate it.

screens.explanation: Roughly-equal peaks strengthen the double top read, descriptively.

screens.question: Tap the second peak of the double top.
screens.explanation: The fourth candle is the second peak, stalling at the same resistance as the first.

screens.scenario: Someone calls it a clean double top even though the second peak is far higher than the first.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: If the second high is far above the first, the peaks aren't at the same level — it's a weaker "double" read (and may just be a breakout).
A higher second peak always makes a stronger double top.
Peak heights never matter for a double top.
screens.explanation: The "double" read depends on the two peaks being at about the same level.

lessons.title: Reading the Two Troughs
lessons.celebration: You can judge whether the troughs match!

screens.title: Are They Really Equal?
screens.text: The same idea applies to a double bottom: two troughs at about the same low. A second trough much lower weakens the "double" read.

screens.question: If the second trough is much lower than the first, the double bottom read is...
options: Weaker — the troughs aren't at the same level.
screens.explanation: The pattern relies on the two troughs being at about the same level.

screens.question: For a clean double bottom, the two troughs should be at [___] the same low.
screens.explanation: "About the same" low is the practical standard.

screens.question: Tap the second trough of the double bottom.
screens.explanation: The fourth candle is the second trough, holding at the same support as the first.

screens.question: The two troughs on the chart above hold at about the same level. What does that support?

options.label: A cleaner double bottom read, since support held twice at the same level
A guaranteed rally
options.wrong_explanation: Equal troughs strengthen the read, not guarantee it.

options.label: That the pattern is invalid
options.wrong_explanation: Equal troughs support the pattern.

screens.explanation: Roughly-equal troughs strengthen the double bottom read, descriptively.

screens.scenario: Someone calls it a clean double bottom even though the second trough is far below the first.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A lower second trough always strengthens the pattern.
If the second low is far below the first, the troughs aren't at the same level — a weaker "double" read (and may just be a breakdown).
screens.explanation: The "double" read depends on the two troughs being at about the same level.

lessons.title: When the Pattern Fails
lessons.celebration: You understand failed double patterns!

screens.title: Not Every M or W Follows Through
screens.text: Sometimes price forms two peaks but then breaks up through resistance instead of down — the double top "fails". Patterns are clues, never guarantees.

screens.question: Every double top is guaranteed to lead to a reversal down.
screens.explanation: Patterns are descriptive clues; a double top can fail if price breaks up instead.

screens.question: A double top "fails" when...
options: Price breaks up through the resistance instead of turning down.
The two peaks are at the same level.
A neckline forms between the peaks.
screens.explanation: Breaking up through the level is the opposite of the expected reversal, so the pattern fails.

screens.question: Because patterns are clues and not guarantees, a double top can still [___].
screens.explanation: Any pattern can fail — that's why it's read as a clue, not a certainty.

screens.question: Why treat a double top as a clue rather than a certainty?

options.label: Because the pattern controls the market
options.wrong_explanation: A pattern describes; it doesn't control price.

options.label: Because price can still break the level instead of reversing
Because patterns always work
options.wrong_explanation: This is exactly the overconfidence to avoid.

screens.explanation: Any pattern can fail, so it's read as a probability-shaped clue, not a guarantee.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a double top means a reversal is certain and ignores that price broke upward.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Breaking upward confirms the double top.
Price broke up through the level — the double top failed. Treating it as certain ignored that outcome.
A double top can never fail.
screens.explanation: When price breaks up instead of down, the double top has failed — patterns aren't guarantees.

lessons.title: Identification Drill: Tops vs. Bottoms
lessons.celebration: You can classify double patterns fast!

screens.title: Name the Pattern
screens.text: Read each chart and identify the double pattern (or what it actually is).

screens.explanation: Two troughs at the same support is a double bottom.

screens.explanation: The fourth candle is the second trough at support.

screens.explanation: The fourth candle is the second peak at resistance.

screens.question: The chart above shows a double bottom.
screens.explanation: This is a single support bounce (one touch), not a two-touch double bottom.

lessons.title: What the Pattern Suggests
lessons.celebration: You can read what double patterns suggest!

screens.title: From Shape to Meaning
screens.text: Read what each completed pattern suggests — always descriptively, never as a buy/sell instruction.

screens.question: A double bottom on the chart above has held support twice. Descriptively, that suggests...

options.label: Nothing can be said about the level
options.wrong_explanation: Two holds at a level is meaningful context.

options.label: A guaranteed rally
options.wrong_explanation: Descriptive, not a promise.

options.label: Sellers failed to push below the level twice — buyers defended it
options.detail: A read of the two tests

screens.explanation: Two successful defenses of support is descriptive context, not a certainty.

screens.question: A double top on the chart above has failed at resistance twice. Descriptively, that suggests...

options.label: A guaranteed crash
options.wrong_explanation: Descriptive, not a promise.

options.label: That resistance no longer exists
options.wrong_explanation: The level held twice, so it's still relevant.

options.label: Buyers failed to push above the level twice — sellers defended it
options.detail: A read of the two tests

screens.explanation: Two failed pushes above resistance is descriptive context, not a certainty.

screens.question: Reading "what a pattern suggests" is about description, not a signal to act.
screens.explanation: This whole course stays descriptive — patterns inform reading, not trade commands.

screens.question: Match each pattern to its descriptive read.
pairs: Resistance defended twice; buyers failed above it
Support defended twice; sellers failed below it
Price broke the level instead of reversing
screens.explanation: Each is a descriptive read of how the level behaved.

screens.scenario: Someone turns "a double bottom suggests buyers defended support" into "definitely buy now."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: The descriptive read and a guaranteed buy are the same thing.
That converts a descriptive read into a certainty and a trade command — the pattern is context, not a guaranteed signal.
screens.explanation: A descriptive read isn't a guaranteed signal; treating it as one overstates certainty.

lessons.title: Mixed Pattern Recognition
lessons.celebration: You can read double patterns in any context!

screens.text: A full mix — identify the pattern and read the level behavior.

A double top needs two clear peaks at about the same resistance after an up-move — not any small wiggle.

lessons.title: What Is a Head & Shoulders?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a head & shoulders on a chart!

screens.title: Three Peaks, Middle Highest
screens.text: A head & shoulders is commonly described as three peaks: a left shoulder, a higher head, then a right shoulder at about the shoulder's height. It's read as a possible reversal after an up-move.

screens.question: The chart above shows three peaks with the middle one highest. This shape is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: Three peaks with a higher middle "head" is the head & shoulders shape.

screens.question: In a head & shoulders, the middle and highest peak is called the [___].
screens.explanation: The tallest, central peak is the "head".

screens.question: A head & shoulders is commonly described as forming after an up-move.
screens.explanation: Like other reversal patterns, it appears after price has risen into it.

screens.question: Tap the head (the highest peak).
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is the head — the tallest of the three peaks.

screens.question: What does a head & shoulders describe, on its own?

options.label: A guaranteed crash
options.wrong_explanation: A pattern describes; it doesn't guarantee the move.

options.label: That the middle peak is the lowest
options.wrong_explanation: The head (middle) is the highest, not the lowest.

options.label: Three peaks with a higher middle — a possible reversal shape

screens.explanation: A head & shoulders describes a three-peak shape — context, not certainty.

screens.scenario: Someone calls a two-peak chart a "head & shoulders."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: The number of peaks doesn't matter.
Two peaks is enough for a head & shoulders.
A head & shoulders needs three peaks (with a higher middle) — two peaks is a double top.
screens.explanation: Head & shoulders is a three-peak pattern; two peaks is a double top.

lessons.title: The Three Peaks
lessons.celebration: You can name each peak of a head & shoulders!

screens.title: Left Shoulder, Head, Right Shoulder
screens.text: The three peaks each have a name: left shoulder, head (highest), and right shoulder (about the same height as the left). Reading them in order is the skill.

screens.question: Match each peak to its description.
pairs: The first peak, lower than the head
The third peak, about the left shoulder's height
screens.explanation: Naming the three peaks in order is the core of reading the pattern.

screens.question: Tap BOTH shoulders (the outer two peaks).
screens.explanation: The 2nd and 6th candles are the left and right shoulders — the outer, lower peaks.

screens.question: The right shoulder is commonly at about the [___] height as the left shoulder.
screens.explanation: Roughly-equal shoulders are part of a clean head & shoulders.

screens.question: Which peak is the tallest in a head & shoulders?
screens.explanation: The head, in the middle, is the highest of the three.

screens.question: Tap the head.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is the head — the tallest peak.

screens.scenario: Someone says the right shoulder should be much taller than the head.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: The head is the tallest; the shoulders are lower and roughly equal to each other.
The head should be the shortest peak.
The right shoulder is always the tallest.
screens.explanation: The head is the highest peak; shoulders sit lower and are roughly equal.

lessons.title: The Neckline
lessons.celebration: You understand the neckline!

screens.title: The Line Under the Pattern
screens.text: The neckline connects the two troughs between the peaks. A head & shoulders is commonly said to "complete" only when price breaks the neckline.

screens.question: Drag the line to the neckline (along the two troughs).
screens.explanation: The neckline runs along the lows between the shoulders and head.

screens.question: Why is the neckline important in a head & shoulders?
options: The pattern is commonly said to complete only when price breaks the neckline.
The neckline is unrelated to the pattern.
The neckline guarantees the next candle's direction.
screens.explanation: Breaking the neckline is the commonly cited confirmation step, descriptively.

screens.question: The neckline connects the two [___] between the peaks.
screens.explanation: The neckline runs along the lows (troughs), not the peaks.

screens.question: A head & shoulders is commonly called confirmed the moment the right shoulder forms, before any neckline break.
screens.explanation: Confirmation is commonly tied to the neckline breaking, not just the right shoulder appearing.

screens.question: Which best describes the neckline's role?

options.label: A guarantee the pattern plays out
options.wrong_explanation: A break is a clue, not a guarantee.

options.label: The exact future price target
options.wrong_explanation: The neckline is a level, not a prediction.

options.label: A level whose break is commonly read as confirming the pattern

screens.explanation: The neckline is the confirmation level — described, not a certainty.

lessons.title: Inverse Head & Shoulders
lessons.celebration: You can spot an inverse head & shoulders!

screens.title: The Upside-Down Version
screens.text: An inverse head & shoulders is the mirror image: three troughs, with the middle (head) lowest, after a down-move. It's read as a possible reversal upward.

screens.question: The chart above shows three troughs with the middle one lowest. This is commonly called an...
screens.explanation: Three troughs with a lower middle "head" is the inverse head & shoulders.

screens.question: An inverse head & shoulders commonly forms after a down-move.
screens.explanation: The inverse version appears after price has fallen into it.

screens.question: Tap the head (the lowest trough).
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is the head — the lowest of the three troughs.

screens.question: Drag the line to the neckline (along the two peaks).
screens.explanation: In an inverse head & shoulders, the neckline runs along the peaks between the troughs.

screens.question: How does an inverse head & shoulders differ from the regular one?

options.label: It has only one trough
options.wrong_explanation: It has three troughs, not one.

options.label: It's identical to the regular version
options.wrong_explanation: One is peaks-up, the other troughs-down.

options.label: It's three troughs with the lowest in the middle, after a down-move

screens.explanation: The inverse is the upside-down mirror — three troughs with a lower head.

screens.scenario: Someone calls an inverse head & shoulders a "regular head & shoulders".
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Troughs and peaks don't change the name.
The two patterns are the same thing.
This is three troughs with a lower middle (inverse), not three peaks with a higher middle.
screens.explanation: Peaks-up is the regular pattern; troughs-down is the inverse.

lessons.title: Reading Symmetry
lessons.celebration: You can judge a head & shoulders' symmetry!

screens.title: Are the Shoulders Balanced?
screens.text: A cleaner head & shoulders has two shoulders at about the same height, with the head clearly above both. Lopsided shoulders weaken the read.

screens.question: For a clean head & shoulders, the two shoulders should be...
options: At about the same height, both below the head.
screens.explanation: Roughly-equal shoulders below a clear head make the cleanest pattern.

screens.question: Tap BOTH shoulders.
screens.explanation: The 2nd and 6th candles are the two shoulders — read whether they're about equal.

screens.question: The head should be clearly [___] both shoulders.
screens.explanation: The head is the highest peak, above both shoulders.

screens.question: If the "head" is actually lower than a shoulder, the head & shoulders read is weaker (or invalid).
screens.explanation: The head must be the highest peak; if it isn't, it's not a clean head & shoulders.

screens.scenario: Someone calls it a clean head & shoulders even though the middle peak is lower than both outer peaks.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: If the middle peak isn't the highest, it isn't a head & shoulders — the head must top both shoulders.
The head can be the lowest peak.
screens.explanation: The defining feature is a head that stands above both shoulders.

lessons.title: Head & Shoulders vs. Double Top
lessons.celebration: You can tell these two apart!

screens.title: Count the Peaks
screens.text: A double top has two peaks at the same level. A head & shoulders has three peaks, with a higher middle. Counting the peaks tells them apart.

screens.question: The chart above has two peaks at the same level. This is best described as...
screens.explanation: Two equal peaks is a double top; three peaks (higher middle) would be head & shoulders.

screens.question: The chart above has three peaks with a higher middle. This is best described as...
screens.explanation: Three peaks with a taller middle is a head & shoulders.

screens.question: The main difference between a double top and a head & shoulders is the number of peaks.
screens.explanation: Two peaks = double top; three peaks (higher middle) = head & shoulders.

screens.template: A double top has [__1__] peaks; a head & shoulders has [__2__].
screens.explanation: Counting the peaks separates the two patterns.

screens.question: Reading the chart above, which fits?

options.label: No pattern at all
options.wrong_explanation: Three peaks with a higher middle is a recognizable pattern.

options.label: Two peaks — a double top
options.wrong_explanation: There are three peaks here, not two.

options.label: Three peaks with a higher middle — a head & shoulders

screens.explanation: Three peaks with a higher middle is a head & shoulders, not a double top.

screens.scenario: Someone labels a clear three-peak (higher middle) chart a "double top."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A double top and head & shoulders are identical.
Three peaks with a higher middle is a head & shoulders — they undercounted the peaks.
screens.explanation: The peak count (and the higher middle) is exactly what distinguishes them.

lessons.title: Confirmation
lessons.celebration: You understand head & shoulders confirmation!

screens.title: The Neckline Break
screens.text: A head & shoulders is commonly said to "confirm" only when price breaks the neckline after the right shoulder. Until then, it's a forming pattern, not a completed one.

screens.question: When is a head & shoulders commonly considered confirmed?
options: When price breaks the neckline after the right shoulder.
The instant the left shoulder forms.
screens.explanation: The neckline break after the right shoulder is the commonly cited confirmation.

screens.question: Before the neckline breaks, a head & shoulders is commonly described as still forming, not confirmed.
screens.explanation: Confirmation is tied to the neckline break, so before that it's a forming pattern.

screens.question: The commonly described sequence of a head & shoulders:
items: Left shoulder forms
Head forms (higher)
Right shoulder forms (about the shoulder height)
Price breaks the neckline (confirmation)
correct_order: Left shoulder forms
Head forms (higher)
Right shoulder forms (about the shoulder height)
Price breaks the neckline (confirmation)
screens.explanation: This order — shoulders, head, shoulder, then neckline break — is how the pattern is commonly read.

screens.question: Why wait for the neckline break before calling it confirmed?

options.label: Because until the neckline breaks, the pattern can still fail
Because the pattern is always confirmed at the head
options.wrong_explanation: The head forming isn't the confirmation step.

options.label: Because confirmation guarantees the outcome
options.wrong_explanation: Even a confirmed pattern can fail.

screens.explanation: The neckline break is the commonly cited confirmation; before it, the pattern can still fail.

lessons.title: When It Fails
lessons.celebration: You understand failed head & shoulders!

screens.title: Not Every Pattern Follows Through
screens.text: Sometimes a head & shoulders forms but price never breaks the neckline — or breaks back the other way. Patterns are clues, never guarantees.

screens.question: Every head & shoulders is guaranteed to lead to a reversal.
screens.explanation: Patterns are descriptive clues; a head & shoulders can fail if the neckline doesn't break as expected.

screens.question: A head & shoulders "fails" when...
options: Price doesn't break the neckline as expected (or breaks back the other way).
The head is the highest peak.
screens.explanation: Not following through at the neckline is what makes the pattern fail.

screens.question: Because patterns are clues, a head & shoulders can still [___].
screens.explanation: Any pattern can fail — that's why it's read as a clue.

screens.question: Why treat a head & shoulders as a clue rather than a certainty?

options.label: Because price can still fail to break the neckline
Because patterns always work
options.wrong_explanation: This is the overconfidence to avoid.

options.label: Because the pattern controls price
options.wrong_explanation: A pattern describes; it doesn't control the market.

screens.explanation: Any pattern can fail, so it's read as a probability-shaped clue, not a guarantee.

lessons.title: Identification Drill
lessons.celebration: You can identify head & shoulders parts fast!

screens.title: Read the Charts
screens.text: Identify the pattern and its parts across a few charts.

screens.question: Which pattern is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Three peaks with a higher middle is a head & shoulders.

screens.question: Which pattern is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Three troughs with a lower middle is an inverse head & shoulders.

screens.question: Tap the head of this head & shoulders.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is the head — the tallest peak.

screens.question: Tap BOTH shoulders.
screens.explanation: The 2nd and 6th candles are the left and right shoulders.

screens.question: Drag the line to the neckline.
screens.explanation: The neckline runs along the two troughs.

lessons.title: What It Suggests
lessons.celebration: You can read what a head & shoulders suggests!

screens.title: From Shape to Meaning
screens.text: Read what a completed head & shoulders suggests — descriptively, never as a buy/sell command.

screens.question: A head & shoulders has completed on the chart above (neckline broke). Descriptively, that suggests...

options.label: That resistance no longer exists
options.wrong_explanation: The structure is exactly what's being read.

options.label: A guaranteed crash
options.wrong_explanation: Descriptive, not a promise.

options.label: Buyers made a higher high (head) but couldn't sustain it, and the level gave way

screens.explanation: The failed higher high plus a neckline break is descriptive context, not a certainty.

screens.question: An inverse head & shoulders has completed on the chart above. Descriptively, that suggests...

options.label: Sellers made a lower low (head) but couldn't sustain it, and the level gave way upward
Nothing can be read from it
options.wrong_explanation: The structure is meaningful context.

options.label: A guaranteed rally
options.wrong_explanation: Descriptive, not a promise.

screens.explanation: The failed lower low plus an upward neckline break is descriptive context.

screens.question: Reading "what a pattern suggests" is description, not a signal to act.
screens.explanation: This course stays descriptive — patterns inform reading, not trade commands.

screens.scenario: Someone turns "a head & shoulders suggests a failed higher high" into "definitely short it now."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: That converts a descriptive read into a certainty and a trade command — the pattern is context, not a guaranteed signal.
A descriptive read and a trade command are the same.
screens.explanation: A descriptive read isn't a guaranteed signal; treating it as one overstates certainty.

lessons.title: Mixed Recognition
lessons.celebration: You can read head & shoulders in any context!

screens.title: Put It Together
screens.text: A full mix — identify the pattern and its parts.

screens.question: Which pattern is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Three troughs with a lower middle is an inverse head & shoulders.

screens.question: Tap the head (lowest trough) of this inverse head & shoulders.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is the head — the lowest trough.

screens.question: The chart above shows a head & shoulders (three peaks, higher middle).
screens.explanation: That's the head & shoulders shape.

screens.question: Match each pattern to its one-line description.
pairs: The level whose break confirms either one
screens.explanation: Recognizing shape plus the confirmation level is the intermediate skill.

screens.question: Drag the line to the neckline of this inverse head & shoulders.
screens.explanation: In the inverse pattern, the neckline runs along the two peaks.

lessons.title: Head & Shoulders Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered head & shoulders!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of head & shoulders, the inverse, the neckline, and confirmation.

screens.question: A head & shoulders is three peaks (higher middle); the inverse is three troughs (lower middle).
screens.explanation: That's the core of both patterns.

screens.question: The level connecting the two troughs, whose break confirms the pattern, is the [___].
screens.explanation: Reviewing the confirmation level.

screens.question: What do a head & shoulders and its inverse have in common?
options: Both are three-peak (or three-trough) reversal shapes confirmed by a neckline break.
screens.explanation: Three turning points plus a neckline break is the shared idea; neither guarantees an outcome.

screens.question: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The outer two peaks/troughs, roughly equal
The level whose break confirms the pattern
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's vocabulary.

screens.template: Head & shoulders patterns are read as [__1__] clues confirmed by a neckline break, not [__2__] outcomes.
screens.explanation: The unit treats the pattern as a descriptive, confirmation-based clue.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: A three-peak reversal shape confirmed by a neckline break — useful context, not a guaranteed signal
A replacement for reading levels
options.wrong_explanation: It's read together with the neckline.

options.label: A pattern that guarantees the next move
options.wrong_explanation: This contradicts the unit.

screens.explanation: This descriptive, confirmation-aware reading is the throughline of the unit.

screens.scenario: Someone finishes this unit and starts calling every three-bar wiggle a "head & shoulders."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: The neckline and peak heights don't matter.
Any three candles form a head & shoulders.
A head & shoulders needs three clear peaks with a higher middle and a neckline — not any small wiggle.
screens.explanation: The pattern has specific requirements (three peaks, higher middle, neckline); random wiggles don't qualify.

lessons.title: What Is an Ascending Triangle?
lessons.celebration: You can spot an ascending triangle!

screens.title: Flat Top, Rising Lows
screens.text: An ascending triangle is commonly described as a flat resistance on top with rising lows underneath — price squeezing up toward the level. It's read as a possible continuation upward.

screens.question: The chart above has a flat top and rising lows. This is commonly called an...
screens.explanation: A flat resistance with rising lows is the ascending triangle shape.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat resistance the highs keep testing.
screens.explanation: The flat top of an ascending triangle is the resistance being tested repeatedly.

screens.question: An ascending triangle has rising lows underneath a flat resistance.
screens.explanation: Rising lows squeezing up under a flat top define the ascending triangle.

screens.question: The lows of an ascending triangle are commonly [___] while the top stays flat.
screens.explanation: Rising lows plus a flat top is the defining structure.

screens.question: What does an ascending triangle describe, on its own?

options.label: That the top is falling
options.wrong_explanation: The top is flat, not falling.

options.label: Buyers pushing lows higher while sellers hold a flat level — a squeeze
A guaranteed breakout up
options.wrong_explanation: Triangles can break either way; nothing is guaranteed.

screens.explanation: An ascending triangle describes a squeeze — context, not certainty.

lessons.title: What Is a Descending Triangle?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a descending triangle!

screens.title: Flat Bottom, Falling Highs
screens.text: A descending triangle is the mirror: a flat support on the bottom with falling highs above — price squeezing down toward the level. It's read as a possible continuation downward.

screens.question: The chart above has a flat bottom and falling highs. This is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: A flat support with falling highs is the descending triangle shape.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat support the lows keep testing.
screens.explanation: The flat bottom of a descending triangle is the support being tested repeatedly.

screens.question: The highs of a descending triangle are commonly [___] while the bottom stays flat.
screens.explanation: Falling highs plus a flat bottom is the defining structure.

screens.question: The chart above shows a flat top with rising lows.
screens.explanation: A descending triangle has a flat BOTTOM with falling highs — the opposite.

screens.scenario: Someone calls a flat-bottom, falling-highs chart an "ascending triangle."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: The two triangles are the same.
Flat bottom with falling highs is a descending triangle; ascending has a flat top with rising lows.
screens.explanation: Which side is flat (top vs bottom) separates ascending from descending.

lessons.title: What Is a Symmetrical Triangle?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a symmetrical triangle!

screens.title: Both Sides Converging
screens.text: A symmetrical triangle has lower highs and higher lows converging toward a point — neither side is flat. It's read as a squeeze that can break either way.

screens.question: The chart above has lower highs AND higher lows converging. This is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: Both sides converging (no flat side) is a symmetrical triangle.

screens.question: A symmetrical triangle has lower highs and [___] lows converging together.
screens.explanation: Lower highs and higher lows narrowing is the symmetrical shape.

screens.question: A symmetrical triangle has one perfectly flat side.
screens.explanation: Neither side is flat — both converge. A flat side would make it ascending or descending.

screens.question: How does a symmetrical triangle differ from an ascending one?

options.label: Both sides converge; an ascending triangle has a flat top
options.detail: No flat side vs a flat side

options.label: They are identical
options.wrong_explanation: One has a flat side, the other doesn't.

options.label: A symmetrical triangle only has rising lows
options.wrong_explanation: It has lower highs too, both converging.

screens.explanation: A symmetrical triangle converges on both sides; ascending/descending have one flat side.

lessons.title: The Flat Side Is the Level
lessons.celebration: You can find the level in a triangle!

screens.title: Read the Flat Side
screens.text: In ascending and descending triangles, the flat side is a support or resistance being tested again and again. Marking that level is a key reading skill.

screens.question: Tap the candles that touch the flat resistance on top.
screens.explanation: The 1st, 3rd, and 5th candles push up into the flat resistance.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance in this ascending triangle.
screens.explanation: The repeated highs mark the flat resistance level.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support in this descending triangle.
screens.explanation: The repeated lows mark the flat support level.

screens.question: In an ascending triangle, the flat side is a...
options: support level being tested by the lows.
resistance level being tested by the highs.
screens.explanation: The flat top of an ascending triangle is a resistance being retested.

screens.question: In a descending triangle, the flat side is a support level.
screens.explanation: The flat bottom of a descending triangle is a support being retested.

lessons.title: Which Way Does It Break?
lessons.celebration: You can read triangles without over-predicting!

screens.title: Bias, Not Certainty
screens.text: Ascending triangles are commonly associated with an upward break and descending with a downward break — but triangles can break either way. It's a bias, never a guarantee.

screens.question: An ascending triangle guarantees an upward breakout.
screens.explanation: It's commonly associated with an upward break, but nothing is guaranteed — it can break either way.

screens.question: What's the honest way to read an ascending triangle's direction?
options: It's commonly associated with an upward break, but can still break down.
screens.explanation: A commonly-cited bias isn't a guarantee; triangles can break either way.

screens.question: A triangle's expected break direction is a [___], not a certainty.
screens.explanation: Descriptive bias, not a promise, is the honest read.

screens.scenario: Someone bets everything on an ascending triangle "definitely" breaking up.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: An ascending triangle is associated with an upward break but doesn't guarantee it — treating it as certain overstates the read.
screens.explanation: A bias isn't a guarantee; triangles can and do break either way.

lessons.title: Triangle Identification Drill
lessons.celebration: You can classify triangles fast!

screens.title: Name the Triangle
screens.text: Read each chart and name the triangle.

screens.question: Which triangle is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Flat top with rising lows is ascending.

screens.question: Which triangle is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Flat bottom with falling highs is descending.

screens.question: Which triangle is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Lower highs and higher lows converging, no flat side, is symmetrical.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat resistance of this triangle.
screens.explanation: The flat top is the resistance.

screens.question: The chart above shows a symmetrical triangle.
screens.explanation: This is a descending triangle (flat bottom), not a symmetrical one.

lessons.title: Triangles Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered triangles!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of ascending, descending, and symmetrical triangles.

screens.question: Match each triangle to its shape.
pairs: Lower highs and higher lows converging
screens.explanation: The flat side (or lack of one) names each triangle.

screens.template: Ascending and descending triangles each have one [__1__] side; a symmetrical triangle has [__2__].
screens.explanation: A flat side marks ascending/descending; symmetrical has none.

screens.question: What do all three triangles have in common?
options: They describe price squeezing into a narrowing range before a break.
They all guarantee an upward breakout.
They all have a flat top.
screens.explanation: A converging squeeze is the shared idea; break direction isn't guaranteed.

screens.question: Which best summarizes triangles?

options.label: A squeeze into a narrowing range — with a break-direction bias, not a guarantee
Shapes unrelated to support and resistance
options.wrong_explanation: The flat sides ARE levels.

options.label: Patterns that guarantee the breakout direction
options.wrong_explanation: Contradicts the unit.

screens.explanation: A squeeze with a bias (not a guarantee) is the throughline.

screens.scenario: Someone calls every little sideways wiggle a "triangle."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Any sideways movement is a triangle.
A triangle needs converging (or one flat) trendlines — not just any sideways drift.
screens.explanation: Triangles have specific converging structure; random drift doesn't qualify.

lessons.title: What Is a Bull Flag?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a bull flag!

screens.title: Pole, Then a Pause
screens.text: A bull flag is a strong up move (the pole) followed by a small, gentle pullback (the flag) that drifts down or sideways — then price often continues up. It's a continuation pattern.

screens.question: The chart above shows a sharp rise, a small drift down, then more rise. This is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: A strong up pole plus a small downward flag is a bull flag.

screens.question: Tap the start of the pole (the first strong up candle).
screens.explanation: The 1st candle begins the strong up move — the pole.

screens.question: In a bull flag, the strong initial up-move is called the [___].
screens.explanation: The pole is the sharp initial move; the flag is the small pause after it.

screens.question: A bull flag is commonly described as a continuation pattern.
screens.explanation: The small pause after the pole often continues in the pole's direction.

screens.question: What does a bull flag describe, on its own?

options.label: A guaranteed continuation
options.wrong_explanation: It's a common tendency, not a guarantee.

options.label: A strong move, a small pause, and often continuation the same way
A reversal down
options.wrong_explanation: A bull flag is a continuation-up pattern, not a reversal.

screens.explanation: A bull flag describes a pause in an up-move that often continues — context, not certainty.

lessons.title: What Is a Bear Flag?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a bear flag!

screens.title: The Mirror Image
screens.text: A bear flag is a strong down move (the pole) followed by a small drift up (the flag) — then price often continues down. It's the bull flag's mirror.

screens.question: The chart above shows a sharp drop, a small drift up, then more drop. This is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: A strong down pole plus a small upward flag is a bear flag.

screens.question: Tap the start of the pole (the first strong down candle).
screens.explanation: The 1st candle begins the strong down move — the pole.

screens.question: A bear flag drifts slightly UP against a strong down-move.
screens.explanation: The flag drifts gently against the pole's direction — up, in a bear flag.

screens.question: A bear flag is commonly read as a [___] pattern.
screens.explanation: Like the bull flag, it's a continuation of the pole's direction.

screens.scenario: Someone calls a strong-down-then-small-up chart a "bull flag."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Bull and bear flags are the same.
A down pole with an upward flag is a bear flag; a bull flag has an up pole.
screens.explanation: The pole's direction (up vs down) names the flag.

lessons.title: Pole and Flag
lessons.celebration: You can read the parts of a flag!

screens.title: Two Parts
screens.text: Every flag has two parts: the pole (a sharp, strong move) and the flag (a small consolidation drifting against it). The flag is much smaller than the pole.

screens.question: Match each part of a flag to its description.
pairs: The small consolidation drifting against the pole
Price often resuming the pole's direction
screens.explanation: Pole then flag then continuation is the commonly described sequence.

screens.question: Compared to the pole, the flag is...
screens.explanation: The flag is a small consolidation relative to the strong pole.

screens.question: Tap the start of the pole.
screens.explanation: The first strong candle is the pole's start.

screens.question: The flag drifts [___] the pole's direction, as a small pause.
screens.explanation: The flag consolidates gently against the pole before continuing.

screens.question: The flag portion is usually larger than the pole.
screens.explanation: The flag is a small pause; the pole is the large, strong move.

lessons.title: Pennants
lessons.celebration: You understand pennants!

screens.title: A Tiny Triangle After a Pole
screens.text: A pennant is like a flag, but the pause forms a small symmetrical triangle (converging) instead of a rectangle. Same idea: a pole, a small pause, then often continuation.

screens.question: A pennant's pause looks like a small...
screens.explanation: A pennant's consolidation converges like a small symmetrical triangle.

screens.question: A pennant and a flag both follow a strong [___].
screens.explanation: Both are continuation pauses after a strong pole.

screens.question: Match each continuation pause to its shape.
pairs: A small rectangle drifting against the move
A brief pause after a strong pole
screens.explanation: Flag vs pennant differ in the pause's shape, not the overall idea.

screens.question: A pennant is a reversal pattern, unlike a flag.
screens.explanation: Both flags and pennants are continuation pauses, not reversals.

lessons.title: Continuation, Not Reversal
lessons.celebration: You can read flags without over-predicting!

screens.title: A Pause, Then Often More
screens.text: Flags and pennants are continuation patterns — a pause that often (not always) resumes the prior move. They're clues, never guarantees.

screens.question: A bull flag guarantees price continues up.
screens.explanation: Continuation is a common tendency, not a guarantee — the flag can fail.

screens.question: The honest read of a bull flag is...
options: A pause that often continues up, but can still fail.
screens.explanation: Continuation is a tendency, not a certainty.

screens.question: Flags and pennants are read as [___] patterns, not guaranteed outcomes.
screens.explanation: They describe a pause that often continues — descriptively.

screens.scenario: Someone treats a bull flag as a certain continuation and ignores that it broke down.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A flag's continuation is a tendency, not a guarantee — it can fail and break the other way.
screens.explanation: Continuation patterns are clues, not guarantees.

lessons.title: Flags & Pennants Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered flags and pennants!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of bull flags, bear flags, pennants, and continuation.

Down pole, small upward flag, often continues down
A small converging triangle after a pole
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's shapes.

screens.question: What do flags and pennants have in common?
options: Both are continuation pauses after a strong pole.
screens.explanation: A pause-then-often-continue is the shared idea; neither guarantees the outcome.

screens.explanation: Pole first, then a continuation-style pause.

options.label: Reversal patterns
options.wrong_explanation: They're continuation patterns.

options.wrong_explanation: Contradicts the unit.

screens.explanation: A pause with a continuation tendency (not a guarantee) is the throughline.

screens.scenario: Someone calls a huge, slow sideways range a "bull flag."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A flag is a small pause after a sharp pole — not a large, slow range with no pole.
Any sideways move is a flag.
screens.explanation: A flag needs a strong pole and a small pause; a big slow range isn't one.

lessons.title: What Is a Rising Wedge?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a rising wedge!

screens.title: Rising, But Narrowing
screens.text: A rising wedge has higher highs and higher lows, but the lines converge (the lows rise faster). Despite rising, it's commonly read as a possible reversal down.

screens.question: The chart above rises but the two lines converge. This is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: Rising highs and lows that converge is a rising wedge.

screens.question: A rising wedge is commonly associated with a possible reversal downward, despite rising.
screens.explanation: Even though it rises, the converging structure is commonly read as weakening — a possible down reversal.

screens.question: A rising wedge has higher highs and higher lows, but the lines [___].
screens.explanation: Converging (narrowing) lines are what make it a wedge, not a channel.

screens.question: What makes a rising wedge different from a plain uptrend?

options.label: It always goes straight up forever
options.wrong_explanation: The converging shape is the point.

options.label: It has no highs or lows
options.wrong_explanation: It has both; they just converge.

options.label: Its lines converge (narrow) rather than staying parallel

screens.explanation: Convergence distinguishes a wedge from a parallel trend.

lessons.title: What Is a Falling Wedge?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a falling wedge!

screens.title: Falling, But Narrowing
screens.text: A falling wedge has lower highs and lower lows that converge (the highs fall faster). Despite falling, it's commonly read as a possible reversal up.

screens.question: The chart above falls but the two lines converge. This is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: Falling highs and lows that converge is a falling wedge.

screens.question: A falling wedge is commonly associated with a possible reversal upward, despite falling.
screens.explanation: The converging structure is commonly read as a possible up reversal, even though it falls.

screens.question: A falling wedge has lower highs and lower lows, but the lines [___].
screens.explanation: Converging lines make it a wedge.

screens.scenario: Someone calls a falling wedge "just a downtrend, nothing more."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A wedge and a plain downtrend are identical.
The converging (narrowing) lines make it a wedge — a specific structure, not just any downtrend.
screens.explanation: The converging shape is what distinguishes a wedge from a plain trend.

lessons.title: What Is a Channel?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a channel!

screens.title: Parallel Lines
screens.text: A channel is a trend where the highs and lows move within parallel lines — an ascending channel (up) or descending channel (down). Unlike a wedge, the lines stay parallel, not converging.

screens.question: The chart above rises within parallel boundaries. This is commonly called an...
screens.explanation: A rising trend within parallel lines is an ascending channel.

screens.question: A channel's boundary lines stay [___], unlike a wedge's converging lines.
screens.explanation: Parallel boundaries define a channel; converging ones define a wedge.

screens.question: The chart above shows a descending channel.
screens.explanation: A falling trend within parallel boundaries is a descending channel.

screens.question: Match each to whether its lines converge or stay parallel.
screens.explanation: Parallel vs converging is the key structural difference.

lessons.title: Wedge vs. Channel
lessons.celebration: You can tell wedges and channels apart!

screens.title: Converging or Parallel?
screens.text: The key question: do the two trendlines converge (wedge) or stay parallel (channel)? That one read tells them apart.

screens.question: Two rising trendlines that stay parallel form a...
screens.explanation: Parallel lines make a channel; converging lines make a wedge.

screens.question: Two rising trendlines that converge (narrow) form a...
screens.explanation: Converging lines make a wedge; parallel ones make a channel.

screens.template: A wedge's lines [__1__]; a channel's lines [__2__].
screens.explanation: Convergence vs parallel is the deciding read.

screens.question: A rising wedge and an ascending channel are the same thing.
screens.explanation: A rising wedge converges; an ascending channel stays parallel — different structures.

screens.question: Reading the chart above, converging lines mean it's a...

options.label: channel — parallel lines
options.wrong_explanation: These lines converge, so it's a wedge.

options.label: triangle with a flat side
options.wrong_explanation: Both lines move; neither is flat here.

options.label: wedge — the lines narrow

screens.explanation: Converging trendlines make it a wedge, not a channel.

lessons.title: Wedges & Channels Identification Drill
lessons.celebration: You can classify wedges and channels!

screens.title: Name the Structure
screens.text: Read each chart and name the structure.

screens.question: Which structure is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Rising and converging is a rising wedge.

screens.question: Which structure is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Falling and converging is a falling wedge.

screens.question: Which structure is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: A rising trend within parallel boundaries is an ascending channel.

screens.question: The chart above shows a falling wedge.
screens.explanation: This is a descending channel (parallel), not a converging falling wedge.

lessons.title: Wedges & Channels Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered wedges and channels!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of rising/falling wedges and channels, and the convergence-vs-parallel read.

screens.question: Match each structure to its description.
pairs: Rising, converging — often read as a down reversal
Falling, converging — often read as an up reversal
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's structures.

options: Whether price is green or red.
Whether the two trendlines converge or stay parallel.
screens.explanation: Converging vs parallel lines is the deciding structural read.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

Wedges and channels guarantee their next move

screens.scenario: Someone calls every rising chart a "rising wedge."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Any rising chart is a wedge.
A rising wedge specifically has converging lines; a plain rising trend within parallel lines is a channel.
screens.explanation: The converging structure — not just rising — is what makes a wedge.

lessons.title: What Is a Trendline?
lessons.celebration: You understand trendlines!

screens.title: Connecting the Turns
screens.text: A trendline is a straight line drawn along a trend's turning points: connecting the higher lows in an uptrend, or the lower highs in a downtrend. It's a diagonal guide, not a flat level.

screens.question: In an uptrend, a trendline is commonly drawn along the...
screens.explanation: An uptrend line connects the rising (higher) lows.

screens.question: A trendline is a diagonal line, unlike a flat horizontal support or resistance.
screens.explanation: Trendlines slope with the trend; horizontal levels are flat.

screens.question: In a downtrend, a trendline connects the [___].
screens.explanation: A downtrend line connects the falling (lower) highs.

screens.question: What does a trendline describe?

options.label: A guarantee price will follow it forever
options.wrong_explanation: A trendline is a guide, not a promise.

options.label: A diagonal guide along a trend's turning points
The exact future price
options.wrong_explanation: It marks structure, not a prediction.

screens.explanation: A trendline is a descriptive guide along the trend's turns.

lessons.title: The Uptrend Line
lessons.celebration: You can read an uptrend line!

screens.title: Along the Higher Lows
screens.text: An uptrend line runs under the higher lows. Each pullback that holds above the line keeps the uptrend's structure intact.

screens.question: Tap the higher low (the pullback that stayed above the prior low).
screens.explanation: The 3rd candle is the pullback that made a higher low, keeping the uptrend intact.

screens.question: An uptrend line stays intact as long as pullbacks make...
screens.explanation: Higher lows holding above the line keep the uptrend structure.

screens.question: An uptrend line is drawn under the rising [___].
screens.explanation: The line connects the higher lows beneath price.

screens.question: If price makes a lower low that breaks below the uptrend line, that's commonly read as the line breaking.
screens.explanation: A lower low breaking the line is commonly read as the uptrend structure weakening.

lessons.title: The Downtrend Line
lessons.celebration: You can read a downtrend line!

screens.title: Along the Lower Highs
screens.text: A downtrend line runs above the lower highs. Each bounce that fails below the line keeps the downtrend's structure intact.

screens.question: Tap the lower high (the bounce that failed below the prior high).
screens.explanation: The 3rd candle is the bounce that made a lower high, keeping the downtrend intact.

screens.question: A downtrend line stays intact as long as bounces make...
screens.explanation: Lower highs staying below the line keep the downtrend structure.

screens.question: A downtrend line is drawn above the falling [___].
screens.explanation: The line connects the lower highs above price.

screens.scenario: Someone draws a downtrend line along the lows instead of the highs.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: It doesn't matter which points you connect.
Downtrend lines go along the lows.
A downtrend line is drawn along the lower highs (above price), not the lows.
screens.explanation: Downtrend lines connect the lower highs; uptrend lines connect the higher lows.

lessons.title: Touches Make It Valid
lessons.celebration: You know what makes a trendline valid!

screens.title: More Touches, More Meaningful
screens.text: A trendline is commonly considered more meaningful when price has touched it multiple times. A line through only one point isn't really established yet.

screens.question: A trendline is commonly considered more meaningful when it has...
screens.explanation: Multiple touches make a trendline more established and meaningful.

screens.question: A line drawn through a single point is already a well-established trendline.
screens.explanation: One point isn't enough — multiple touches are commonly needed to establish a line.

screens.question: More [___] generally make a trendline more meaningful.
screens.explanation: Repeated touches confirm the line matters.

screens.question: Why prefer a trendline with several touches?

options.label: A single touch is always enough
options.wrong_explanation: One point doesn't establish a line.

options.label: Repeated touches show price is respecting that line
Touches don't matter at all
options.wrong_explanation: Touches are the evidence a line is meaningful.

screens.explanation: Multiple touches are the evidence that a trendline is being respected.

lessons.title: Breaking a Trendline
lessons.celebration: You can read a trendline break!

screens.title: When the Line Gives Way
screens.text: A trendline "break" is commonly read as a possible shift in structure — but like any signal, it's descriptive, not a guarantee.

screens.question: Breaking an uptrend line is commonly read as...
options: a possible shift in the uptrend's structure.
screens.explanation: A break is a commonly-cited possible shift — descriptive, not a guarantee.

screens.question: A trendline break guarantees a full reversal.
screens.explanation: A break is a possible shift, not a guaranteed reversal.

screens.question: A trendline break is read as a [___] shift, not a certainty.
screens.explanation: It's a descriptive, possible shift in structure.

screens.scenario: Someone treats a single trendline break as a guaranteed reversal and bets everything on it.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A trendline break is a possible shift, not a guaranteed reversal — treating it as certain overstates it.
A break always means a full reversal.
screens.explanation: A break is descriptive context, not a guarantee.

lessons.title: Trendlines Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered trendlines!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of uptrend lines, downtrend lines, touches, and breaks.

screens.explanation: Higher lows for up, lower highs for down.

screens.question: What makes a trendline more meaningful?
options: More touches, showing price respects the line.
screens.explanation: Multiple touches are the evidence a line matters.

screens.question: Which best summarizes trendlines?

options.label: Diagonal guides along a trend's turns, more meaningful with more touches
Lines that guarantee where price goes
options.wrong_explanation: Contradicts the unit.

options.wrong_explanation: Trendlines are diagonal, not flat.

screens.explanation: Descriptive diagonal guides, validity from touches, is the throughline.

lessons.title: What Is a Range?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a range!

screens.title: Between Two Levels
screens.text: A range (or consolidation) is price moving sideways between a support below and a resistance above — bouncing between the two without a clear trend.

screens.question: The chart above bounces between a floor and a ceiling. This is commonly called a...
screens.explanation: Sideways movement between support and resistance is a range.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance (the ceiling) of this range.
screens.explanation: The top of the range is the resistance price keeps failing to break.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support (the floor) of this range.
screens.explanation: The bottom of the range is the support price keeps bouncing from.

screens.question: A range is bounded by a support below and a [___] above.
screens.explanation: Support below, resistance above, bound a range.

screens.question: A range has a clear, strong trend in one direction.
screens.explanation: A range is sideways — the opposite of a strong one-directional trend.

lessons.title: Range-Bound vs. Trending
lessons.celebration: You can tell ranges from trends!

screens.title: Sideways or Directional?
screens.text: The core question: is price range-bound (sideways between levels) or trending (making progress in one direction)? Reading which regime you're in is a key skill.

screens.question: The chart above bounces sideways between two levels. It is...
screens.explanation: Sideways between levels is range-bound, not trending.

screens.question: The chart above makes higher highs and higher lows. It is...
screens.explanation: Progress in one direction (higher highs/lows) is trending, not range-bound.

screens.question: A range-bound market and a trending market are read the same way.
screens.explanation: They're different regimes — sideways vs directional — and read differently.

screens.template: A [__1__] market moves sideways between levels; a [__2__] market makes progress one way.
screens.explanation: Range-bound = sideways; trending = directional.

screens.scenario: Someone treats a clearly sideways range as a strong uptrend.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Bouncing sideways between levels is range-bound, not a strong uptrend — the regime was misread.
screens.explanation: Reading the regime (range vs trend) correctly is the skill.

lessons.title: Reading Range Boundaries
lessons.celebration: You can read a range's boundaries!

screens.title: The Floor and Ceiling
screens.text: In a range, price commonly bounces down from resistance and up from support. Reading where those boundaries are is how you read the range.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance of this range.
screens.explanation: The ceiling the highs keep testing is the range's resistance.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support of this range.
screens.explanation: The floor the lows keep testing is the range's support.

screens.question: Within a range, price commonly bounces DOWN from the...
screens.explanation: Resistance caps the range; price bounces down from it.

screens.question: Within a range, price commonly bounces UP from support.
screens.explanation: Support is the floor price bounces up from within the range.

lessons.title: Breaking Out of a Range
lessons.celebration: You understand range breakouts!

screens.title: Leaving the Box
screens.text: Eventually price often leaves the range by breaking above resistance or below support — a breakout. The direction isn't guaranteed in advance.

screens.question: The chart above pushes above the range's resistance and keeps going. This is a...
screens.explanation: Clearing resistance and continuing is a breakout from the range.

screens.question: You can always know in advance which way a range will break.
screens.explanation: Break direction isn't guaranteed in advance — it's read as it happens.

screens.question: Leaving a range by clearing a boundary is called a [___].
screens.explanation: Clearing support or resistance out of the range is a breakout.

screens.question: What does a range breakout describe?

options.label: That the range never existed
options.wrong_explanation: The breakout is defined relative to the range.

options.label: Price leaving the range by clearing a boundary
A guaranteed big trend afterward
options.wrong_explanation: Breakouts can also fail; nothing is guaranteed.

screens.explanation: A breakout describes price leaving the range — context, not a guaranteed trend.

lessons.title: False Breakouts
lessons.celebration: You can recognize a false breakout!

screens.title: A Break That Doesn't Hold
screens.text: Sometimes price pokes past a range boundary, then falls back inside — a false breakout (or fakeout). It's why a break isn't a guarantee.

screens.question: The chart above pokes above resistance, then falls back inside the range. This is a...
screens.explanation: A poke past the level that fails back inside is a false breakout.

screens.question: A false breakout is one reason a boundary break isn't a guarantee.
screens.explanation: Because breaks can be false, a break is read as a clue, not a certainty.

screens.question: A break that fails back inside the range is commonly called a [___] breakout.
screens.explanation: "False breakout" (or fakeout) is the standard term.

screens.scenario: Someone treats every poke past resistance as a guaranteed breakout.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Some pokes are false breakouts that fail back inside — a poke isn't a guaranteed breakout.
Every poke past a level always continues.
screens.explanation: False breakouts are exactly why a break isn't a guarantee.

lessons.title: Ranges Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered ranges!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of ranges, boundaries, breakouts, and false breakouts.

A break that fails back inside
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's vocabulary.

screens.explanation: Reviewing the range's ceiling.

screens.question: What best describes a range?
options: Sideways movement between a support and a resistance.
screens.explanation: Sideways between two levels is the definition of a range.

screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Higher highs and higher lows is a trend, not a sideways range between fixed levels.
Trends and ranges are the same.
