lessons.title: What Is a Breakout?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a breakout!

screens.title: Clearing the Level
screens.text: A breakout is price clearing a resistance (or support) with momentum and continuing past it. It's read as price escaping a level — not a guaranteed trend.

screens.question: The chart above clears resistance with a strong candle and keeps going. This is a...
screens.explanation: Clearing the level with momentum and continuing is a breakout.

screens.question: Tap the breakout candle (the strong one clearing the level).
screens.explanation: The 4th candle clears resistance with momentum — the breakout candle.

screens.question: A breakout is price [___] a level and continuing past it.
screens.explanation: Clearing the level (not bouncing) is what makes a breakout.

screens.question: A breakout guarantees a large trend afterward.
screens.explanation: Breakouts can fail; nothing after a breakout is guaranteed.

lessons.title: What Is a Breakdown?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a breakdown!

screens.title: Breaking Support
screens.text: A breakdown is the downside version: price clearing a support and continuing lower. Same idea as a breakout, opposite direction.

screens.question: The chart above breaks below support and keeps falling. This is a...
screens.explanation: Clearing support downward and continuing is a breakdown.

screens.question: Tap the breakdown candle (the one clearing support).
screens.explanation: The 4th candle breaks below support — the breakdown candle.

screens.question: A breakdown clears a support level to the downside.
screens.explanation: A breakdown is price clearing support and continuing lower.

screens.question: A breakdown is a breakout to the [___] side.
screens.explanation: A breakdown is the downside version of a breakout.

lessons.title: The Retest
lessons.celebration: You understand the retest!

screens.title: Coming Back to the Level
screens.text: After a breakout, price often returns to retest the level it broke — the old resistance now acting as support — before continuing. The highlighted candle is the retest.

screens.question: Tap the retest candle (where price returns to the broken level).
screens.explanation: The 4th candle pulls back to retest the level that was just broken.

screens.question: A retest is when price, after a breakout...
options: returns to the broken level before continuing.
screens.explanation: A retest is the return to the broken level to test it as new support/resistance.

screens.question: After a breakout, returning to the broken level is called a [___].
screens.explanation: "Retest" is the standard term for returning to the broken level.

screens.question: A retest often shows the old resistance acting as new support.
screens.explanation: After breaking up, the old resistance commonly acts as new support on the retest.

lessons.title: Support/Resistance Flip
lessons.celebration: You understand the level flip!

screens.title: Roles Reverse
screens.text: When a level breaks, its role commonly flips: broken resistance often becomes support, and broken support often becomes resistance. The retest is where this flip is tested.

screens.question: Drag the line to the level that was resistance and is now being retested as support.
screens.explanation: The broken level — old resistance, now support — is what price retests.

screens.question: When resistance breaks and holds, it commonly becomes...
screens.explanation: Broken resistance commonly flips to act as support.

screens.question: Broken support can commonly flip to act as resistance.
screens.explanation: The flip works both ways — broken support often becomes resistance.

screens.question: A broken level commonly [___] its role (support ↔ resistance).
screens.explanation: The level's role commonly flips after a clean break.

lessons.title: Clean vs. Weak Breakouts
lessons.celebration: You can judge a breakout's strength!

screens.title: How Convincing Is It?
screens.text: A "clean" breakout clears the level with a strong, decisive candle. A "weak" one barely pokes through and struggles. Reading strength is descriptive context, not a guarantee.

screens.question: A clean breakout is commonly described as...
options: clearing the level with a strong, decisive candle.
screens.explanation: A decisive, strong candle through the level reads as a cleaner breakout.

screens.question: The chart above only pokes past the level, then falls back. This looks like a...
screens.explanation: A poke that fails back is a weak or false breakout, not a clean one.

screens.question: Even a clean-looking breakout can still fail.
screens.explanation: Strength is descriptive context; a clean breakout is not a guarantee.

screens.question: Reading breakout strength is [___] context, not a guarantee.
screens.explanation: It informs the read; it doesn't promise the outcome.

lessons.title: Breakouts & Retests Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered breakouts and retests!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of breakouts, breakdowns, retests, and the level flip.

screens.question: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Returning to the broken level before continuing
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's vocabulary.

screens.question: Tap the retest candle.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is the retest of the broken level.

screens.question: When resistance breaks and holds, its role commonly...
screens.explanation: A broken level commonly flips its role.

screens.template: A breakout clears a [__1__]; a retest returns to that broken [__2__].
screens.explanation: Clear the level, then retest that same level.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Breakouts that guarantee a big move
options.wrong_explanation: Contradicts the unit.

options.label: Price clears a level, often retests it as a flipped role, and continues — read descriptively
Levels that never change roles
options.wrong_explanation: Broken levels commonly flip roles.

screens.explanation: Clear, retest, flip — descriptively — is the throughline.

screens.scenario: Someone treats every breakout as a guaranteed trend and never watches for a retest or failure.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Breakouts can fail or retest first — treating every one as a guaranteed trend ignores that.
screens.explanation: Breakouts are descriptive clues that can fail or retest, not guarantees.

lessons.title: What Is a Pullback?
lessons.celebration: You understand pullbacks!

screens.title: A Pause Against the Trend
screens.text: A pullback is a temporary counter-move within a trend — a small dip in an uptrend, or a small bounce in a downtrend — before the trend often resumes.

screens.question: The chart above rises, dips briefly, then rises again. The brief dip is a...
screens.explanation: A temporary counter-move within a trend is a pullback.

screens.question: Tap the pullback (the dip within the uptrend).
screens.explanation: The 3rd candle is the brief dip — the pullback — before the uptrend resumes.

screens.question: A pullback is a temporary move against the trend, not necessarily a reversal.
screens.explanation: A pullback pauses the trend briefly; it isn't automatically a reversal.

screens.question: In an uptrend, a pullback is a temporary [___] before price often rises again.
screens.explanation: A pullback in an uptrend is a small dip against the up-move.

lessons.title: Higher Lows Continue the Uptrend
lessons.celebration: You can read a healthy uptrend!

screens.title: Each Dip Holds Higher
screens.text: In a healthy uptrend, each pullback bottoms at a higher low than the last — the dips get bought before reaching the previous low.

screens.question: Tap the higher low (the pullback that held above the prior low).
screens.explanation: The 3rd candle makes a higher low, keeping the uptrend healthy.

screens.question: A healthy uptrend makes a series of...
screens.explanation: Higher highs and higher lows define a healthy uptrend.

screens.question: Each pullback in a healthy uptrend bottoms at a [___] low.
screens.explanation: Higher lows keep the uptrend structure intact.

screens.question: If a pullback makes a LOWER low than the previous one, the uptrend structure is weakening.
screens.explanation: A lower low breaks the higher-low pattern, commonly read as weakening.

lessons.title: Lower Highs Continue the Downtrend
lessons.celebration: You can read a healthy downtrend!

screens.title: Each Bounce Fails Lower
screens.text: In a healthy downtrend, each bounce tops at a lower high than the last — the bounces get sold before reaching the previous high.

screens.question: Tap the lower high (the bounce that failed below the prior high).
screens.explanation: The 3rd candle makes a lower high, keeping the downtrend healthy.

screens.question: A healthy downtrend makes a series of...
screens.explanation: Lower highs and lower lows define a healthy downtrend.

screens.question: Each bounce in a healthy downtrend tops at a [___] high.
screens.explanation: Lower highs keep the downtrend structure intact.

screens.scenario: Someone sees a bounce make a HIGHER high and still calls the downtrend perfectly healthy.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Higher highs keep a downtrend healthy.
A higher high breaks the lower-high pattern — that's commonly read as the downtrend weakening, not healthy.
The highs don't matter in a downtrend.
screens.explanation: Lower highs keep a downtrend intact; a higher high weakens it.

lessons.title: Pullback vs. Reversal
lessons.celebration: You can tell a pullback from a reversal!

screens.title: Pause or Turn?
screens.text: A pullback pauses the trend but keeps its structure (higher lows / lower highs). A reversal breaks that structure. Reading which is happening is a key skill.

screens.question: The chart above dips but still makes a higher low, then continues up. This is a...
screens.explanation: A dip that holds a higher low and continues up is a pullback, not a reversal.

screens.question: The chart above breaks below the prior low and keeps falling. This is closer to a...
screens.explanation: Breaking the prior low breaks the up-structure — closer to a reversal.

screens.question: A pullback keeps the trend's structure; a reversal breaks it.
screens.explanation: That's the core difference — structure intact (pullback) vs broken (reversal).

screens.template: A [__1__] keeps higher lows intact; a [__2__] breaks them.
screens.explanation: Pullbacks preserve structure; reversals break it.

lessons.title: Continuation After a Pullback
lessons.celebration: You understand continuation!

screens.title: The Trend Resumes
screens.text: After a healthy pullback, the trend often continues in its original direction. "Often," not "always" — it's a tendency, not a guarantee.

screens.question: After a healthy pullback in an uptrend, price commonly...
screens.explanation: Continuation is the common tendency after a healthy pullback — not a guarantee.

screens.question: Continuation after a pullback is guaranteed.
screens.explanation: It's a common tendency, not a certainty — the trend can still fail.

screens.question: After a healthy pullback, the trend often [___] its original direction.
screens.explanation: The trend commonly resumes after a healthy pullback.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes every pullback is guaranteed to continue the trend and ignores a broken structure.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Continuation is a tendency, not a guarantee — a broken structure can mean a reversal instead.
screens.explanation: Continuation is likely after a healthy pullback but not guaranteed, especially if structure breaks.

lessons.title: Pullbacks Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered pullbacks & continuation!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of pullbacks, higher lows / lower highs, and continuation.

screens.question: Match each to its meaning.
pairs: A temporary counter-move within a trend
A pullback bottom above the prior low (uptrend intact)
The trend resuming after a pullback
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's ideas.

screens.question: What keeps an uptrend "healthy" through its pullbacks?
options: Each pullback makes a higher low.
Each pullback makes a lower low.
screens.explanation: Higher lows through the pullbacks keep an uptrend healthy.

screens.template: A pullback [__1__] the trend's structure; continuation is a [__2__], not a guarantee.
screens.explanation: Pullbacks preserve structure; continuation is a tendency.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Trends pause with pullbacks and often continue if structure holds — descriptively
Pullbacks that guarantee continuation
options.wrong_explanation: Contradicts the unit.

options.label: Pullbacks identical to full reversals
options.wrong_explanation: Pullbacks keep structure; reversals break it.

screens.explanation: Structure-preserving pauses with likely (not guaranteed) continuation is the throughline.

lessons.title: Reading Momentum From Bodies
lessons.celebration: You can read momentum off a chart!

screens.title: Big Bodies, Strong Moves
screens.text: A large candle body reflects momentum — price moved decisively one way. Reading body size is a quick read of how strong a move is.

screens.question: The big, near-wickless candle highlighted above reflects...
screens.explanation: A large body (marubozu) reflects decisive momentum.

screens.question: Tap the strong-momentum candle (the big body).
screens.explanation: The 2nd candle is the big-bodied momentum candle.

screens.question: A [___] body reflects stronger momentum.
screens.explanation: Bigger bodies reflect stronger, more one-sided moves.

screens.question: A large candle body reflects a decisive, one-sided move.
screens.explanation: The full body shows price pushed one way and held.

lessons.title: Exhaustion: Long Wicks
lessons.celebration: You can read exhaustion from wicks!

screens.title: Pushed, Then Rejected
screens.text: A long wick shows a push that got rejected — a sign a move may be running out of steam (exhaustion) at that extreme.

screens.question: The long upper wick highlighted above shows...
options: an up-push that got rejected back down.
screens.explanation: A long upper wick shows buyers were rejected at the highs.

screens.question: Tap the rejection candle (the long upper wick).
screens.explanation: The 2nd candle's long upper wick shows the rejected push up.

screens.question: A long wick is commonly read as a sign of possible [___] at that extreme.
screens.explanation: A rejected push suggests the move may be running out of steam there.

screens.question: A long lower wick shows a down-push that got rejected (buyers stepped in).
screens.explanation: A long lower wick shows sellers were rejected and buyers recovered price.

lessons.title: Indecision: Doji & Spinning Top
lessons.celebration: You can read indecision candles!

screens.title: Neither Side Wins
screens.text: Small-bodied candles like the doji and spinning top reflect indecision — momentum stalling, with neither side in control.

screens.question: The tiny-bodied candle highlighted above reflects...
screens.explanation: A doji's tiny body reflects a balance — indecision.

screens.question: The small-bodied candle with wicks on both sides above reflects...
screens.explanation: A spinning top's small body and balanced wicks reflect indecision.

screens.question: A doji reflects strong one-directional momentum.
screens.explanation: A doji reflects balance/indecision — the opposite of strong momentum.

screens.question: Small-bodied candles reflect momentum [___], not a strong move.
screens.explanation: A small body means neither side pushed decisively — momentum stalling.

lessons.title: Strong vs. Weak Candles
lessons.celebration: You can compare candle strength!

screens.title: Decisive or Hesitant?
screens.text: Comparing candles: a big body = decisive momentum; a tiny body = hesitation. Reading relative strength is descriptive context.

screens.question: Which reflects more momentum: a big-bodied marubozu or a tiny-bodied doji?
screens.explanation: A big body reflects far more momentum than a tiny doji body.

screens.question: Tap the more decisive candle on this chart.
screens.explanation: The big-bodied 2nd candle is the more decisive, higher-momentum one.

screens.template: A big body reflects [__1__]; a tiny body reflects [__2__].
screens.explanation: Body size is a quick read of momentum vs hesitation.

screens.question: Reading candle strength is descriptive context, not a guaranteed prediction.
screens.explanation: Strength informs the read; it doesn't guarantee what comes next.

lessons.title: Momentum Into a Level
lessons.celebration: You can read momentum meeting a level!

screens.title: When a Push Meets Resistance
screens.text: Momentum into a level can either break it or get rejected. A strong push that then rejects (long wick) at resistance is a common exhaustion read.

screens.question: The chart above pushes up into resistance, then gets rejected. This is commonly read as...
screens.explanation: A rejected push at resistance is a common exhaustion read — descriptive.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance the push was rejected at.
screens.explanation: The level where the push got rejected is the resistance.

screens.question: A rejection at resistance guarantees price falls.
screens.explanation: A rejection is a descriptive clue about exhaustion, not a guarantee.

screens.question: A strong push that rejects at a level is a common [___] read.
screens.explanation: A rejected push at a level commonly reads as exhaustion there.

lessons.title: Momentum Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered momentum & exhaustion!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of momentum (bodies), exhaustion (wicks), and indecision (small bodies).

screens.question: Match each candle read to what it reflects.
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's candle reads.

screens.question: What do momentum and exhaustion reads have in common?
options: Both are descriptive context from candles, not guarantees.
screens.explanation: Both read the candles descriptively; neither guarantees the outcome.

screens.template: A big body reflects [__1__]; a long wick reflects a rejected push and possible [__2__].
screens.explanation: Bodies read momentum; wicks read rejection/exhaustion.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Candle shape tells you nothing
options.wrong_explanation: Shape reflects momentum and exhaustion.

options.label: Read momentum, exhaustion, and indecision from candle shape — descriptively
Candle shape guarantees the next move
options.wrong_explanation: Contradicts the unit.

screens.explanation: Descriptive candle-strength reading is the throughline.

lessons.title: What Is Confluence?
lessons.celebration: You understand confluence!

screens.title: When Signals Line Up
screens.text: Confluence is when two or more readings point the same way at the same spot — for example, a support level AND a bounce candle together. More agreement makes a stronger read (still not a guarantee).

screens.question: Confluence means...
options: a single reading on its own.
two or more readings lining up at the same spot.
screens.explanation: Confluence is multiple factors agreeing at once.

screens.question: More confluence makes a read stronger, but still not guaranteed.
screens.explanation: Agreement strengthens the read; it doesn't make it a certainty.

screens.question: Confluence is when [___] or more readings agree at the same spot.
screens.explanation: Confluence requires at least two agreeing factors.

screens.question: Why is confluence useful to read?

options.label: It guarantees the outcome
options.wrong_explanation: More agreement isn't a guarantee.

options.label: Several readings agreeing is stronger evidence than one alone
It replaces reading the chart
options.wrong_explanation: Confluence IS reading several chart factors together.

screens.explanation: Confluence stacks evidence — stronger, but never a guarantee.

lessons.title: Level + Candle Signal
lessons.celebration: You can read level-plus-candle confluence!

screens.title: A Bounce at Support
screens.text: One common confluence: price reaches a support level AND prints a bounce (like a long lower wick) there. The level and the candle agree.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support where price bounced.
screens.explanation: The level price bounced from is the support — one half of the confluence.

screens.question: "Support level + a bounce candle there" is an example of...
screens.explanation: The level and the candle agreeing is confluence.

screens.question: A bounce candle right at a support level is stronger evidence than a bounce with no level nearby.
screens.explanation: The level plus the candle agreeing (confluence) is stronger than the candle alone.

screens.question: A support level and a bounce candle together is an example of [___].
screens.explanation: Two agreeing factors at one spot is confluence.

lessons.title: Level + Pattern
lessons.celebration: You can read level-plus-pattern confluence!

screens.title: A Pattern at a Level
screens.text: Another confluence: a pattern forming right at a key level — like a double top forming at resistance. The pattern and the level reinforce each other.

screens.question: A double top forming right at a resistance level is an example of...
screens.explanation: The pattern and the level agreeing at the same spot is confluence.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance this double top is testing.
screens.explanation: The resistance the two peaks test is the level reinforcing the pattern.

screens.question: A pattern at a key level is stronger evidence than the same pattern in empty space.
screens.explanation: The pattern plus the level (confluence) is stronger than the pattern alone.

screens.question: A double top at resistance combines a pattern with a [___].
screens.explanation: The resistance level plus the double top pattern is confluence.

lessons.title: Trend + Pullback
lessons.celebration: You can read trend-plus-pullback confluence!

screens.title: A Pullback in a Trend
screens.text: Confluence also shows up as a healthy pullback within a trend — the trend direction and the higher-low pullback agree on the up-bias.

screens.question: Tap the higher-low pullback that agrees with the uptrend.
screens.explanation: The higher-low pullback within the uptrend is the two factors (trend + pullback) agreeing.

screens.question: An uptrend plus a higher-low pullback is an example of...
screens.explanation: The trend and the pullback both pointing up is confluence.

screens.question: A higher-low pullback within an uptrend is [___] with the trend.
screens.explanation: The pullback and the trend agree — they're aligned (confluence).

screens.question: A pullback that agrees with the trend adds confluence to an up-bias read.
screens.explanation: Trend plus an aligned pullback is two factors agreeing — confluence.

lessons.title: More Confluence, Stronger Read
lessons.celebration: You can weigh confluence honestly!

screens.title: Stronger, Not Certain
screens.text: The more independent readings that agree, the stronger the read — but even lots of confluence is never a guarantee. It stacks probability, not certainty.

screens.question: Stacking more agreeing readings makes a read...
screens.explanation: More agreement strengthens the read without guaranteeing it.

screens.question: Enough confluence eventually makes an outcome guaranteed.
screens.explanation: Confluence stacks probability, never certainty — nothing is guaranteed.

screens.question: Confluence stacks [___], not certainty.
screens.explanation: More agreeing factors raise the odds in the read, not a guarantee.

screens.scenario: Someone finds three agreeing signals and bets everything, sure it "can't fail."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Even strong confluence isn't a guarantee — treating it as "can't fail" overstates the read.
screens.explanation: Confluence improves the read's odds but never removes uncertainty.

lessons.title: Confluence Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered confluence!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of confluence — stacking agreeing readings for a stronger (not certain) view.

screens.question: Match each example to the factors it combines.
screens.explanation: Each is two factors agreeing — confluence.

screens.question: What is the honest limit of confluence?
options: It has no effect on a read.
It guarantees the outcome once you have enough.
It stacks probability but never guarantees an outcome.
screens.explanation: Confluence strengthens the read without ever making it certain.

screens.template: Confluence combines [__1__] agreeing readings for a [__2__] read — never a guarantee.
screens.explanation: Multiple agreeing factors make a stronger, not certain, read.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Confluence means ignoring the chart
options.wrong_explanation: It's reading several chart factors together.

options.label: Confluence guarantees the outcome
options.wrong_explanation: Contradicts the unit.

options.label: Stacking agreeing readings makes a stronger, still-uncertain read

screens.explanation: Stronger-but-never-certain, from agreeing factors, is the throughline.

screens.scenario: Someone treats one signal alone as if it were full confluence.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: The number of factors doesn't matter.
One signal is always full confluence.
Confluence needs two or more agreeing readings — a single signal on its own isn't confluence.
screens.explanation: Confluence requires multiple agreeing factors, not a lone signal.

lessons.title: What Is a Gap?
lessons.celebration: You can spot a gap!

screens.title: A Jump With No Trading
screens.text: A gap is a jump in price where one candle opens well away from the previous candle — leaving an empty space with no trading in between. It often happens between sessions or on news.

screens.question: The chart above shows a candle opening well above the previous candle, leaving empty space. This is a...
screens.explanation: A jump leaving empty space between candles is a gap.

screens.question: Tap the gap candle (the one that jumped away from the previous candle).
screens.explanation: The 3rd candle opens above the prior candle's high — the gap candle.

screens.question: A gap leaves an empty space with no [___] in between.
screens.explanation: Price jumped, so no trades happened across the gap.

screens.question: A gap up opens above the previous candle's high.
screens.explanation: A gap up jumps above the prior candle, leaving space below the new open.

lessons.title: Gap Up vs. Gap Down
lessons.celebration: You can tell gap direction!

screens.title: Which Way Did It Jump?
screens.text: A gap up opens above the prior candle's high; a gap down opens below the prior candle's low. Direction is just which way the jump went.

screens.question: The chart above opens well below the previous candle's low. This is a...
screens.explanation: Opening below the prior low is a gap down.

screens.question: Tap the gap-down candle.
screens.explanation: The 3rd candle opens below the prior candle's low — the gap down.

screens.question: A gap down opens below the previous candle's low.
screens.explanation: A gap down jumps below the prior candle.

screens.template: A gap [__1__] opens above the prior high; a gap [__2__] opens below the prior low.
screens.explanation: Up = above prior high; down = below prior low.

lessons.title: Why Gaps Happen
lessons.celebration: You understand why gaps form!

screens.title: News and Session Breaks
screens.text: Gaps commonly form when price can't trade continuously — overnight between sessions, or when news hits and the next available price is far from the last.

screens.question: Gaps commonly form because of...
options: session breaks or news, when trading isn't continuous.
screens.explanation: When price can't trade continuously (overnight, news), the next price can be far away — a gap.

screens.question: Gaps commonly appear between sessions or around news.
screens.explanation: Non-continuous trading (overnight/news) is a common cause of gaps.

screens.question: A gap forms when trading isn't [___], so the next price is far from the last.
screens.explanation: Discontinuous trading lets price jump, forming a gap.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes gaps only appear randomly for no reason.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Gaps commonly have causes — session breaks or news — not pure randomness.
Gaps only depend on candle color.
screens.explanation: Gaps usually reflect non-continuous trading (sessions/news), not randomness.

lessons.title: The Gap Fill
lessons.celebration: You understand gap fills!

screens.title: Returning to the Gap
screens.text: A "gap fill" is when price later returns to trade back through the empty gap space. It happens often but not always — a tendency, never a guarantee.

screens.question: A "gap fill" is when price...
options: returns to trade back through the gap's empty space.
screens.explanation: Filling the gap means price comes back through the empty space.

screens.question: Every gap is guaranteed to fill.
screens.explanation: Gaps fill often but not always — it's a tendency, not a guarantee.

screens.question: A gap fill happens [___], not always.
screens.explanation: Gap fills are a common tendency, not a certainty.

screens.question: How should you read "gaps often fill"?

options.label: As something that never happens
options.wrong_explanation: Gap fills are common, just not guaranteed.

options.label: As a common tendency, not a guarantee
As a certainty every time
options.wrong_explanation: Not every gap fills.

screens.explanation: "Often fills" is a descriptive tendency, never a guarantee.

lessons.title: Gaps Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered gaps!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of gaps, direction, causes, and gap fills.

screens.question: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Opens above the prior candle's high
Opens below the prior candle's low
Price returning through the gap's empty space
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's vocabulary.

screens.question: Tap the gap candle.
screens.explanation: The 3rd candle is the one that gapped away from the previous candle.

screens.question: What causes most gaps?
options: Non-continuous trading — session breaks or news.
screens.explanation: Discontinuous trading is the common cause of gaps.

screens.question: Which best summarizes gaps?

options.label: Jumps leaving empty space, from discontinuous trading, that often (not always) fill
Gaps that always fill immediately
options.wrong_explanation: Not every gap fills.

options.label: Random marks with no cause
options.wrong_explanation: Gaps usually have a cause.

screens.explanation: Cause + a fill tendency (not guarantee) is the throughline.

lessons.title: What Is a Timeframe?
lessons.celebration: You understand timeframes!

screens.title: Each Candle's Duration
screens.text: A timeframe is how much time each candle represents — a 1-minute candle, an hourly candle, a daily candle. The same market looks different on different timeframes.

screens.question: A "timeframe" describes...
options: how much time each candle represents.
screens.explanation: Timeframe is the duration each candle covers (1m, 1h, 1d, …).

screens.question: The same market can look different on different timeframes.
screens.explanation: A move that's a blip on a daily chart can be a whole trend on a 1-minute chart.

screens.question: A daily candle represents [___] time than a 1-minute candle.
screens.explanation: Each daily candle covers a full day, far more than a minute.

screens.question: Which is a "higher" timeframe?
screens.explanation: Higher timeframes cover more time per candle (daily > hourly > 1-minute).

lessons.title: Higher vs. Lower Timeframe
lessons.celebration: You can compare timeframes!

screens.title: Zoomed Out vs. Zoomed In
screens.text: A higher timeframe (daily) is the zoomed-out big picture; a lower timeframe (1-minute) is the zoomed-in detail. Both describe the same market at different scales.

screens.question: The higher timeframe shows...
screens.explanation: Higher timeframes are the big-picture, zoomed-out view.

screens.question: The lower timeframe shows...
screens.explanation: Lower timeframes zoom in on fine detail within the bigger move.

screens.template: A higher timeframe is more [__1__]; a lower timeframe is more [__2__].
screens.explanation: Higher = zoomed out (big picture); lower = zoomed in (detail).

screens.question: Higher and lower timeframes describe the same market at different scales.
screens.explanation: They're the same price data viewed zoomed out vs zoomed in.

lessons.title: Trends Can Differ by Timeframe
lessons.celebration: You can read trends across timeframes!

screens.title: Up Here, Down There
screens.text: A market can be in an uptrend on the higher timeframe while showing a short-term downtrend on a lower one. A pullback on the daily can look like a full downtrend on the 1-minute.

screens.question: The chart above is a higher-timeframe uptrend with a dip. On a lower timeframe, that dip might look like a...
screens.explanation: A higher-timeframe pullback can appear as a full downtrend when zoomed in.

screens.question: A pullback on a higher timeframe can look like a downtrend on a lower timeframe.
screens.explanation: Zooming into a pullback can show a complete small downtrend.

screens.question: A market can trend one way on a higher timeframe and [___] on a lower one.
screens.explanation: Trends can differ across timeframes for the same market.

screens.scenario: Someone reads only the 1-minute chart and ignores the daily trend entirely.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Ignoring the higher timeframe misses the big-picture trend the short-term move sits inside.
screens.explanation: The higher-timeframe context frames what the lower-timeframe move means.

lessons.title: Top-Down Reading
lessons.celebration: You understand top-down reading!

screens.title: Big Picture First
screens.text: "Top-down" reading means checking the higher timeframe first for the big-picture trend and key levels, then zooming into a lower one for detail. Context first, detail second.

screens.question: Top-down reading starts with the...
screens.explanation: Top-down means big-picture (higher timeframe) first, then detail.

screens.question: A top-down reading process:
items: Check the higher timeframe for the big-picture trend
Note the higher-timeframe key levels
Zoom into a lower timeframe for detail
Read the lower-timeframe move inside that context
correct_order: Check the higher timeframe for the big-picture trend
Note the higher-timeframe key levels
Zoom into a lower timeframe for detail
Read the lower-timeframe move inside that context
screens.explanation: Context first (higher timeframe), then zoom in — that's top-down.

screens.question: Top-down reading checks the big-picture timeframe before the detail one.
screens.explanation: Big picture first, then detail, is the top-down idea.

screens.question: Top-down reading sets [___] from the higher timeframe first.
screens.explanation: The higher timeframe provides the context to read the detail within.

lessons.title: Timeframe Alignment
lessons.celebration: You can read timeframe alignment!

screens.title: When They Agree
screens.text: When multiple timeframes point the same way — say, an uptrend on both the higher and lower timeframe — that agreement is a form of confluence. It's stronger, but still not a guarantee.

screens.question: When the higher and lower timeframe both trend up, that agreement is a form of...
screens.explanation: Agreement across timeframes is confluence — a stronger read.

screens.question: Timeframe agreement makes a read stronger but not guaranteed.
screens.explanation: Alignment stacks evidence (confluence), which is stronger but never certain.

screens.question: When timeframes agree, it adds [___] to the read.
screens.explanation: Agreeing timeframes are another agreeing factor — confluence.

screens.scenario: Someone sees both timeframes agree and assumes the trade "can't lose."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Timeframe agreement is stronger evidence but never a guarantee — "can't lose" overstates it.
screens.explanation: Even aligned timeframes only stack probability, not certainty.

lessons.title: Multi-Timeframe Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered multi-timeframe basics!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of timeframes, higher vs lower, top-down reading, and alignment.

screens.question: Match each idea to its meaning.
screens.explanation: A quick recap of the unit's ideas.

screens.template: Read the [__1__] timeframe for context, then the [__2__] one for detail.
screens.explanation: Higher for context, lower for detail — top-down.

screens.question: Why check more than one timeframe?
options: To make the chart more colorful.
Because lower timeframes are the only ones that matter.
The big picture frames what the short-term move means.
screens.explanation: Context from the higher timeframe frames the lower-timeframe detail.

screens.question: Which best summarizes multi-timeframe reading?

options.label: Only the lowest timeframe matters
options.wrong_explanation: Context comes from higher timeframes.

options.label: Timeframe agreement guarantees the outcome
options.wrong_explanation: Alignment isn't a guarantee.

options.label: Read big-picture context first, then detail — alignment adds confluence, not certainty

screens.explanation: Context-first reading with alignment as confluence (not certainty) is the throughline.

lessons.title: Pattern Speed Round
lessons.celebration: You can name any pattern fast!

screens.title: Name What You See
screens.text: Rapid-fire identification across everything you've learned. Read each chart and name it.

screens.question: Which pattern is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Two peaks at the same resistance is a double top.

screens.question: Which pattern is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Three peaks with a higher middle is a head & shoulders.

screens.question: Which pattern is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Flat top with rising lows is an ascending triangle.

screens.question: Which pattern is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: A strong up pole with a small downward flag is a bull flag.

screens.question: Which structure is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Falling and converging is a falling wedge.

lessons.title: Level Reading Round
lessons.celebration: You can mark levels anywhere!

screens.title: Find the Level
screens.text: Read the key level on each chart and mark it.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance on this chart.
screens.explanation: The level the highs were rejected at is the resistance.

screens.question: Drag the line to the support on this chart.
screens.explanation: The level the lows bounced from is the support.

screens.question: Drag the line to the flat resistance of this triangle.
screens.explanation: The flat top of the ascending triangle is the resistance.

screens.question: Drag the line to the range's support.
screens.explanation: The floor of the range is the support.

screens.question: Drag the line to the neckline of this head & shoulders.
screens.explanation: The neckline runs along the two troughs of the head & shoulders.

lessons.title: Candle Reading Round
lessons.celebration: You can read any candle!

screens.title: Tap the Candle
screens.text: Read each chart and tap the candle described.

screens.question: Tap the doji.
screens.explanation: The middle candle's tiny body with wicks both sides is the doji.

screens.question: Tap the hammer.
screens.explanation: The last candle — small body up top, long lower wick — is the hammer.

screens.question: Tap the shooting star.
screens.explanation: The last candle — small body down low, long upper wick — is the shooting star.

screens.question: Tap the engulfing candle.
screens.explanation: The larger down candle covering the prior up candle is the bearish engulfing.

screens.question: Tap the big-momentum candle.
screens.explanation: The big-bodied, near-wickless candle is the momentum (marubozu) candle.

lessons.title: Multi-Candle Round
lessons.celebration: You can tap groups of candles!

screens.title: Tap All That Match
screens.text: Some reads need more than one candle. Tap every candle that matches.

screens.question: Tap BOTH peaks of the double top.
screens.explanation: The 2nd and 4th candles are the two peaks at resistance.

screens.question: Tap BOTH troughs of the double bottom.
screens.explanation: The 2nd and 4th candles are the two troughs at support.

screens.question: Tap BOTH shoulders of the head & shoulders.
screens.explanation: The 2nd and 6th candles are the left and right shoulders.

screens.question: Tap the three touches of the flat resistance.
screens.explanation: The 1st, 3rd, and 5th candles push into the flat resistance.

lessons.title: Reversal or Continuation?
lessons.celebration: You can classify the setup type!

screens.title: Turn or Keep Going?
screens.text: Classify each chart as a reversal shape (a possible turn) or a continuation shape (a likely resume) — descriptively.

screens.question: Is a head & shoulders commonly read as a reversal or a continuation shape?
options: Reversal (a possible turn after an up-move).
screens.explanation: Head & shoulders is commonly read as a reversal shape.

screens.question: Is a bull flag commonly read as a reversal or a continuation shape?
options: Continuation (a pause that often resumes up).
screens.explanation: Flags are continuation patterns.

screens.question: Is a double bottom commonly read as a reversal or continuation shape?
options: Reversal (a possible turn up after a down-move).
screens.explanation: A double bottom is commonly read as a reversal shape.

screens.question: Match each to its usual category.
screens.explanation: Reversal shapes suggest a turn; continuation shapes suggest a resume.

screens.question: Every reversal shape guarantees a reversal.
screens.explanation: Categories describe tendencies; nothing is guaranteed.

lessons.title: Putting It All Together
lessons.celebration: You can read a full chart!

screens.title: Everything at Once
screens.text: Combine pattern, level, and candle reads on each chart — the whole intermediate skillset.

screens.question: On the chart above, two peaks stall at resistance and roll over. Best read?

options.label: A double top at resistance — a reversal shape at a level (confluence)
A bull flag
options.wrong_explanation: This is two peaks at resistance, not a pole-and-flag.

options.label: A guaranteed crash
options.wrong_explanation: Confluence isn't a guarantee.

screens.explanation: Pattern + level agreeing is a confluent, descriptive read — not a guarantee.

screens.question: Drag the line to the resistance in this double top.
screens.explanation: The two peaks mark the resistance being tested.

screens.question: Tap the second peak.
screens.explanation: The 4th candle is the second peak at resistance.

screens.question: A pattern that lines up with a key level is stronger evidence than the pattern alone.
screens.explanation: Pattern-plus-level is confluence — stronger than either alone.

screens.scenario: Someone reads one perfect pattern and ignores the level, the trend, and the candles around it.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A full read combines pattern, level, trend, and candles — not one factor in isolation.
screens.explanation: The strongest reads combine several agreeing factors, not a lone signal.

lessons.title: Intermediate Mastery Review
lessons.celebration: You've completed the Intermediate level!

screens.title: You Can Read Charts
screens.text: You've learned patterns, levels, candles, structure, and confluence — and to read them all descriptively, never as guarantees. A final check.

screens.question: What ties this whole level together?
options: Reading charts descriptively — patterns, levels, and candles as clues, not guarantees.
screens.explanation: Descriptive, context-aware chart reading is the throughline of the level.

screens.question: Match each skill to what it reads.
pairs: Shapes like double tops, triangles, flags
screens.explanation: A recap of the three core reading skills.

screens.template: The strongest reads combine [__1__] agreeing factors, but are still [__2__] guarantees.
screens.explanation: Confluence is stronger but never a guarantee.

screens.question: Which best summarizes the Intermediate level?

options.label: Read patterns, levels, and candles together — descriptively, as probabilities, not certainties
A system of guaranteed signals
options.wrong_explanation: Nothing here is guaranteed.

options.label: A list of shapes with no context
options.wrong_explanation: Context and confluence are the point.

screens.explanation: Context-aware, descriptive, probability-minded reading is what this level built.

screens.scenario: Someone finishes this level and starts treating every pattern as a guaranteed trade.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Context stops mattering after this level.
Everything here is a descriptive clue read with context — never a guaranteed trade.
screens.explanation: The whole level teaches probability-minded, descriptive reading — not guarantees.

lessons.title: What Is Risk Per Trade?
lessons.celebration: You understand risk per trade!

screens.title: How Much Is on the Line
screens.text: Risk per trade describes how much of your capital could be lost on a single trade if it goes against you.

screens.question: Risk per trade describes how much capital could be lost on a single trade if it goes against you.
screens.explanation: That's the standard definition of risk per trade.

screens.question: Risking a larger portion of your account on one trade is generally considered [___] risk.
screens.explanation: A bigger portion of capital at stake means a larger risk for that trade.

screens.question: Why is thinking about risk per trade useful, in general terms?
options: It helps quantify how much a single loss could realistically cost.
It guarantees the trade will be profitable.
It removes the need for a stop-loss entirely.
screens.explanation: Quantifying potential loss is the whole point of thinking about risk per trade.

screens.question: Match the risk framing to its description.
pairs: How much could be lost on one specific trade
The combined risk across all open positions
How much loss someone is generally comfortable with
screens.explanation: These related concepts together build a fuller risk picture.

screens.template: Risking 10% of an account on one trade is generally considered a [__1__] risk than risking [__2__]%.
screens.explanation: A larger percentage risked per trade means a bigger potential impact from one loss.

screens.question: A simple way to think through risk before placing a trade:
items: Decide the maximum dollar amount you're willing to risk
Compare that amount to your total account size
Express it as a percentage of your account
Use that percentage to inform your position size
correct_order: Decide the maximum dollar amount you're willing to risk
Compare that amount to your total account size
Express it as a percentage of your account
Use that percentage to inform your position size
screens.explanation: This process turns an abstract risk tolerance into a concrete plan.

screens.question: Which best describes "risk per trade"?

options.label: A guarantee of how much you will actually lose
options.wrong_explanation: It's the potential loss if things go against you, not a guaranteed outcome.

options.label: How much of your capital could be lost if a single trade goes against you
The total amount of money in your account
options.wrong_explanation: That's your total account size, not the risk on one trade.

screens.explanation: Risk per trade specifically describes the potential loss on a single position.

screens.scenario: Someone risks 50% of their account on a single trade because they feel very confident about it.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should have felt even more confident before risking that much.
Risking such a large portion of an account on one trade exposes it to severe damage from a single loss.
They should have risked their entire account instead.
screens.explanation: Confidence in an outcome doesn't remove risk — a single loss at that size could be very damaging.

lessons.title: Position Sizing Basics
lessons.celebration: You understand position sizing!

screens.title: How Much to Put In
screens.text: Position sizing is the process of deciding how much capital to allocate to a single trade, commonly derived from your risk tolerance.

screens.question: Position size is commonly derived from your risk tolerance and stop-loss level.
screens.explanation: A sound position size is commonly calculated backward from how much you're willing to risk.

screens.question: The amount of capital allocated to a single trade is commonly called its [___].
screens.explanation: "Position size" describes how much of your capital a single trade uses.

screens.question: What is a commonly cited way to calculate an appropriate position size?
options: Start from your maximum acceptable dollar risk, then work out the size that keeps a stop-loss hit within that amount.
Always use the same position size regardless of the stop-loss distance.
Randomly pick a size that feels right in the moment.
screens.explanation: Working backward from acceptable risk is a commonly cited, methodical approach.

screens.question: Match the risk concept to its description.
pairs: How much capital is allocated to a single trade
How far price can move before the risk limit is hit
The most you're willing to lose on that trade
screens.explanation: These three concepts together determine an appropriate position size.

screens.template: A wider stop-loss distance generally calls for a [__1__] position size, to keep the same dollar [__2__].
screens.explanation: If the stop is further away, a smaller size keeps the total dollar risk the same.

screens.question: A simple way to calculate position size before a trade:
items: Decide the maximum dollar amount you're willing to risk
Decide where your stop-loss level would be
Calculate the position size that keeps the loss within that maximum if the stop is hit
Only then consider the position size final
correct_order: Decide the maximum dollar amount you're willing to risk
Decide where your stop-loss level would be
Calculate the position size that keeps the loss within that maximum if the stop is hit
Only then consider the position size final
screens.explanation: Position size is commonly derived from your risk tolerance and stop level, not chosen randomly.

screens.question: Which of these two hypothetical trades has the better risk-to-reward ratio, as described?

options.label: Risking $100 to potentially make $100 (1:1)
options.wrong_explanation: Reward here is equal to risk, not more favorable.

options.label: Risking $100 to potentially make $50 (2:1 against)
options.wrong_explanation: This risks more than it could potentially gain.

options.label: Risking $100 to potentially make $300 (1:3)
options.detail: Reward is three times the risk

screens.explanation: A higher reward relative to the risk taken is generally considered a more favorable ratio, on paper.

screens.scenario: Someone uses the exact same position size on every trade, regardless of how far away their stop-loss is.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should always use an even bigger position size instead.
They should remove stop-losses to simplify things.
A fixed position size regardless of stop distance means dollar risk varies unpredictably between trades.
screens.explanation: Adjusting position size to the stop-loss distance is how consistent dollar risk is commonly maintained.

lessons.title: Risk/Reward Ratio
lessons.celebration: You understand risk/reward ratios!

screens.title: What You Could Lose vs. Gain
screens.text: A risk/reward ratio compares the potential loss on a trade to its potential gain — pure math, not a signal.

screens.question: A "2:1 risk-to-reward ratio" means the potential reward is twice the potential risk.
screens.explanation: That's the standard meaning of a 2:1 (or similarly stated) risk/reward ratio.

screens.question: A trade risking $100 to potentially make $200 has a risk/reward ratio of [___].
screens.explanation: $100 of risk against $200 of potential reward is a 1:2 ratio (risk:reward).

screens.question: What does a favorable risk/reward ratio generally describe?
options: A guarantee that the trade will be profitable.
The exact number of shares being traded.
Potential reward that is larger than the potential risk taken.
screens.explanation: Risk/reward describes the relationship between potential loss and gain, not a guaranteed outcome.

screens.question: Match the risk/reward description to its general reading.
pairs: Generally considered a more favorable ratio
Generally considered a less favorable ratio
screens.explanation: Comparing potential reward to potential risk is the core of this concept.

screens.template: A [__1__] risk/reward ratio means more potential reward for the same [__2__] taken.
screens.explanation: A higher ratio means a larger potential payoff relative to the risk.

screens.question: A simple way to calculate a trade's risk/reward ratio before entering:
items: Identify your planned entry price
Identify your planned stop-loss level (the risk)
Identify your planned target level (the reward)
Compare the two distances as a ratio
correct_order: Identify your planned entry price
Identify your planned stop-loss level (the risk)
Identify your planned target level (the reward)
Compare the two distances as a ratio
screens.explanation: This calculation can be done in advance, before a trade is even placed.

screens.question: Which best describes what risk/reward ratio measures, on its own?

options.label: The relationship between potential loss and potential gain on a trade
options.detail: A math comparison, not a certainty

options.label: The total dollar amount in your account
options.wrong_explanation: That's your account size, not a per-trade ratio.

options.label: A guarantee of how the trade will actually turn out
options.wrong_explanation: It's a ratio of possibilities, not a guaranteed outcome.

screens.explanation: Risk/reward is a mathematical comparison, not a prediction of the outcome.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a favorable risk/reward ratio guarantees the trade will be profitable.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should look for an even higher ratio to be sure.
They should ignore risk/reward ratios entirely.
A favorable ratio describes the potential payoff structure, not a guarantee that the trade succeeds.
screens.explanation: Risk/reward is about the shape of possible outcomes, not a certainty about which one happens.

lessons.title: Stop-Loss Placement Logic
lessons.celebration: You understand where stop-losses are commonly placed!

screens.title: Not Just a Random Number
screens.text: Stop-loss placement is commonly tied to a specific reason — like a nearby support/resistance level — rather than an arbitrary number.

screens.question: A stop-loss level is commonly chosen completely at random, with no specific reasoning.
screens.explanation: Stop-loss levels are commonly tied to a specific reason, like a nearby support or resistance level.

screens.question: Placing a stop-loss just beyond a nearby support or resistance level is a commonly cited [___].
screens.explanation: This is a commonly cited approach, among several, for placing a stop-loss with a clear reason behind it.

screens.question: Why might a stop-loss be placed just beyond a nearby support level?
options: If that level breaks, it may suggest the original reason for the trade no longer holds.
It guarantees the stop will never be triggered.
It has no relationship to the trade's original reasoning.
screens.explanation: Tying the stop to a meaningful level gives it a clear, describable reason.

screens.question: Match the stop-loss placement idea to its reasoning.
pairs: Tied to a level that would invalidate the original idea
Tied to a consistent risk amount regardless of chart structure
Commonly cited as being triggered by normal price noise
screens.explanation: These are different commonly discussed approaches to stop-loss placement.

screens.template: A stop-loss placed too [__1__] may get triggered by normal price [__2__], not a meaningful shift.
screens.explanation: A stop set with too little room can be triggered by ordinary fluctuations rather than a real change in the picture.

screens.question: A simple way to think through stop-loss placement:
items: Identify the specific reason for the trade
Identify what price level would suggest that reason no longer holds
Place the stop-loss just beyond that level
Confirm the resulting risk fits your position sizing plan
correct_order: Identify the specific reason for the trade
Identify what price level would suggest that reason no longer holds
Place the stop-loss just beyond that level
Confirm the resulting risk fits your position sizing plan
screens.explanation: This ties the stop-loss to a specific reason rather than an arbitrary number.

screens.question: Which best describes a stop-loss placed "just beyond a nearby support level"?

options.label: A completely random number with no logic behind it
options.wrong_explanation: This approach is specifically about having a clear reason.

options.label: A guarantee the position will never lose money
options.wrong_explanation: A stop-loss limits risk; it doesn't guarantee no loss ever occurs.

options.label: Tied to a level that would suggest the original trade idea no longer holds

screens.explanation: Tying the stop to a meaningful level gives it a clear, describable rationale.

screens.scenario: Someone sets a stop-loss extremely close to their entry price, with no particular reasoning behind the distance.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A stop placed too close with no reasoning can get triggered by normal price noise rather than a meaningful shift.
They should remove the stop-loss entirely instead.
They should place it even closer for extra safety.
screens.explanation: Stop-loss placement is commonly tied to a specific, reasoned level rather than an arbitrarily tight distance.

lessons.title: Overleveraging Danger
lessons.celebration: You understand the danger of overleveraging!

screens.title: Amplifying Both Directions
screens.text: Leverage amplifies both potential gains and potential losses — overleveraging describes using more than a comfortable, risk-appropriate amount.

screens.question: Leverage only amplifies potential gains, never potential losses.
screens.explanation: Leverage amplifies both directions — potential gains and potential losses alike.

screens.question: Using more leverage than is appropriate for your risk tolerance is commonly called [___].
screens.explanation: "Overleveraging" describes taking on leverage beyond what fits your risk tolerance.

screens.question: Why is overleveraging commonly cited as a significant danger?
options: It guarantees larger profits with no added risk.
It has no effect on the size of potential losses.
It amplifies losses, potentially causing much larger damage from a single adverse move.
screens.explanation: Amplified losses are the commonly cited core danger of overleveraging.

screens.question: Match the leverage concept to its description.
pairs: A tool that amplifies both potential gains and losses
Using more leverage than fits one's risk tolerance
Sized to fit an individual's risk tolerance and plan
screens.explanation: Leverage itself is a neutral tool; overleveraging describes misusing it relative to one's own risk tolerance.

screens.template: Leverage can [__1__] both potential gains and potential [__2__] from the same price move.
screens.explanation: This dual amplification is the core mechanism behind leverage's risk.

screens.question: A simple way to think through leverage before using it:
items: Understand that leverage amplifies both gains and losses
Consider your own risk tolerance and capital
Choose a leverage level that fits that risk tolerance
Avoid leverage levels that would cause outsized damage from a single move
correct_order: Understand that leverage amplifies both gains and losses
Consider your own risk tolerance and capital
Choose a leverage level that fits that risk tolerance
Avoid leverage levels that would cause outsized damage from a single move
screens.explanation: This keeps leverage decisions tied to individual risk tolerance rather than chasing amplified gains alone.

screens.question: Which best describes "overleveraging"?

options.label: A guarantee of larger losses no matter what
options.wrong_explanation: It raises risk, but exact outcomes still depend on what actually happens.

options.label: Using any leverage at all, under any circumstances
options.wrong_explanation: Leverage itself isn't inherently overleveraging; it's about fit with risk tolerance.

options.label: Using more leverage than fits your own risk tolerance
options.detail: A mismatch between leverage and personal risk capacity

screens.explanation: Overleveraging specifically describes a mismatch between leverage used and one's own risk tolerance.

screens.scenario: Someone uses very high leverage because "it worked out fine last time."
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should use even higher leverage next time to be consistent.
Past luck with high leverage doesn't reduce the risk of amplified losses on a future adverse move.
They should assume high leverage always works out.
screens.explanation: One favorable past outcome doesn't change the underlying amplified risk that leverage carries.

lessons.title: Drawdowns
lessons.celebration: You understand drawdowns!

screens.title: The Dip From a Peak
screens.text: A drawdown measures how far an account has fallen from a prior peak value — a normal part of any trading account's history.

screens.question: A drawdown measures how far an account has fallen from its prior peak value.
screens.explanation: That's the standard definition of a drawdown.

screens.question: The percentage decline from an account's highest value to a subsequent low point is called a [___].
screens.explanation: "Drawdown" is the standard term for this kind of decline.

screens.question: Why is understanding drawdowns commonly considered useful?
options: It helps set realistic expectations that account value doesn't move in a straight line.
It only applies to accounts that have never had any losses.
It guarantees an account will never decline again.
screens.explanation: Understanding drawdowns helps build realistic expectations about a normal account's ups and downs.

screens.question: Match the drawdown concept to its description.
pairs: The highest point an account has reached so far
A subsequent lower point after the peak
The percentage decline from peak to trough
screens.explanation: These three concepts together define how a drawdown is measured.

screens.template: Even accounts that are [__1__] over the long run commonly experience some [__2__] along the way.
screens.explanation: Drawdowns are a normal part of most account histories, even ones that end up profitable overall.

screens.question: A simple way to calculate a drawdown:
items: Identify the account's peak value so far
Identify the lowest value reached after that peak
Calculate the percentage decline between the two
Describe that percentage as the drawdown
correct_order: Identify the account's peak value so far
Identify the lowest value reached after that peak
Calculate the percentage decline between the two
Describe that percentage as the drawdown
screens.explanation: This is a straightforward, descriptive calculation based on account history.

screens.question: Which best describes a "20% drawdown"?

options.label: A rule requiring the account to close
options.wrong_explanation: A drawdown is a descriptive measurement, not a mandated action.

options.label: A guarantee the account will recover fully
options.wrong_explanation: A drawdown describes what happened, not a guaranteed recovery.

options.label: The account has fallen 20% from its prior peak value

screens.explanation: A drawdown specifically measures the decline from peak, nothing more or less.

screens.scenario: Someone panics and assumes any drawdown means their overall trading approach has permanently failed.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Drawdowns are a normal, expected part of most account histories, even ones that are profitable overall.
They should avoid ever checking their account value again.
They should assume every drawdown means immediate, permanent failure.
screens.explanation: A single drawdown doesn't by itself indicate a permanent failure of an overall approach.

lessons.title: Losing Streaks Are Normal
lessons.celebration: You understand that losing streaks happen!

screens.title: Even With a Sound Plan
screens.text: A string of losing trades in a row can happen even to a reasonable, well-thought-out approach — it's a normal part of trading, not proof of failure.

screens.question: A losing streak automatically proves that a trading approach is fundamentally flawed.
screens.explanation: Losing streaks can happen even with a reasonable approach — they don't automatically prove it's flawed.

screens.question: A string of consecutive losing trades is commonly called a losing [___].
screens.explanation: "Losing streak" is the standard term for this kind of consecutive-loss sequence.

screens.question: Why might a losing streak happen even with a reasonable approach?
options: A losing streak is mathematically impossible with any sound approach.
No approach wins every single time; some losses in a row can occur by chance alone.
Losing streaks only happen to beginners.
screens.explanation: Even a reasonable approach with a positive long-run track record can still see a run of losses.

screens.question: Match the concept to a commonly cited description.
pairs: A run of consecutive losing trades
The idea that some losses in a row can occur even with a sound plan
Abandoning a reasonable plan solely because of a losing streak
screens.explanation: These concepts together explain why a losing streak doesn't automatically mean a plan has failed.

screens.template: A losing streak is commonly described as [__1__], not automatic proof that a plan is [__2__].
screens.explanation: Some run of losses is statistically possible even with a reasonable, well-thought-out approach.

screens.question: A calmer way to respond to a losing streak:
items: Pause before making any big changes
Review whether the original plan was actually followed
Consider whether anything specific needs adjusting
Avoid abandoning a reasonable plan based on short-term results alone
correct_order: Pause before making any big changes
Review whether the original plan was actually followed
Consider whether anything specific needs adjusting
Avoid abandoning a reasonable plan based on short-term results alone
screens.explanation: A measured review is commonly recommended over an immediate, emotional overhaul.

screens.question: Which best reflects a balanced way to think about a losing streak?

options.label: "This can happen even with a reasonable plan; worth a calm review"
"Losing streaks are impossible with any sound approach"
options.wrong_explanation: Losing streaks can happen even with reasonable approaches.

options.label: "This proves my plan is completely worthless"
options.wrong_explanation: A losing streak alone doesn't prove that.

screens.explanation: The balanced view treats a losing streak as possible and worth reviewing, not an automatic verdict.

screens.scenario: Someone abandons a carefully planned approach entirely after just two losing trades in a row.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: They should never review their plan under any circumstances.
Two losses in a row can happen even with a reasonable approach — it doesn't necessarily mean the approach has failed.
They should have taken on much more risk instead.
screens.explanation: A short losing streak alone is often not enough evidence to conclude a reasonable plan has failed.

lessons.title: Capital Preservation Mindset
lessons.celebration: You understand capital preservation!

screens.title: Protecting What You Have
screens.text: Capital preservation describes prioritizing protection of existing capital, commonly viewed as foundational to being able to trade over the long term.

screens.question: Capital preservation describes prioritizing protection of existing capital.
screens.explanation: That's the standard descriptive meaning of a capital preservation mindset.

screens.question: Protecting your existing capital is commonly viewed as foundational to trading over the [___] term.
screens.explanation: Without capital, there's nothing left to trade with — preservation supports staying in the game long-term.

screens.question: Why might capital preservation be commonly emphasized alongside potential gains?
options: Capital preservation has no relationship to risk management.
Without sufficient capital remaining, there's nothing left to trade with going forward.
Preserving capital guarantees higher returns than any other approach.
screens.explanation: Capital preservation is commonly linked to risk management, since capital is needed to keep participating at all.

screens.question: Match the mindset to its general focus.
pairs: Prioritizing potential gains, often with less protection
Weighing both protection and potential upside together
screens.explanation: These represent different general postures toward risk and capital.

screens.template: A capital preservation mindset is commonly linked to sound [__1__] management, not the complete avoidance of all [__2__].
screens.explanation: Preservation doesn't mean avoiding all risk — it means managing it deliberately.

screens.question: A simple way to build a capital preservation mindset into a plan:
items: Define an acceptable risk per trade in advance
Use position sizing consistent with that risk
Avoid outsized risk on any single trade
Review the overall plan periodically
correct_order: Define an acceptable risk per trade in advance
Use position sizing consistent with that risk
Avoid outsized risk on any single trade
Review the overall plan periodically
screens.explanation: These steps together support protecting capital while still participating in the market.

screens.question: Which best describes a capital preservation mindset?

options.label: Avoiding all risk entirely, under every circumstance
options.wrong_explanation: Preservation is about managing risk deliberately, not eliminating it entirely.

options.label: Guaranteeing profits no matter what
options.wrong_explanation: Preservation focuses on protecting capital, not guaranteeing gains.

options.label: Prioritizing protection of existing capital as foundational to trading long-term

screens.explanation: Capital preservation is about deliberate protection, not the total avoidance of risk or a guarantee of profit.

screens.scenario: Someone dismisses capital preservation as unnecessary because they're only focused on maximizing potential gains.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Without capital remaining, there's nothing left to generate future gains with — preservation and growth are commonly linked.
They should ignore risk management entirely from now on.
They should take on the maximum possible risk on every trade instead.
screens.explanation: Capital preservation is commonly viewed as foundational to being able to keep participating and pursuing gains long-term.

lessons.title: Risk Management Drill
lessons.celebration: You can apply risk concepts to hypothetical scenarios!

screens.title: Practice Round
screens.text: Practice applying risk management concepts to a few hypothetical situations.

screens.question: A trader has $10,000 and wants to risk no more than 1% on a single trade. What's the maximum dollar risk on that trade?

options.wrong_explanation: 0.1% of $10,000 is $10, not the 1% requested.
10% of $10,000 is $1,000, not the 1% requested.

screens.explanation: 1% of a $10,000 account is $100 in maximum dollar risk.

screens.question: A wider stop-loss distance generally requires a smaller position size to keep the same dollar risk.
screens.explanation: If the stop is further from entry, a smaller size is needed to cap the dollar loss at the same amount.

screens.question: Which of two hypothetical trades has a more favorable risk/reward ratio?
screens.explanation: A $50 risk for a $150 potential reward is a 1:3 ratio, more favorable than 1:1 or worse.

screens.question: Setting aside a maximum acceptable dollar loss before placing a trade is part of sound [___] management.
screens.explanation: Planning a maximum acceptable loss in advance is a core part of risk management.

screens.question: Match the risk scenario to a commonly cited response.
pairs: A losing streak of several trades in a row
Pause and review calmly rather than panic
A trade with a very unfavorable risk/reward ratio
Position size that would risk 20% of the account
Reduce size to fit a smaller risk percentage
screens.explanation: These are commonly cited, level-headed responses to each situation.

screens.scenario: Someone increases their position size significantly right after a big win, without changing their stop-loss plan.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Increasing size without adjusting the plan can unintentionally increase dollar risk beyond what was originally intended.
They should increase their position size even further.
They should remove their stop-loss to simplify things.
screens.explanation: Position size changes should stay tied to a consistent risk plan, not be driven by a recent win.

lessons.title: Risk Management Review
lessons.celebration: You've completed the Risk Management unit!

screens.title: Bringing It All Together
screens.text: A final review of risk per trade, position sizing, risk/reward, leverage, drawdowns, and capital preservation.

screens.question: Everything in this unit is about managing potential loss, not guaranteeing profit.
screens.explanation: That's the common thread across every concept in this unit.

screens.question: The process of deciding how much capital to allocate to a trade is called [___].
screens.explanation: Reviewing the core term from earlier in this unit.

screens.question: What do risk per trade, position sizing, and risk/reward ratio all have in common?

screens.text: To turn a risk percent into dollars: multiply the account size by the percent. On a $10,000 account, 1% risk = $100.

screens.title: R = The Amount Risked
screens.text: "R" is shorthand for the amount you risked on a trade. If you risk $100, then 1R = $100. Measuring results in R lets you compare trades of different sizes.

screens.question: If you risk $100 on a trade, then 1R equals...
screens.explanation: 1R is simply the amount risked — here, $100.

screens.question: "R" stands for the amount you [___] on the trade.
screens.explanation: R is the risk amount; results are measured in multiples of it.

screens.question: If you risk $250 on a trade, then 1R equals...
screens.explanation: 1R = the amount risked = $250.

screens.question: Measuring results in R lets you compare trades of different dollar sizes.
screens.explanation: R normalizes results, so a "2R win" means the same regardless of position size.

lessons.title: Reward in R
lessons.celebration: You can measure reward in R!

screens.title: Wins as Multiples of Risk
screens.text: A win is measured in R too. If you risk $100 (1R) and gain $200, that's a +2R result. A loss of the full risk is −1R.

screens.question: You risk $100 and the trade gains $200. That result is...
screens.explanation: A $200 gain on $100 risk is twice the risk — +2R.

screens.question: You risk $100 and the trade loses the full risk. That result is...
screens.explanation: Losing the full amount risked is −1R.

screens.question: A gain of three times your risk is a [___] result.
screens.explanation: Three times the risk gained is +3R.

screens.question: You risk $200 and gain $600. That result is...
screens.explanation: $600 gain on $200 risk is three times the risk — +3R.

screens.question: A full loss is −1R, since you lost exactly the amount you risked.
screens.explanation: Losing the whole risked amount is by definition −1R.
