A gain of twice the risk
Chosen so a stopped-out loss equals the planned risk
screens.explanation: A recap of the unit's core math.

screens.template: Dollar risk = account size × risk [__1__]; results are measured in multiples of [__2__].
screens.explanation: Percent gives dollar risk; R measures the results.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Risk a small consistent percent, size from the stop, and measure results in R
Size randomly and hope
options.wrong_explanation: The unit is about a consistent method.

options.label: Bigger size always means bigger profit
options.wrong_explanation: Size sets risk, not guaranteed profit.

screens.explanation: Consistent percent risk, stop-based sizing, and R measurement is the throughline.

lessons.title: Win Rate Isn't Everything
lessons.celebration: You understand why win rate alone misleads!

screens.title: How Often vs. How Much
screens.text: Win rate is how often you win. But it ignores how much you win or lose. A high win rate with tiny wins and huge losses can still lose money overall.

screens.question: Win rate measures...
screens.explanation: Win rate is the frequency of wins, not their size.

screens.question: A high win rate always means a profitable system.
screens.explanation: If wins are tiny and losses are huge, even a high win rate can lose overall.

screens.question: Win rate ignores how [___] you win or lose per trade.
screens.explanation: Win rate is frequency only; it ignores the size of wins and losses.

screens.question: Why isn't win rate enough on its own?

options.label: Because it's always wrong
options.wrong_explanation: Win rate is useful, just incomplete.

options.label: Because it ignores the size of the wins and losses
Because winning never matters
options.wrong_explanation: Both how often and how much matter.

screens.explanation: You need both how often (win rate) and how much (R) to judge results.

lessons.title: Combining Win Rate and R
lessons.celebration: You can combine win rate and R!

screens.title: Frequency Meets Size
screens.text: The honest picture combines win rate (how often) with average R (how much). A lower win rate can still come out ahead if the average win in R is large enough.

screens.question: To judge a system honestly, combine win rate with...
screens.explanation: Win rate plus average R (size) gives the honest picture.

screens.question: A 40% win rate can still be profitable if the average winner is large in R.
screens.explanation: Big average wins (in R) can outweigh more frequent small losses.

screens.template: Combine how [__1__] you win with how [__2__] you win to judge a system.
screens.explanation: Frequency (win rate) and size (R) together tell the story.

screens.question: A system wins 40% of the time but averages +3R on wins and −1R on losses. This can be...
options: profitable overall, thanks to the large average win.
guaranteed to lose because win rate is under 50%.
screens.explanation: Large average wins can more than offset frequent small losses.

lessons.title: What Is Expectancy?
lessons.celebration: You understand expectancy!

screens.title: Average Result Per Trade
screens.text: Expectancy is the average result per trade, measured in R, over many trades. A positive expectancy means the average trade gains R over the long run.

screens.question: Expectancy is the...
options: average result per trade (in R) over many trades.
screens.explanation: Expectancy is the long-run average result per trade.

screens.question: A positive expectancy means the average trade, over many trades, gains R.
screens.explanation: Positive expectancy = the average trade comes out ahead in R over the long run.

screens.question: Expectancy is the average result per trade measured in [___].
screens.explanation: Expressed in R, expectancy compares across position sizes.

screens.question: Why is expectancy a long-run idea?

options.label: Because it's an average that only holds over many trades, not any single one
Because it predicts the next trade exactly
options.wrong_explanation: It says nothing certain about one trade.

options.label: Because it ignores wins and losses
options.wrong_explanation: It's built from wins and losses.

screens.explanation: Expectancy is an average over many trades, not a promise about any single one.

lessons.title: Winning With Under 50% Wins
lessons.celebration: You understand how low win rates can still win!

screens.title: Big Wins, Small Losses
screens.text: A system can be profitable with a win rate below 50% if its winners are much larger (in R) than its losers. Size can outweigh frequency.

screens.question: A system with a 35% win rate can still be profitable if...
options: its winners are much larger in R than its losers.
screens.explanation: Large winners in R can outweigh more frequent, smaller losers.

screens.question: You must win more than half your trades to be profitable.
screens.explanation: With large enough winners in R, a sub-50% win rate can still profit.

screens.question: A low win rate can still win if the [___] are much larger in R.
screens.explanation: Larger winners in R can more than offset frequent small losses.

screens.scenario: Someone dismisses a system purely because its win rate is under 50%, without checking the average R.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Win rate alone isn't enough — a sub-50% system with large winners in R can still have positive expectancy.
screens.explanation: Both win rate and average R matter; ignoring R misjudges the system.

lessons.title: Sample Size Matters
lessons.celebration: You understand sample size!

screens.title: A Few Trades Prove Little
screens.text: Expectancy and win rate only mean something over a large enough sample. A handful of trades can look great or terrible purely by chance.

screens.question: Expectancy is meaningful only over...
options: a large enough sample of trades.
screens.explanation: Averages need many trades to be meaningful; small samples are noisy.

screens.question: Three winning trades in a row prove a system has positive expectancy.
screens.explanation: A tiny sample can happen by chance; it doesn't prove long-run expectancy.

screens.question: A small [___] of trades can look great or terrible purely by chance.
screens.explanation: Small samples are dominated by luck, not the true average.

screens.question: Why be careful with a small sample?

options.label: Because small samples are always accurate
options.wrong_explanation: They're the least reliable.

options.label: Because chance can make a few trades misleading in either direction
Because sample size never matters
options.wrong_explanation: It's central to trusting an average.

screens.explanation: Small samples are dominated by luck, so they can badly mislead.

lessons.title: Expectancy & Edge Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered expectancy & edge!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of win rate, R, expectancy, and sample size.

screens.question: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: How much trades win or lose, in R
The average result per trade over many trades
screens.explanation: A recap of the unit's core ideas.

screens.question: What two things must you combine to judge a system honestly?
options: Candle color and time of day.
screens.explanation: Frequency (win rate) plus size (average R) gives the honest picture.

screens.template: A system can profit with a [__1__] win rate if its winners are [__2__] in R.
screens.explanation: Large winners in R can offset a lower win rate.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Judge a system by win rate alone
options.wrong_explanation: Win rate alone can mislead.

options.label: Judge a system by expectancy — win rate and R together, over a large sample
A few trades prove everything
options.wrong_explanation: Sample size matters.

screens.explanation: Expectancy (win rate × R over many trades) is the honest measure.

screens.scenario: Someone judges a brand-new system as "amazing" after two lucky wins.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Two trades is far too small a sample to judge expectancy — that's chance, not proof.
Two wins prove a positive expectancy.
screens.explanation: Expectancy needs a large sample; a couple of wins prove nothing.

lessons.title: Trending, Ranging, or Volatile?
lessons.celebration: You can classify market conditions!

screens.title: Three Broad Conditions
screens.text: Markets are commonly classified into broad conditions: trending (directional), ranging (sideways between levels), and volatile (large, erratic swings). Reading the condition guides how you read everything else.

screens.question: The chart above makes steady higher highs and higher lows. This condition is...
screens.explanation: Directional progress (higher highs/lows) is a trending condition.

screens.question: The chart above bounces sideways between two levels. This condition is...
screens.explanation: Sideways between support and resistance is a ranging condition.

screens.question: The chart above shows large, erratic swings with no clear direction. This condition is...
screens.explanation: Big, erratic swings with no clear direction is a volatile condition.

screens.question: Match each condition to its description.
screens.explanation: These three broad conditions describe most markets.

lessons.title: Classifying a Trend
lessons.celebration: You can classify a trend!

screens.title: Direction and Structure
screens.text: A trending condition shows directional structure — higher highs and higher lows (up) or lower highs and lower lows (down).

screens.question: The chart above makes lower highs and lower lows. It is a...
screens.explanation: Lower highs and lower lows is a downtrend.

screens.question: An uptrend shows higher highs and higher lows.
screens.explanation: Rising highs and lows define an uptrend.

screens.question: Tap the lower high on this downtrend.
screens.explanation: The 3rd candle is the bounce that made a lower high, confirming the downtrend.

screens.question: A trending condition has a clear [___] in one direction.
screens.explanation: Directional progression is what makes it a trend.

lessons.title: Classifying a Range
lessons.celebration: You can classify a range!

screens.title: Sideways Between Levels
screens.text: A ranging condition moves sideways between a support and resistance, without directional progress.

screens.question: The chart above stays between a floor and ceiling. It is...
screens.explanation: Sideways between two levels is ranging.

screens.question: Drag the line to the range's resistance.
screens.explanation: The ceiling of the range is its resistance.

screens.question: A ranging market makes strong directional progress.
screens.explanation: Ranging is sideways — the opposite of directional progress.

screens.question: A range moves [___] between support and resistance.
screens.explanation: Sideways bounded movement is a range.

lessons.title: Classifying Volatile
lessons.celebration: You can classify volatile conditions!

screens.title: Big, Erratic Swings
screens.text: A volatile condition shows large, fast swings in both directions — big candles and long wicks — without a clean trend or tidy range.

screens.question: The chart above shows large swings both ways with no clean direction. It is...
screens.explanation: Big erratic two-way swings is a volatile condition.

screens.question: Volatile conditions have larger, faster swings than a calm range.
screens.explanation: Volatility means bigger, faster moves than a calm, tight range.

screens.question: Volatile conditions show large, [___] swings in both directions.
screens.explanation: Large erratic two-way swings define volatility.

screens.scenario: Someone treats a wildly volatile chart as a calm, tidy range.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Volatile and calm ranges are the same.
Big erratic swings are volatile, not a calm range — the condition was misread.
screens.explanation: Volatile conditions have far larger, more erratic swings than a tidy range.

lessons.title: Why Classification Matters
lessons.celebration: You understand why condition matters!

screens.title: Read the Room First
screens.text: The market condition frames everything else. A level that "holds" in a range may get blown through in a volatile spell. Reading the condition first is a core advanced skill.

screens.question: Why classify the market condition first?
options: Because it frames how you read levels, patterns, and candles.
Because it changes the candle colors.
Because it has no effect on anything.
screens.explanation: The condition sets the context for every other read.

screens.question: The same level can behave differently in a range vs a volatile condition.
screens.explanation: A level that holds calmly in a range can be blown through when volatile.

screens.question: The market condition [___] how you read everything else.
screens.explanation: Condition is the context that frames the rest of the read.

screens.question: Which best captures the role of condition?

options.label: It's the context you read first, before levels and patterns
It's irrelevant to reading a chart
options.wrong_explanation: It's central context.

options.label: It guarantees the next move
options.wrong_explanation: It frames, it doesn't guarantee.

screens.explanation: Condition is the first-read context that frames every other read.

lessons.title: Classification Drill & Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered market classification!

screens.title: Read the Condition
screens.text: A final round — classify each chart's condition.

screens.question: Which condition is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Higher highs and higher lows is trending up.

screens.question: Which condition is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Sideways between levels is ranging.

screens.question: Which condition is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Large erratic swings is volatile.

screens.question: Which condition is shown on the chart above?
screens.explanation: Lower highs and lower lows is trending down.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Classify trending, ranging, or volatile first — it frames every other read
Classification guarantees the next move
options.wrong_explanation: It frames, not guarantees.

options.label: Condition never matters
options.wrong_explanation: It's core context.

screens.explanation: Condition-first reading is the throughline.

lessons.title: What Is a Moving Average?
lessons.celebration: You understand moving averages!

screens.title: The Average of Recent Prices
screens.text: A moving average (MA) is the average of the last N prices, recalculated each candle. A 20-period MA averages the last 20 closes. It's a smoothed line that follows price.

screens.question: A moving average is the...
options: average of the last N prices, updated each candle.
screens.explanation: An MA averages the most recent N prices and updates as new ones arrive.

screens.question: A 20-period moving average averages the last [___] prices.
screens.explanation: The number is how many recent prices it averages.

screens.question: A moving average updates as each new candle arrives.
screens.explanation: It's "moving" because it recalculates with each new price.

screens.question: What does a moving average give you?

options.label: The exact future value
A smoothed line summarizing recent price
A guarantee of the next price

screens.explanation: An MA smooths recent price into a line; it doesn't predict the future.

lessons.title: Smoothing Out Noise
lessons.celebration: You understand smoothing!

screens.title: Less Jitter, Clearer Direction
screens.text: Because it averages, a moving average smooths out the candle-to-candle jitter, making the broader direction easier to see.

screens.question: Averaging recent prices makes a moving average...
screens.explanation: Averaging smooths the noise, so the line is steadier than raw price.

screens.question: A moving average [___] out short-term noise.
screens.explanation: Averaging reduces the jitter, smoothing the line.

screens.question: A longer moving average is generally smoother than a shorter one.
screens.explanation: Averaging more prices smooths more, so longer MAs are steadier.

screens.question: Smoothing makes the broader [___] easier to see.
screens.explanation: With less noise, the general direction is clearer.

lessons.title: The Slope Reflects Trend
lessons.celebration: You can read an MA's slope!

screens.title: Rising, Falling, or Flat
screens.text: A moving average's slope reflects the trend: a rising MA reflects an uptrend, a falling MA a downtrend, and a flat MA a range. It's a smoothed read of direction.

screens.question: On a rising market like the chart above, a moving average would be...
screens.explanation: In an uptrend, the average of recent prices rises — the MA slopes up.

screens.question: A falling moving average reflects a downtrend.
screens.explanation: When recent prices fall, their average falls — the MA slopes down.

screens.question: A flat moving average most likely reflects a...
screens.explanation: Sideways price keeps the average roughly flat — a range.

screens.question: A moving average's [___] reflects the trend direction.
screens.explanation: The slope (up/down/flat) mirrors the trend.

lessons.title: Price Above vs. Below the MA
lessons.celebration: You can read price against the MA!

screens.title: Which Side Is Price On?
screens.text: Price trading above a rising MA is commonly described as strength; below a falling MA as weakness. It's a descriptive read, not a signal to act.

screens.question: Price holding above a rising moving average is commonly described as...
screens.explanation: Staying above a rising MA is commonly read as strength — descriptively.

screens.question: Price below a falling MA is commonly described as relative weakness.
screens.explanation: Trading under a falling average is commonly read as weakness.

screens.question: Price vs the MA is a [___] read, not a signal to act.
screens.explanation: It describes strength/weakness; it isn't an automatic buy/sell.

screens.scenario: Someone treats "price above the MA" as an automatic, guaranteed buy signal.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: The MA guarantees the next move.
Price above the MA is a descriptive strength read, not a guaranteed signal to act on.
screens.explanation: An MA read is descriptive context, never a guaranteed signal.

lessons.title: Short vs. Long MAs
lessons.celebration: You understand fast vs slow MAs!

screens.title: Fast and Slow
screens.text: A short MA (few periods) reacts quickly to price — it's "fast." A long MA (many periods) reacts slowly — it's "smooth and slow." Each shows a different scale of trend.

screens.question: A short-period MA is...
options: fast — it reacts quickly to price.
screens.explanation: Fewer periods means quicker reaction — a "fast" MA.

screens.question: A long-period MA is...
screens.explanation: More periods means slower reaction — a "slow," smooth MA.

screens.template: A short MA is [__1__]; a long MA is [__2__].
screens.explanation: Short = fast reaction; long = slow, smooth.

screens.question: A short MA hugs price more closely than a long MA.
screens.explanation: Reacting faster, the short MA tracks price more tightly.

lessons.title: MA Crossovers
lessons.celebration: You understand MA crossovers!

screens.title: When Fast Crosses Slow
screens.text: A "crossover" is when a fast MA crosses a slow MA. It's commonly used as a descriptive trend cue — but MAs are lagging (built from past prices), so crossovers are not guaranteed signals.

screens.question: An MA crossover is when...
options: a fast MA crosses a slow MA.
screens.explanation: A crossover is the fast and slow MAs crossing each other.

screens.question: Moving averages are lagging, since they're built from past prices.
screens.explanation: An MA is an average of past prices, so it lags current price.

screens.question: Because MAs are built from past prices, they are [___].
screens.explanation: Averaging past prices makes MAs lag, not lead.

screens.question: How should a crossover be read?

options.label: As a descriptive, lagging trend cue — not a guaranteed signal
As a leading predictor of price
options.wrong_explanation: MAs lag; they don't lead.

options.label: As a guaranteed entry
options.wrong_explanation: Crossovers lag and can whipsaw.

screens.explanation: A crossover is a lagging, descriptive cue, never a guarantee.

lessons.title: Moving Averages Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered moving averages!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of what an MA is, smoothing, slope, price-vs-MA, and crossovers.

screens.question: Match each idea to its meaning.
pairs: The average of the last N prices
Fast MA crossing slow MA (a lagging cue)
screens.explanation: A recap of the unit's core ideas.

screens.question: What does an MA's slope reflect?
screens.explanation: Slope up/down/flat mirrors the trend.

screens.template: A moving average [__1__] price and [__2__] the current price (it's lagging).
screens.explanation: MAs smooth and lag; they don't predict.

screens.question: Which best summarizes moving averages?

options.label: A predictor of the next price
options.wrong_explanation: MAs lag, they don't predict.

options.label: Unrelated to price
options.wrong_explanation: An MA is built directly from price.

options.label: A smoothed, lagging line whose slope reads the trend — descriptive, not predictive

screens.explanation: Smoothed, lagging, descriptive trend reading is the throughline.

lessons.title: What Is an Oscillator?
lessons.celebration: You understand oscillators!

screens.title: A Bounded, Derived Measure
screens.text: An oscillator is an indicator derived from price that moves within a bounded range. It summarizes something about price (like the speed of moves) rather than showing price itself.

screens.question: An oscillator is...
options: a price-derived measure that moves in a bounded range.
screens.explanation: Oscillators are derived measures bounded within a range (e.g., 0–100).

screens.question: An oscillator is [___] from price, not the price itself.
screens.explanation: Oscillators are calculated from price data.

screens.question: An oscillator shows the raw price directly.
screens.explanation: It shows a derived measure about price, not the price line itself.

screens.question: An oscillator moves within a [___] range.
screens.explanation: Oscillators are bounded (e.g., 0–100 for RSI).

lessons.title: What RSI Measures
lessons.celebration: You understand RSI!

screens.title: Speed and Size of Moves
screens.text: RSI (Relative Strength Index) is an oscillator from 0 to 100 that measures the speed and size of recent price moves. Higher RSI = stronger recent up-moves; lower = stronger down-moves.

screens.question: RSI measures the...
options: speed and size of recent price moves, on a 0–100 scale.
screens.explanation: RSI summarizes recent up vs down move strength from 0 to 100.

screens.question: RSI is bounded between 0 and [___].
screens.explanation: RSI runs from 0 to 100.

screens.question: A higher RSI reflects stronger recent up-moves.
screens.explanation: RSI rises when recent gains dominate recent losses.

screens.question: RSI is an example of a(n)...
screens.explanation: RSI is a bounded, price-derived oscillator.

lessons.title: Overbought & Oversold Zones
lessons.celebration: You can read RSI zones honestly!

screens.title: Labels, Not Signals
screens.text: RSI above ~70 is commonly labeled "overbought" and below ~30 "oversold." These are descriptive labels, not buy/sell signals — a strong trend can stay "overbought" for a long time.

screens.question: RSI above ~70 is commonly labeled...
screens.explanation: High RSI (~70+) is commonly labeled overbought — a description.

screens.question: "Overbought" is a guaranteed sell signal.
screens.explanation: It's a descriptive label; a strong uptrend can stay overbought for a long time.

screens.question: "Overbought" and "oversold" are descriptive [___], not signals to act.
screens.explanation: They describe RSI's zone; they aren't automatic trade signals.

screens.scenario: Someone shorts every time RSI hits "overbought," sure it must reverse.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Overbought always means an immediate reversal.
"Overbought" is a label, not a signal — strong trends can stay overbought a long time.
screens.explanation: Zones describe RSI; they don't guarantee a reversal.

lessons.title: What MACD Shows
lessons.celebration: You understand MACD!

screens.title: Two Moving Averages' Relationship
screens.text: MACD is built from the relationship between two moving averages (a fast and a slow one). It summarizes momentum — how the fast MA is pulling away from or converging with the slow one.

screens.question: MACD is derived from...
options: the relationship between two moving averages.
screens.explanation: MACD tracks how a fast and slow MA relate — a momentum read.

screens.question: MACD is built from moving averages, so it is also lagging.
screens.explanation: Because it's built from MAs (past prices), MACD lags too.

screens.question: MACD summarizes [___] from two moving averages.
screens.explanation: The gap/relationship between the MAs reads as momentum.

screens.question: Since MACD comes from moving averages, it is...
screens.explanation: MA-based indicators lag price.

lessons.title: Divergence
lessons.celebration: You understand divergence!

screens.title: When Price and Indicator Disagree
screens.text: Divergence is when price and an oscillator move in different directions — e.g., price makes a higher high but RSI makes a lower high. It's a descriptive "disagreement," not a guaranteed reversal.

screens.question: Divergence is when price and the indicator...
screens.explanation: Divergence is a disagreement between price and the oscillator.

screens.question: Divergence guarantees a reversal.
screens.explanation: It's a descriptive disagreement — a clue, never a guarantee.

screens.question: Divergence is price and an oscillator [___] on direction.
screens.explanation: The two disagreeing on direction is divergence.

screens.question: How should divergence be read?

options.label: As a descriptive disagreement worth noting — not a guarantee
As proof the data is broken
options.wrong_explanation: It's a normal, valid reading.

options.label: As a guaranteed reversal
options.wrong_explanation: Divergence can persist without a reversal.

screens.explanation: Divergence is a descriptive clue, not a guaranteed signal.

lessons.title: Oscillators Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered oscillators!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of oscillators, RSI, its zones, MACD, and divergence.

screens.question: Match each to its meaning.
pairs: A 0–100 oscillator of recent move strength
A momentum read from two moving averages
screens.explanation: A recap of the unit's core ideas.

screens.question: What do RSI and MACD have in common?
options: Both are indicators derived from price (and both lag it).
Both are the raw price line.
screens.explanation: Both are derived, lagging indicators — not guarantees.

screens.template: Oscillators are [__1__] from price and their extreme zones are [__2__], not signals.
screens.explanation: Derived measures with descriptive zones, not automatic signals.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Oscillators derive momentum reads from price; their zones and divergence are descriptive, not guarantees
Oscillators lead price
options.wrong_explanation: They're derived and lagging.

options.label: Oscillators are guaranteed signal generators
options.wrong_explanation: They describe, they don't guarantee.

screens.explanation: Descriptive, derived, lagging — never guaranteed — is the throughline.

lessons.title: What Is a Trade Plan?
lessons.celebration: You understand trade plans!

screens.title: Decide Before, Not During
screens.text: A trade plan decides the key things in advance: the idea (why), the invalidation (where you're wrong), the target (planned exit), and the size (risk). Planning ahead keeps decisions off the emotional moment.

screens.question: A trade plan is best decided...
options: in the heat of the moment.
screens.explanation: Planning ahead keeps decisions out of the emotional moment.

screens.question: Match each part of a plan to what it defines.
pairs: Where the idea is proven wrong
screens.explanation: Idea, invalidation, target (and size) are the core of a plan.

screens.question: A plan decides the key things [___] entering.
screens.explanation: The point of a plan is deciding in advance.

screens.question: A trade plan includes where the idea would be proven wrong.
screens.explanation: Invalidation — where you're wrong — is a core part of a plan.

lessons.title: Invalidation
lessons.celebration: You understand invalidation!

screens.title: Where the Idea Is Wrong
screens.text: Invalidation is the price/level where your trade idea is proven wrong. It's what a stop is commonly based on — not an arbitrary number.

screens.question: Invalidation is the point where...
options: the trade is guaranteed to win.
the trade idea is proven wrong.
screens.explanation: Invalidation marks where the reasoning no longer holds.

screens.question: A stop is commonly based on where the idea is invalidated, not a random number.
screens.explanation: Tying the stop to invalidation gives it a clear, reasoned basis.

screens.question: Invalidation is where the trade idea is [___].
screens.explanation: It's the level that disproves the idea.

screens.scenario: Someone enters a trade with no idea of where they'd be wrong.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Without an invalidation point, there's no clear place to stop or admit the idea failed.
A trade never needs a wrong-point.
screens.explanation: A defined invalidation is what makes risk manageable and the idea testable.

lessons.title: Process Over Prediction
lessons.celebration: You understand process over prediction!

screens.title: You Control the Process, Not the Outcome
screens.text: You can't control whether one trade wins — only whether you followed your process. Good process with a bad outcome is still good process; the edge shows over many trades.

screens.question: In trading, you directly control...
options: the outcome of any single trade.
screens.explanation: You control the process; outcomes vary trade to trade.

screens.question: A good process can still produce a losing trade.
screens.explanation: Any single outcome is uncertain; process is judged over many trades.

screens.question: You control the [___], not the outcome of one trade.
screens.explanation: Process is the controllable part; outcomes vary.

screens.question: Why focus on process over outcome?

options.label: Because the edge shows over many trades, not any single one
Because outcomes are fully controllable
options.wrong_explanation: You can't control a single result.

options.label: Because process never matters
options.wrong_explanation: Process is the controllable edge.

screens.explanation: Process is what you control; the edge appears over a large sample.

lessons.title: A Pre-Trade Checklist
lessons.celebration: You can build a pre-trade checklist!

screens.title: Same Questions Every Time
screens.text: A checklist asks the same questions before every trade: what's the condition, is there a level, is there a signal, and what's the risk? Consistency comes from repeating the process.

screens.question: A simple pre-trade checklist order:
items: Classify the market condition
Identify the key level
Look for a signal at that level
Define the risk (invalidation and size)
correct_order: Classify the market condition
Identify the key level
Look for a signal at that level
Define the risk (invalidation and size)
screens.explanation: Condition, level, signal, risk — a repeatable pre-trade sequence.

screens.question: The point of a checklist is to...
options: ask the same questions consistently every time.
screens.explanation: Consistency, not a guarantee, is the value of a checklist.

screens.question: A checklist brings [___] to the pre-trade process.
screens.explanation: Repeating the same checks each time builds consistency.

screens.question: A checklist guarantees profitable trades.
screens.explanation: It brings consistency to the process; it can't guarantee outcomes.

lessons.title: Sticking to the Plan
lessons.celebration: You understand plan discipline!

screens.title: Follow It, Even When Tempted
screens.text: A plan only helps if you follow it. Moving your stop, skipping your checklist, or abandoning the idea mid-trade undoes the plan's whole purpose.

screens.question: A trade plan only helps if you...
screens.explanation: The plan's value comes from following it consistently.

screens.question: Widening your stop mid-trade to avoid a loss undermines the plan.
screens.explanation: Moving the stop breaks the invalidation the plan was built on.

screens.question: A plan helps only if you [___] it.
screens.explanation: Following the plan is what gives it value.

screens.scenario: Someone hits their planned invalidation but moves the stop further away to avoid taking the loss.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Invalidation is optional once you're in.
Moving the stop is following the plan.
Moving the stop past invalidation abandons the plan and lets a small planned loss grow.
screens.explanation: Honoring invalidation is core discipline; moving it undoes the plan.

lessons.title: Trade Planning Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered trade planning & process!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of plans, invalidation, process, checklists, and discipline.

screens.question: Match each to its meaning.
pairs: Idea, invalidation, target, and size decided in advance
Controlling the process, not the outcome
screens.explanation: A recap of the unit's core ideas.

screens.question: What's the core of "process over prediction"?
options: You control the process; outcomes vary over many trades.
screens.explanation: Process is controllable; the edge shows over a large sample.

screens.template: A plan defines things in [__1__], and it only helps if you [__2__] it.
screens.explanation: Plan ahead, then follow it.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Predict each outcome and control it
options.wrong_explanation: You can't control single outcomes.

options.label: Plan the idea, invalidation, target, and size in advance — then follow the process
Wing it and hope
options.wrong_explanation: The unit is about a repeatable process.

screens.explanation: Plan-in-advance plus disciplined process is the throughline.

lessons.title: What Is VWAP?
lessons.celebration: You understand VWAP!

screens.title: The Volume-Weighted Average
screens.text: VWAP is the Volume-Weighted Average Price — the average price over a session, weighted by how much volume traded at each price. It's commonly used intraday as a reference "fair value" line.

screens.question: VWAP stands for...
screens.explanation: VWAP is the volume-weighted average price over a session.

screens.question: VWAP weights each price by its [___].
screens.explanation: More volume at a price gives it more weight in the average.

screens.question: VWAP is commonly used as an intraday reference for average price.
screens.explanation: VWAP is a common intraday "fair value" reference line.

screens.question: How does VWAP differ from a simple moving average?
options: It only uses the highest price.
It weights prices by volume, not just by time.
screens.explanation: VWAP weights by volume; a simple MA weights each period equally.

lessons.title: Reading Price vs. VWAP
lessons.celebration: You can read price against VWAP!

screens.title: Above or Below Fair Value
screens.text: Price trading above VWAP is commonly described as trading above the session's average (relative strength); below as relative weakness. It's descriptive context, not a signal.

screens.question: Price above VWAP is commonly described as...
options: trading above the session average (relative strength).
screens.explanation: Above the volume-weighted average is commonly read as relative strength.

screens.question: Price below VWAP is commonly described as relative weakness.
screens.explanation: Below the session's average price reads as relative weakness.

screens.question: Price vs VWAP is a [___] read, not a signal to act.
screens.explanation: It describes strength/weakness; it isn't an automatic trade.

screens.scenario: Someone treats "price above VWAP" as an automatic guaranteed buy.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Above VWAP is a descriptive strength read, not a guaranteed signal to buy.
screens.explanation: VWAP context is descriptive, never a guaranteed signal.

lessons.title: What Are Bollinger Bands?
lessons.celebration: You understand Bollinger Bands!

screens.title: A Band Around a Moving Average
screens.text: Bollinger Bands draw a moving average with an upper and lower band set a number of standard deviations away. The bands measure how far price is straying from its average.

screens.question: Bollinger Bands are built around a...
options: moving average, with bands set by standard deviation.
screens.explanation: The middle is an MA; the bands are standard deviations from it.

screens.question: The Bollinger band width is based on [___] deviation.
screens.explanation: The bands are placed a number of standard deviations from the MA.

screens.question: The middle Bollinger line is a moving average.
screens.explanation: Bollinger Bands center on a moving average, with bands around it.

screens.question: The bands measure how far price is straying from its...
screens.explanation: The bands quantify deviation from the moving-average center.

lessons.title: Bands Widen and Narrow
lessons.celebration: You can read band width!

screens.title: Width Reflects Volatility
screens.text: When volatility rises, the bands widen; when it's calm, they narrow. Band width is a quick read of how volatile price is right now.

screens.question: Wide Bollinger Bands reflect...
screens.explanation: Bigger deviations (volatility) push the bands wider.

screens.question: Narrow ("squeezing") Bollinger Bands reflect...
screens.explanation: Small deviations (calm) pull the bands narrow.

screens.question: Band width is a quick read of current volatility.
screens.explanation: Width tracks how far price is deviating — i.e., volatility.

screens.template: Bands [__1__] when volatile and [__2__] when calm.
screens.explanation: Volatility widens the bands; calm narrows them.

lessons.title: Price at the Bands
lessons.celebration: You can read price at the bands honestly!

screens.title: Touching a Band Isn't a Signal
screens.text: Price touching the upper or lower band shows it's stretched far from its average — but in a strong trend, price can "ride" a band for a long time. It's descriptive, not a reversal signal.

screens.question: Price touching the upper band means price is...
screens.explanation: An upper-band touch means price is far above the moving-average center.

screens.question: A band touch is a guaranteed reversal signal.
screens.explanation: In a strong trend, price can ride a band for a long time — no guarantee.

screens.question: A band touch shows price is [___] from its average, not a guaranteed reversal.
screens.explanation: It describes stretch/deviation, not an automatic turn.

screens.scenario: Someone sells every time price touches the upper band, sure it must revert.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Price can ride the upper band in a strong trend — a touch isn't a guaranteed reversal.
screens.explanation: Band touches are descriptive stretch reads, not guaranteed reversals.

lessons.title: VWAP & Bollinger Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered VWAP & Bollinger Bands!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of VWAP and Bollinger Bands.

screens.question: Match each tool to what it shows.
screens.explanation: A recap of the unit's tools.

screens.question: What do VWAP and Bollinger Bands have in common?
options: Both are averages of price (with extra context), read descriptively.
Both are the raw price line.
screens.explanation: Both are average-based, descriptive tools — not guarantees.

screens.template: VWAP weights price by [__1__]; Bollinger band width reflects [__2__].
screens.explanation: VWAP = volume-weighted average; band width = volatility.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Tools that guarantee reversals at the bands
options.wrong_explanation: Price can ride the bands.

options.label: Average-based reference tools read descriptively — never guaranteed signals
The raw price line themselves
options.wrong_explanation: They're derived averages, not raw price.

screens.explanation: Descriptive, average-based context — not signals — is the throughline.

lessons.title: What Is a Drawdown?
lessons.celebration: You understand drawdowns!

screens.title: The Drop From a Peak
screens.text: A drawdown is the percentage decline from an account's peak value to a later low. Every account has drawdowns — they're a normal part of the equity curve.

screens.question: A drawdown measures the decline from an account's...
options: peak value to a later low.
screens.explanation: A drawdown is the drop from a prior peak to a subsequent low.

screens.question: A drawdown is measured as a [___] decline from the peak.
screens.explanation: Drawdowns are commonly expressed as a percent from peak.

screens.question: Every account experiences drawdowns at some point.
screens.explanation: Drawdowns are a normal part of any equity curve.

screens.question: A 20% drawdown means the account is down 20% from its...
screens.explanation: Drawdown is measured from the prior peak value.

lessons.title: Recovery Math
lessons.celebration: You understand recovery math!

screens.title: Losses Need Bigger Gains Back
screens.text: A key fact: a loss needs a larger percentage gain to recover. A 50% loss needs a 100% gain to break even. This is why limiting drawdowns matters.

screens.question: A 50% loss requires what gain to break even?
screens.explanation: Halving your account means you must double what's left — a 100% gain.

screens.question: A 20% loss requires roughly what gain to break even?
screens.explanation: From 80% of the start, you need +25% (0.80 × 1.25 = 1.00).

screens.question: A loss needs a larger percentage gain than the loss itself to recover.
screens.explanation: You're gaining on a smaller base, so the required percent is larger.

screens.question: The bigger the drawdown, the [___] the gain needed to recover.
screens.explanation: Deeper losses require disproportionately larger recovery gains.

screens.scenario: Someone assumes a 50% loss just needs a 50% gain to get back.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: A 50% loss needs a 100% gain to recover, since you're rebuilding from a smaller base.
screens.explanation: Recovering a loss requires a larger percent gain than the loss itself.

lessons.title: Losing Streaks Are Normal
lessons.celebration: You understand losing streaks!

screens.title: Even a Good System Loses in a Row
screens.text: A string of losses in a row happens even with a positive-expectancy system — purely by chance. A losing streak alone doesn't prove the system is broken.

screens.question: A losing streak with a sound system is...
options: normal — it can happen by chance.
screens.explanation: Even a good system sees losing streaks by chance.

screens.question: A few losses in a row proves a system has negative expectancy.
screens.explanation: Short streaks happen by chance; they don't prove the long-run expectancy.

screens.question: A losing streak alone doesn't prove a system is [___].
screens.explanation: Streaks are normal variance, not proof of a broken system.

screens.question: Why don't losing streaks prove a system is broken?

options.label: Because systems never lose
options.wrong_explanation: All systems have losing trades.

options.label: Because expectancy doesn't exist
options.wrong_explanation: Expectancy is the long-run measure.

options.label: Because streaks happen by chance even with positive expectancy

screens.explanation: Losing streaks are normal variance, not proof about the long-run edge.

lessons.title: Streaks and Sample Size
lessons.celebration: You understand streaks and chance!

screens.title: Short Runs Are Noisy
screens.text: Over a large sample, expectancy shows through. But short runs are noisy — even a fair coin flips several heads (or tails) in a row sometimes.

screens.question: Short runs of results are...
screens.explanation: Small samples are dominated by luck, not the true average.

screens.question: Even a positive-expectancy system can have a rough short stretch.
screens.explanation: Variance means good systems still have losing stretches short-term.

screens.question: Expectancy shows through only over a [___] sample.
screens.explanation: Averages need many trades to be reliable.

screens.question: Short runs are dominated by [___], not the true average.
screens.explanation: Small samples reflect luck more than the underlying edge.

lessons.title: Capital Preservation Mindset
lessons.celebration: You understand capital preservation!

screens.title: Protect the Base
screens.text: Because losses need bigger gains back and streaks happen, keeping drawdowns small protects the account. A preserved account can keep participating; a blown-up one can't.

screens.question: Keeping drawdowns small matters because...
options: recovery gets much harder as losses deepen.
screens.explanation: Deep drawdowns need disproportionate gains to recover, so limiting them helps.

screens.question: A preserved account can keep participating; a blown-up one cannot.
screens.explanation: Without capital, there's nothing left to trade with.

screens.question: Capital preservation keeps [___] small to protect the account.
screens.explanation: Limiting drawdowns is the core of capital preservation.

screens.question: Why is capital preservation foundational?

options.label: Because losses don't matter
options.wrong_explanation: Losses are exactly what it manages.

options.label: Because it guarantees returns
options.wrong_explanation: It protects, it doesn't guarantee gains.

options.label: Because staying in the game long-term requires not blowing up

screens.explanation: Preserving capital keeps you able to participate over the long run.

lessons.title: Drawdowns Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered drawdowns & streaks!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of drawdowns, recovery math, streaks, and preservation.

screens.question: A 50% loss requires what gain to recover?
screens.explanation: Doubling the remaining half is a 100% gain.

screens.question: Match each idea to its meaning.
pairs: Losses need larger percent gains back
Normal variance, not proof a system is broken
screens.explanation: A recap of the unit's core ideas.

screens.template: Deeper drawdowns need [__1__] gains to recover, so keeping them [__2__] matters.
screens.explanation: Recovery math is why limiting drawdowns is important.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: A 50% loss just needs 50% back
options.wrong_explanation: It needs 100%.

options.label: Drawdowns and streaks are normal; recovery math makes limiting them essential
Losing streaks prove a broken system
options.wrong_explanation: They're normal variance.

screens.explanation: Normal variance plus recovery math driving preservation is the throughline.

lessons.title: Why Journal?
lessons.celebration: You understand journaling!

screens.title: You Can't Improve What You Don't Track
screens.text: A trading journal records what you did and why, so you can review and improve. Memory is unreliable; a written record is honest.

screens.question: The main purpose of a trading journal is to...
options: record trades so you can review and improve.
screens.explanation: Journaling creates a record to learn from — not a profit guarantee.

screens.question: Memory alone is a reliable record of your trading decisions.
screens.explanation: Memory is biased and incomplete; a written journal is more honest.

screens.question: A journal lets you [___] and improve over time.
screens.explanation: Reviewing a written record is how you improve.

screens.question: Why is a written record better than memory?

options.label: Because journaling guarantees profit
options.wrong_explanation: It aids learning, not a guarantee.

options.label: Because memory is perfect
options.wrong_explanation: Memory is unreliable.

options.label: Memory is biased; a written record is honest and complete

screens.explanation: An honest written record beats biased memory for improvement.

lessons.title: What to Log
lessons.celebration: You know what to log!

screens.title: Setup, Plan, Execution, Outcome
screens.text: A useful journal entry logs the setup (why), the plan (entry, invalidation, target, size), the execution (did you follow it?), and the outcome (in R).

screens.question: Match each journal field to what it captures.
screens.explanation: Setup, plan, execution, and outcome make a complete entry.

screens.question: Recording the outcome in R (not just dollars) lets you...
options: compare trades of different sizes fairly.
screens.explanation: R normalizes results across position sizes for fair comparison.

screens.question: A good entry logs whether you actually [___] your plan.
screens.explanation: Logging execution (did you follow the plan?) is key to reviewing process.

screens.question: Logging the outcome in R helps compare trades of different sizes.
screens.explanation: R makes results comparable regardless of position size.

lessons.title: Review Process, Not Just Outcome
lessons.celebration: You can review the right thing!

screens.title: Was the Process Good?
screens.text: The best review asks "did I follow my process?" — separate from whether the trade won. A good process with a losing outcome is still good process.

screens.question: The most useful review question is...
screens.explanation: Process is what you control; reviewing it drives improvement.

screens.question: A losing trade can still be a well-executed, good-process trade.
screens.explanation: Outcomes vary; a plan followed correctly is good process regardless.

screens.question: Review your [___], separate from any single outcome.
screens.explanation: Reviewing process (not just the result) is what improves you.

screens.scenario: Someone only reviews winners and ignores whether they followed their process.
screens.question: What is the mistake?
options: Reviewing outcomes alone misses whether the process was sound — the controllable part.
screens.explanation: The point of review is the process, which you control, not just outcomes.

lessons.title: Finding Patterns in Your Trades
lessons.celebration: You can learn from your journal!

screens.title: Let the Data Talk
screens.text: Over many entries, patterns emerge: maybe your best trades share a condition, or your worst come from breaking the checklist. The journal turns experience into lessons.

screens.question: Over many journal entries, you can look for...
options: patterns in what your best and worst trades share.
screens.explanation: Patterns across many entries reveal what helps or hurts your results.

screens.question: Reviewing many entries can reveal recurring mistakes to fix.
screens.explanation: Patterns across a large sample surface habits worth changing.

screens.question: Patterns emerge only across [___] entries, not one.
screens.explanation: A large sample is needed for reliable patterns.

screens.question: Why review across many entries, not one?

options.label: Because reliable patterns need a large sample
Because journaling guarantees improvement
options.wrong_explanation: It enables it, not guarantees.

options.label: Because one trade proves everything
options.wrong_explanation: One trade is noise.

screens.explanation: Reliable lessons come from patterns across many trades.

lessons.title: The Learning Loop
lessons.celebration: You understand the learning loop!

screens.title: Plan, Do, Review, Repeat
screens.text: Improvement is a loop: plan the trade, do it by the plan, review it honestly, and repeat with what you learned. The journal powers the review step.

screens.question: The learning loop, in order:
items: Plan the trade
Execute it by the plan
Review it honestly in the journal
Apply the lesson to the next plan
correct_order: Plan the trade
Execute it by the plan
Review it honestly in the journal
Apply the lesson to the next plan
screens.explanation: Plan, do, review, repeat is the improvement loop.

screens.question: The journal powers which step of the loop?
screens.explanation: The journal is what makes an honest review possible.

screens.question: Improvement comes from repeating the plan-do-review loop over time.
screens.explanation: Consistent looping, not one trade, drives improvement.

screens.question: The learning loop is plan, do, [___], repeat.
screens.explanation: Review (via the journal) is the third step of the loop.

lessons.title: Journaling Review
lessons.celebration: You've mastered journaling & review!

screens.title: Bringing It Together
screens.text: A final review of why to journal, what to log, reviewing process, patterns, and the loop.

screens.question: Match each to its role.
pairs: An honest record to learn from
screens.explanation: A recap of the unit's core ideas.

screens.question: What should a review focus on most?
screens.explanation: Process is the controllable part that drives improvement.

screens.template: Log setup, plan, execution, and outcome in [__1__]; review your [__2__].
screens.explanation: Log outcomes in R; review the process.

screens.question: Which best summarizes this unit?

options.label: Journal honestly, review your process over many trades, and loop the lessons
Journal to guarantee profits
options.wrong_explanation: It enables improvement, not guarantees.

options.label: Only review winning trades
options.wrong_explanation: Process review covers all trades.

screens.explanation: Honest journaling, process review, and the learning loop is the throughline.

nodes.title: Full Course Review

lessons.title: What Is FOMO?
lessons.celebration: You understand FOMO!

screens.title: The Fear of Missing Out
screens.text: FOMO describes the urge to jump into a trade because price is already moving fast, often without a clear plan.

screens.title: A Move That Doesn't Hold
screens.text: A fakeout is commonly described as a price move beyond a level that quickly reverses, rather than continuing.
